en: 1. The Definition of Points of Defeat (Nigrahasthāna).
Homage to the Destroyer of Obstacles, whose rays from the mass of various jewels of excellent qualities forever dispel the darkness.

Having bowed to the noble Mañjuśrī, who is supremely intent on bringing about the welfare of the entire world by striving most diligently for the sake of obtaining the fruits desired by beings of various kinds,
this pure and concise *Vādanyāyavibhāga* is commenced. 1.

That which is devoid of a purpose is not undertaken by those who act with foresight, such as the mere determination of the presence of a mole; and since this treatise might be suspected of being purposeless, the proponent of logic (nyāyavādin) has set forth the statement beginning with "nyāyavādinaḥ" in order to dispel that suspicion and demonstrate its purpose.
How, then, is the purpose of this [work] shown by this statement? Let this matter rest for now; rather, the meaning is explained:
"Nyāya" is the reasoning characterized by the three-fold mark (*liṅga*).

It is so called because by means of it (*anena*) the accomplishment of the intended object (*vivakṣitārthasiddhi*) is led to or attained. For this very reason, he will immediately state that the logical mark (*liṅga*) has three forms, beginning with "the logical mark is of three kinds.
Others say it refers to the statement (*vacana*) that expresses that [three-formed mark].
One whose nature (*śīla*) is to speak that [mark] is thus described.
They "repress" him as well, meaning they defeat him.

Granted, they might repress an opponent who speaks unreasonably, precisely because he is subject to defeat; however, that they should repress one who speaks reasonably—even though such a person is undeserving of defeat—is not possible.
However, those whose minds are intent on attributing superiority to others defeat even him; thus, the word "even" (*api*) is used either to indicate inclusion or to highlight excellence.
To the question of *in what* they suppress them, he says: *in debates* (vādeṣu)—that is to say, in investigations designated as "proofs" and "refutations."
In some versions, the reading is "vivādeṣu" (in disputes).
In that case, it should be explained as: "vivādāḥ" means contradictory arguments; [the Lord acts] in those. And how are they contradictory?

Since investigations designated as "proofs" (sādhana) and "refutations" (dūṣaṇa) function by establishing meanings contrary to those [of the opponent], how is it that they defeat the proponent of logic (nyāyavādin) through fallacies of the reason (hetudoṣa), such as the unestablished (asiddha)? To this he says:
"by the presentation of non-existent categories."

The "establishments of the non-existent" (asatāṃ vyavasthāḥ) refer to the fallacious positions of the wicked, or "unreal establishments" because they are censured by the virtuous; these are characterized by [fallacious] reasons, [fallacious] examples, and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), and their formal presentations constitute the subject matter.
The analysis of the compound is "those who apply themselves by means of them.
Who, then, are these shameless ones? He says: they are the deceitful, the rogues, the fraudulent—meaning those who are envious of the prosperity of others.

Since they suppress him in such a manner, this treatise is commenced for the purpose of refuting that—namely, the suppression of those deceitful persons, or the presentation of those false doctrines, or that suppression itself, or all three; or rather, the analysis should be understood as "this [treatise] has that very thing as its subject. And when that [suppression] is refuted, correct inquiry proceeds, and all human goals (puruṣārtha) are preceded by that [inquiry]; such is the intended meaning.
However, this context, revolving within [the mind] of one whose object is near, touches upon the subsequent [verse],
because it is fully established as having the nature of an internal thread;
otherwise, if it were not established as having such a nature, there would be no proximity, and thus the employment of the word "this" (*idam*) would be impossible.
If it is asked how there is a reference to the present tense in the expression "it is begun" (ārabhyate),
[the answer is: Pāṇini [states] that "in proximity to the present, the present may optionally be used" (vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavadvā, Pāṇini 3.3.131).

If it is argued that, because of the statement [in the *Nyāyabhāṣya*], "3.31," the relationship (*sambandha*) must also be explicitly stated— otherwise, this [treatise] would be as ungraspable as the prattle of a child or a madman for those who act with foresight— it is true; however,
because it is already included within the purpose (*prayojana*), it is not mentioned separately.
For it is in order to refute that [view] that this [treatise] is commenced. Consequently, this purpose is established by means of this treatise;
thus, it is indicated that the relationship between the purpose and the treatise is characterized as that of the goal and the means (*sādhyasādhanalakṣaṇa*).

As for other types of relationships—such as those characterized by the immediate succession of actions—they need not even be mentioned, because they do not constitute constituent parts of the activity of the treatise.
For even when those [other factors] are present, the treatise is not commenced in the absence of a purpose;
and even when they are absent, it is indeed commenced when a purpose exists.
Therefore, since the commencement of the treatise follows the positive and negative concomitance of the purpose, it is the purpose alone that must be stated by one who acts with foresight.
And when that [purpose] has been stated, it is considered that the relationship is also already expressed;

for wise persons do not proceed without having ascertained the body of the treatise. Therefore, since it is a necessary factor for activity toward a purposeful work, the body of the treatise must indeed be stated.
If this is argued, we reply: this is true, but because it is already implied by the statement of the purpose, it does not deserve a separate mention, just like the relationship.

Since it was stated that this [treatise] is commenced for the purpose of negating that [view], it follows that its "body" (śarīra) is that very negation. And when this is commenced for the purpose of negating that, then the previous reason (*hetu*) becomes unestablished (*asiddha*).
Furthermore, by this, two counter-means of knowledge (*pratipramāṇa*) are indicated; therefore, this treatise ought to be commenced by a discerning person, provided they possess the capacity.

Alternatively, [the treatise] is worthy of being grasped because it possesses a purpose and because it possesses a connection, just like other such treatises; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Having thus stated the purpose, he recites a verse that summarizes the meaning of the entire treatise, beginning with "The statement of what is not a member of the proof" (1b1).

The statement of what is not a constituent of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) and the failure to point out a fault (*adoṣodbhāvana*) are, respectively, the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)—the grounds for loss—for the two parties, the proponent and the opponent. Since the other points of defeat imagined by Akṣapāda, such as the "renunciation of the thesis" (*pratijñāsaṃnyāsa*) and so forth which will be discussed later, are distinct from these [two], they are not accepted as points of defeat; this is understood from the context.
This, first of all, is the meaning of the verse in brief.
With the words "of the desired" (*iṣṭasya*) and so forth, he begins the detailed analysis:
"the desired object," such as "sound is impermanent," is that which is intended as the probandum (*sādhya*).
Its accomplishment (*siddhi*) is its realization (*pratipatti*), which is the means (*sādhana*).
By this, he shows that in this explanation the word "means" (*sādhana*) is intended as the "act of accomplishing" (*bhāva-sādhana*), and not as the "instrumental means" (*karaṇa-sādhana*). He asks:
what is that limb of this means characterized by the accomplishment of the desired object? He replies: [it is] this.
He explains the word *aṅga* as that which brings about or produces; the meaning is that here the word *aṅga* is a synonym for "cause" (*kāraṇa*), not a synonym for "part" (*avayava*).
And that member of the proof (sādhanāṅga) here is called the "reason" (liṅga) whose three characteristics are ascertained.
The statement of this member of the proof is the communication of the three-characterized reason.
The non-statement of that member of the proof—its non-utterance or its non-expression—is what constitutes the "statement of a non-member of the proof" (asādhanāṅgavacana).

By this he explains that one should not understand, according to this interpretation, that "the statement of what is not a member of the proof" (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) refers to the statement of the application (*upanaya*) and so forth— which are themselves members of the proof— but rather that it refers precisely to the non-statement of a member of the proof. That non-statement of a member of the proof constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent.
By this, he explains the first half of the verse.
He asks: "How, then, can the non-utterance of a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) constitute a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)? To this he replies:

"Having accepted that" (1b2). That is to say, having accepted the intended probandum (*sādhya*) with the declaration, "I shall prove this," and then remaining silent due to a lack of confidence (*apratibhā*), which serves as the cause [for the failure].
In this context, "inability" (*apratibhā*) is understood as the forgetting of a previously grasped point and a state of paralysis;

by this, he states that there is a failure to utter any member of the proof in every respect. Alternatively, even if it is uttered, if it is not established, then although spoken, it is as if unspoken because it does not perform its own function. With this intention, he says: "or because of the failure to establish a member of the proof. (1b2)
The word "or" (*vā*) functions as a particle of option (*vikalpārtha*) with reference to the preceding [point],
meaning that the non-justification of a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) consists in the failure to demonstrate certainty regarding all three aspects (*rūpa*).

Therefore, due to silence and the failure to justify the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*), there is a non-utterance of them; and because of that, since the purpose of the thesis (*pratijñātārtha*) is not established, this constitutes a ground for the defeat (*nigrahādhikaraṇa*) of the proponent (*vādin*). This is the connection with the subject at hand.
In some places, however, the reading is "of the proponent" (*vādinaḥ*).
In this context, the word "that" (tat) refers back to the aforementioned non-articulation (*anuccāraṇa*).

But how does it become a failure to support a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*), such that by its opposite—namely, by failing to support [the reason] due to the lack of a cause for the meaning of the thesis—the proponent incurs a ground for defeat (*nigrahādhikaraṇa*)? Anticipating that someone might ask this, the author sets forth the initial framework beginning with "only threefold" (*trividham eva*) in order to avoid that objection. He explains that the sign (*liṅga*), which is the instrument (*aṅga*) of cognition, is indeed of only three types; of what [is it the instrument]? Of the cognition consisting of the realization of the unestablished (*asiddhi*).
To the question "Of what is there accomplishment?", he says:
"of that which is not perceived," meaning of that object which is beyond direct perception and exists as something to be inferred;
furthermore, the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) expresses the exclusion of the four [senses] and so forth.
If it is asked how this restriction— that [the object of inference] is only threefold— is established,

it is because the probandum (*sādhya*) is determined to be twofold by way of affirmation and negation; and that which is of the nature of affirmation may be either of the nature of existence or of the nature of a cause.
There is no other [cause] there,
because a causal connection is impossible;
for it is not logical that the existence of another thing which is not its effect should entail the existence of the [first] thing.
Just as there is no existence of a cloth when a camel is absent,
it is not logical that the cessation of one thing which is neither its cause nor its effect should entail the cessation of another;
for instance, just as there is no cessation of a cloth upon the cessation of a camel.

Furthermore, it is not logical for that which lacks positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to function as a means of valid cognition (*āgamaka*), because that would lead to the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even a cloth could indicate a camel.

However, when there is the presence of a property that constitutes its very nature (*svabhāva-bhūta-dharma*), the presence of another thing that also constitutes its nature is logical; for a thing's own nature does not exist apart from itself.
Because it would follow that there is an absence of the nature of that [cause], and because when that [cause] ceases, the effect also ceases; thus,
it is logical that when the cause exists, the effect also exists.
And when that [cause] ceases, [the effect] ceases; otherwise, because it would exist even without it, that thing would not be its effect, just like anything else.

Therefore, due to the distinction between the nature [of the effect] and the cause which serves as the probans (*sādhana*), the positive formulation of the probandum (*sādhya*) is of only two kinds, because the logical connection (*pratibandha*) of the reason (*hetu*) exists only therein.

One must accept that a reason of essential nature (svabhāvahetu) establishes an object of proof that is its own essential nature, and a reason of effect (kāryahetu) establishes one that is its cause; likewise,
even a negation is established only by the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility.
It will be explained in detail how there is nothing else;

here, however, the summarized meaning of the reality is this: the determination of the indicator (liṅga), which is the subject, depends upon its object, and that object may be either an affirmation or a negation.

In a positive injunction (*vidhi*), either another thing is enjoined or that very thing itself; and even in the case of enjoining another thing, is it the effect, the cause, or neither that is established?

Furthermore, in the presentation of the effect, is it the generality of the cause—such as "mere entity" (*vastumātra*) as excluded from non-clouds and the like—that is stated as the logical mark (*liṅga*), or is it a specific cause whose capacity is unimpeded, such as a cloud?
Furthermore, a negation must be established either by the non-perception or by the perception of that which is intended to be negated.
Even in the case of non-perception, there are the following alternatives: it may consist merely in the cessation of perception;
or it may be of a status equivalent to that [perception], being of the nature of the perception of some other object alone.

In this regard, even a mere cause such as a cloud—which is necessarily accompanied by deep thundering and so forth—does not invariably bring about its effect, such as rain, because there is the possibility of an intervening obstacle;
thus, a mere cause is not a reliable indicator (*gamaka*).

Furthermore, even from a specific cause whose power is unimpeded, the effect itself arises first—intervened only by the recollection of the relationship—before the inferential cognition occurs, and it becomes perceptible to sensory cognition (*akṣajñāna*); therefore, that [effect] also cannot function as a logical mark (*liṅga*).
An effect, moreover, is logically a sign of its cause because of its invariable concomitance with it;
otherwise, by overstepping that [concomitance], it would violate its own possession of a cause.
Neither [the presence] nor the absence [of the probans] can be understood as following from a lack of connection, for that would lead to over-extension;
nor is it logical that even a non-distinct entity is understood through non-deviation.
Furthermore, a negation [of the probans] is not tenable by means of perception, because of contradiction.
For how indeed can it be logically consistent that something is both perceived and non-existent?

Even the mere cessation of the cognition of that object is fallible; however, the conventional usage of "non-existence" is appropriate for that which is perceived in its isolation from a single cognition, because if it were actually present, it would necessarily be perceived as existing.

Furthermore, whatever is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot logically have as its object that which is impossible, just as, for example, a horse's horn. Since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth postulated by others— such as the "conjunction with another" (*anya-saṃyoga*) and other such imagined marks— are objects that are impossible in the manner described, this constitutes a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).
By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the cognition of blue and so forth,

or that very same effect and other such marks (*kāryādiliṅga*), constitute the subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) consisting in the impossibility of the referent of a term having a causal basis (*naimittikaśabdārthānupapatti*).
What, then, is established by this regarding the non-probative nature of other [reasons]?
For instance, "being an object," "being a probans," "being an illuminator," and so forth, are synonyms.
Therefore, since the probandum (sādhya) is of three kinds, it is established that the probans (hetu) which proves it is likewise of exactly three kinds.
To the question "In what way is it threefold?", he says:
"The intrinsic nature" (svabhāva), etc.; the word "and" (ca) has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with respect to the intrinsic nature and the effect (*kārya*).

Furthermore, this demonstration of the intended reasons is threefold—due to the distinctions of essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*)—and serves as a factor for establishing that which is not perceived;
it is not [threefold] due to the distinctions of cause (*kāraṇa*), inherence in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*), contradictory (*virodhi*), and so forth. This is shown for the sake of clarity.
Now, one might object: "Should it not rather be stated as 'non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility' (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptānupalambha*)?"

If it is asked: "Since its establishment as non-perceptual is due to its being a constituent (*aṅga*) according to the logic to be stated later, and not merely because of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) alone, how then can it be said generally?"—it is indeed so; however, because this discussion concerns the constituent of the proof that has been established, even this general term "non-apprehension" refers specifically to the non-apprehension of that which meets the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
For even general terms, through the proximity of other words and the force of the context, come to reside in specific meanings.
As it has been said:

"It is not merely the proximity of a specific term that is the cause for the specific determination of words; rather, factors such as the power of the context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth are also [causes]. Furthermore, he will demonstrate later on that it is impossible for mere non-perception (*anupalambha*) alone to constitute a valid member of a proof (*sādhanāṅga*).
Alternatively, since this discussion concerns the logical mark (*liṅga*) which is the cause for establishing what is not perceived, this objection is simply not to be raised.
What, then, is the support for these three types of members of proof, such that its absence would constitute a lack of support?
To this he says: "Of that," and so forth.

In this context, the word "probandum" (*sādhya*) denotes the property alone, such as impermanence and so forth, by means of a metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) from the whole to its parts; it does not denote the collection of both the property and the locus of the probandum, because that would entail the non-existence of pervasion itself,
since impermanence and other properties as qualified by a specific locus such as sound do not exist in the locus of the example.
Having established pervasion by means of the valid cognition that proves positive and negative concomitance, the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance has been stated;

the proof of existence (*bhāvasādhana*)— meaning the statement of presence— by means of the valid cognition that establishes the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) refers to the subject (*dharmin*), such as sound and so forth, whose specific nature is desired to be known.
By this also, the ascertainment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) has been stated.

But how is it that, having established pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), the existence [of the reason] in the subject (*dharmin*) is then stated? To this, he provides an example, beginning with "yathā" (as follows).
By this summary of "all that," he explains the demonstration of pervasion (vyāpti);
for what purpose?
For the purpose of dispelling misconceptions.

For instance, some who hold opposing views maintain that internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) and external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) are demonstrated with respect to the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) respectively;

however, that is not tenable because pervasion arises from the force of reality (*vastubala*). He asks: "Is there such a rule of sequence here—that one must first establish pervasion with the probandum (*sādhya*) and only afterwards state its presence in the locus (*dharmin*)—or is there not?"

Regarding the passage beginning with "atrāpi" (here too) and so forth: here, in my own view, regarding the establishment of the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*), the word "api" (also/even) is to be connected with the negation in the sense of restriction—
that is to say, there is no such fixed rule of sequence, meaning no fixed order of arrangement, at all.
He asks, "What is the reason? and replies:
"Because there is no difference in the establishment of the desired object in either case.

This means that whether one first states the proof of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and subsequently states the proof of the existence of the locus (*dharmin*), or first states the proof of the existence of the locus and subsequently states the proof of pervasion, there is no difference in the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*).
If this is so, for what purpose is the rule of sequence observed?
It is for the sake of establishing the probandum;
just as in the application of a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of the reason with the probandum is demonstrated.
In the case of the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-vat*), it is stated that the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is necessarily the absence of the reason (*hetu*),
but not that the absence of the reason implies the absence of the probandum.
For what purpose [is this said]?

It is so that there may be no failure to establish the desired object, nor the establishment of its opposite, which would result from failing to demonstrate the reason’s inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*) with the probandum (*sādhya*).
As it has been said:
For in this way, it is possible to demonstrate that the reason exists only in the similar class (sapakṣa) and is entirely absent in the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva),
but not by the reverse.

Just as in the case where "eternality" might be considered "produced" because it is uncreated or because it is subject to destruction— where the pervasion is established even if not explicitly stated— it is there appropriate to rely upon a sequence; but here, since the intended object is accomplished even without this, the Sūtra indicates that there is no fixed rule regarding sequence.
If it is asked why this is so—namely, that there is no difference between the two cases regarding the accomplishment of the desired object—he says:
"Because [the pervasion] of the subject," and so forth;
for it was stated previously that one must establish the pervasion by the probandum.
What, then, is the proof for that pervasion? He says "here," etc.
"Here" refers to the reason consisting of the presence of the subject itself (*svabhāvahetu*).
However, the proof of pervasion for both the effect-reason (*kārya*) and the non-perception (*anupalambha*) would be stated subsequently;

the remainder of the sense is that it concerns the subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) which exists when the reason is present in the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya-viparyaya*). The meaning is that the statement of that [means] by which the reason, being present in the opposite of the probandum, is subverted is what constitutes the proof of pervasion.

What, then, is this demonstration of the subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*)? He says: "If not every entity were existent and produced" (1b5)—this refers back to the two previously stated reasons. [The connection is as follows: "In that case, it would be non-existent," because for a non-momentary entity, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is impossible through either succession or simultaneity (1b5).
Thus it is said: for an entity intended to be momentary, gradual causal efficiency is not tenable, because its nature—which is capable of accomplishing an effect—must exist at all times;
otherwise, it would not produce it even later.
If it is argued that [the cause], without falling away from its prior nature, produces [the effect] upon encountering auxiliary factors just as before,
this is not so; for it is illogical for that which cannot have any excellence added to it and does not relinquish its prior nature to depend upon auxiliary factors.
If it is argued that the auxiliary causes indeed produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) within its own nature, we say no;
for it is impossible for that excellence produced by the auxiliaries to be either identical to or different from [the cause itself]. To explain:
first of all, this excellence cannot be of the same nature as the cause.

Since that [auxiliary] is not distinct from it, there is the consequence that it would arise through the power of the auxiliary, like a specific excellence (*ātmātiśaya*) [inherent in the entity]; and if this were so, its accepted non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*) would be lost. If you say, "Let it be distinct from it," then since the effect would arise from that very excellence of the self, its incapacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*) remains as it was; thus, an unavoidable consequence descends upon you.
One might ask: "How does this [cause] have a relation [to its effect]? Such a doubt indeed enters the field of inquiry.
Even regarding the claim that it "acts by force of its excellence" (*atiśaya*), the same fault raised against the position that requires auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) applies.

If it is argued that, although its nature is already capable and thus no excellence can be added to it, it nevertheless produces the effect by depending on something else—just as a weaver (*kuvinda*) and so forth do—then [the following response follows].
That is not the essence [of the effect],
for the auxiliary conditions are not capable of imparting any excellence (*atiśaya*) to it;
nor is dependence upon a factor that provides no assistance logical, as it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

And thus, it would follow that this [cause] would produce its effect at all times; for even weavers and others would possess that same nature because they produce it, or else a non-producer would possess that nature.
This and more has been stated in the *Hetubindu*, and so it is not discussed here.
Thus, in this way, its causal efficiency is not tenable either successively or simultaneously.

For it is endowed with a nature capable of producing causal efficiency; therefore, if it were to produce an effect both at the same time [as its arising] and subsequently—due to its lack of separation from that very form—then its destruction would occur immediately after its arising.
Furthermore, for that which is accepted as non-momentary, an effect is never observed to be produced all at once, since its production is seen to occur successively.

Thus, this non-momentary entity is not capable, whether successively or simultaneously, of accomplishing even the slightest portion of any causal efficiency whatsoever; therefore, it is indeed non-existent.
If that causal efficiency is not tenable for it, then why should it not be non-existent? To this he says:
"causal efficiency," and so forth.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: that which has the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) as its very definition is "existence" (*sattva*).
Therefore, [the term] means "excluded from," or "distinguished from," existence characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency;
this is because of the scriptural statement regarding the logical reason (*hetu*).
Therefore, regarding this meaning,
how is it further determined that the definition of existence is the capacity for causal efficiency? To this, he says:

"Of all," and so forth: "designation" (*upākhyā*) refers to verbal expression (*śruti*), because it is by means of this that [an object] is designated; its "non-separation" (*aviraha*) is its non-existence (*abhāva*).
That which has this very definition belongs to that which is indefinable (nirupākhya); it is so designated here as well.

In this context, the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of excluding the non-existence of those things—such as jars and the like—which are intended to be momentary, since they possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) through the differentiation of their objects.
If it is argued that the definition of existence (*sattva*) is not the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), but rather the connection with existence (*sattāyoga*), we say no,
because existence itself is absent.
And since that absence has been established elsewhere, it is not stated here;
furthermore, existence itself does not attain existence because of the absence of a connection with existence,
according to the tenet that "universals are devoid of universals."
Furthermore, it is not the case that entities whose intrinsic natures are not of a certain form can attain that very form even upon coming into contact with another nature—
just as crystals or clouds do not take on the color of a hibiscus flower or the like; therefore, this [objection] is trivial,
and only this much needs to be stated regarding the truth of the matter.
If it is argued that "the term *nirupākhya* (denotable) means 'that which is characterized by the absence of all capacity,'" then this is well said; however,

it is understood that this was stated in order to demonstrate that that which is devoid of all capacity is the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent," and for the sake of establishing that the name [of the category] possesses a corresponding meaning, since no word based on capacity could apply to such a thing.

If it is asked, "What would happen if the demonstration of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for the reason (*hetu*) in the case of the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) were not performed? he says: "In this way, when no subverting proof for the reason in the case of the opposite of the probandum is demonstrated, there is simply no cessation of doubt"—this is the connection.
But what is that doubt?

"Would it be produced or eternal? Such types [of arguments] are also found in the *Nyāyabindu*: "Because that is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and because that which has such an intrinsic nature is the reason (*hetu*)," (Tarkabhāṣā, Chapter 3, p. 69; Kashi Sanskrit Series edition). Now, one might object: "If the presence of the reason in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is not perceived, how can there be non-exclusion [of the reason from the counter-example]? To this, he says:

Even if this means of proof (*sādhana*) does not function in the absence [of the object], why would there be no removal of the qualification of the probandum (*sādhya*) when there is a reversal of the sense organs? To address this, he says:
"Because there is no contradiction," and so forth.

The ellipsis is "of the means of proof (sādhana) and the counter-example of the probandum (sādhyavipakṣa). His intention is as follows: if the mutual contradiction between the means of proof and the opposite of the probandum were established, then non-observation alone would suffice; otherwise, since a subverting argument (bādhaka) would not be established, doubt would be unavoidable. Anticipating this objection, he says:
And it is not at all logical that the non-apprehension of everything should be a subverting or negating factor; this is the supplement [to the argument].

Of what entity—that is, of what existence—is there [the subversion]? The remainder, namely "of the reason when its opposite to the probandum," is understood from the context. This is indeed implied by the topic.
This is what is meant: it is precisely the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) that sublates the coexistence of the reason with the absence of the probandum,
as was demonstrated previously.
Nor is there exclusion based on mere non-perception, because for one who perceives all things that are remote, non-perception does not establish non-existence, and so forth.
Therefore, it was well said: "Otherwise, if a subverting proof (*bādhaka*) were unestablished, doubt would be difficult to avoid.
By this, he recalls what was stated previously.

And since it has been stated that "it is thus meaningful because there is no exclusion of non-perception as a means of proving absence," someone might have the following doubt: "What is the purpose of this qualification 'as a means of proving absence,' given that every non-perception whatsoever is a means of proving absence? To dispel that doubt, he says this:

Regarding the passage beginning with "na ca" (1b11), the word *ca* here should be understood in the sense of *hi* (for/indeed); or else, it functions as an emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) in the sense of "not at all. The explanation is as before.

"Now, it might be argued: 'Is it not the case that the pervasion of the subverting proof itself—namely, the impossibility of [causal efficiency] occurring either successively or simultaneously—is not established by its own capacity? Therefore, how can that [proof], whose pervasion is itself unestablished, suffice to establish the pervasion of another reason such as existence?

If you say that the pervasion is established there by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), then surely this very same fault of infinite regress (anavasthā) will follow. Anticipating that an opponent might say this, he says all of the following."
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" (1b11): the word "therein" (*tatra*) serves the purpose of introducing the statement.
It is established that whatever is the characteristic of a real entity (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*) is pervaded by the connection with either succession (*krama*) or simultaneity (*akrama*).

If it is asked why it is precisely by this mode—that wherever there is causal capacity (*sāmarthya*), there must be purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) either successively or simultaneously—it is said: "Because no other alternative is possible" (1b11).
This is because there exists no other alternative distinct from succession and simultaneity.

Therefore, wherever this characteristic of existence—namely, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*)—is present, there it must necessarily occur through either succession or simultaneity.
But how is it established that there is no third category other than succession and simultaneity?
It is established because succession and simultaneity are defined by their mutual exclusion (*anyonyaparihārasthitalakṣaṇatva*), and thus they exclude a third possibility.
We say it is like existence and non-existence.
If it is asked, "Let it be so; but why must it consist precisely of the nature of succession and simultaneity?"—then what else could it be?
If you say, "It might exist," then for what purpose have you fallen into this great calamity of a dilemma, such that you are unable even to name it as being of such-and-such a nature?
Even if it is established that capacity is pervaded by the two modes of succession and simultaneity, if you ask, "What is thereby established? he says:

Since capacity is pervaded by the connection with either succession or simultaneity, there is a non-perception of the pervading property—the connection with succession or simultaneity—when a non-momentary entity is asserted; the meaning is that this [non-perception] subverts or negates capacity.
For indeed, this connection with succession or simultaneity is the pervader of that capacity.

Consequently, upon the cessation of this [succession and simultaneity], there must necessarily be the cessation of its capacity as well; otherwise, it would not follow that succession and simultaneity are the pervaders of this [capacity], since they sublate it. Therefore, because the pervasion is established—by means of the absence of the pervader (the non-existence of succession and simultaneity), which functions as the object, and the absence of the pervaded (the absence of capacity), which functions as the agent—the consequence of an infinite regress does not arise.
Having thus stated the justification for the probative factor (*sādhana-aṅga*) of the essential nature reason (*svabhāva-hetu*), he now concludes.

With the words "In this way" (evam) and so forth, he connects what was previously asserted— that if no justification is provided, that very lack of justification brings about the defeat of the proponent—
with the phrase "the non-justification of that" (tasyāsamarthanam) and so on.
Why is it that the commenced object is not established?
Because a proof that has not been established is incapable of establishing the commenced object, as this would lead to the undesirable consequence of there being no dispute at all.

For instance, since it is possible for qualities such as wisdom (*prajñā*) to reach the limit of excellence through the progressive refinement of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) in the process of establishing omniscient knowledge, they would require a cause that resides in a stable substratum and somehow imparts a specific quality to the self once and for all.

If, then, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this reason is established by demonstrating a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), then in that case, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would follow for you. To dispel this doubt, he sets forth the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "atrāpi" (1b9):
here, "here" refers to the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

For you, who do not accept non-perception as a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), there is no ascertainment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-niścaya*) based on the reason of mere non-perception. By this formulation, the word "also" (*api*) indicates that this applies not only to the fundamental reason (*maula-hetu*) but also to the previous [reason]. The verb phrase is: "Does it not follow that even the previous fundamental reason would be subject to lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*)?"
What is the reason?
It is because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the impossibility of [action] occurring either successively or simultaneously is not established by means of logical capacity (*sāmarthya*).

For if the certainty of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-niścaya*) were not established merely through non-observation, then it would follow that something could both be characterized as existent and possess causal capacity while being devoid of the possibility of acting either successively or simultaneously.

Regarding the question "What is the contradiction between these two?", [the opponent] says: "If the pervasion (vyāpti) is not established in this very subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), even if it were not established here, one might argue that by the force of this [proof], the pervasion will be established for the original reason (*maula-hetu*). To this, he replies:
"The original reason itself would also result in being non-pervasive"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

For instance, a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) that is itself not established by a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*) is not capable of establishing another as a means of valid cognition, because that would entail the [absurd] consequence that everything would be a means of valid cognition.
If this is so, then in this case as well, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be ascertained by another pervading means of valid cognition regarding the pervading [subject]. To this he says:
"In this case too" (1b9); he uses the word "too" (*api*) to indicate that this applies not only to the fundamental reason (*maulahetu*).
Furthermore, if one were to begin a proof [by this method], there would be an infinite regress;
for instance, regarding that subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) which is stated for the sake of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*),
the pervasion therein must also be established by another subverting means of valid cognition.
Because even that [inference] is not itself a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) capable of establishing the validity of another; this can be said regarding that case as well.

If it is argued that its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by yet another [inference], then if this were so, the same argument would apply there too, and thus an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result for you.

Having thus formulated the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he now states the rebuttal (*pratividhāna*) here, beginning with "Not [of] that which proves non-existence" (1b10), with the supplement: "by way of being a proof for negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)."
This is what is meant:

not every non-perception here is rejected, because that which is designated as the "non-perception of the pervader" (vyāpakānupalabdhi), which determines negative concomitance (vyatireka), is not prohibited.
However, as for what was said— that "mere non-perception" means that non-perception establishes the opposite, namely non-existence— [it is not so].

For what reason, and in regard to what, is the non-perception of this probans (*hetu*) in the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) called the subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)?

Because it establishes the contrary (*viruddha-pratyu-pasthāpanāt*). The word "of this" (*asya*) carries over [from the previous context]. For instance, that which lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through either succession or simultaneity does not possess existence characterized by capacity (*sāmarthya-lakṣaṇa-sattva*).
Just as in the case of the son of a barren woman and so forth, so too for momentary things, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is impossible through either succession or simultaneity.

Thus, this "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalambha*), namely that "causal efficiency is impossible through succession or non-succession," is called the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) which establishes the opposite of the probandum—namely, non-existence (*asattva*)—in opposition to the reason "because of existence" (*sattvāt*).
And in the same way, this should be stated accordingly for [the reasons] such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth.
Why is this called a "subverting means of valid cognition" (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) because it establishes the opposite? He says:

For in this way, that reason characterized by existence (*sattva*) and so forth would be established as being absent when that probandum is absent, provided that it is subverted—that is, refuted—therein, in the absence of the probandum, by something contradictory to itself, namely by its own contradictory nature such as non-existence (*asattva*), etc.; that is to say, by what kind of thing? By one possessing a means of valid cognition, i.e., by one endowed with a *pramāṇa*.

To the question, "Why does this [reason] become established in that way? he says: otherwise, if there were no establishment of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*) against this reason when the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) occurs, then doubt would persist;
and the consequence—that it might be both eternal and so forth—would be difficult to avoid. This is the remainder of the sense.

"Obstructed by a subverting [proof]" (*duḥkhena nivāryate*) means "difficult to obstruct" or "difficult to refute. Here, by the term "subverting" (*bādhaka*), a proof that presents a contradictory [property] is intended; or rather, a property contradictory to the reason as presented by a subverting proof.

But surely, since the exclusion of the reason from the opposite of the probandum is ascertained through mere non-perception alone, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) will be free from doubt; so why do you speak of the removal of suspicion? For if a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is not demonstrated, that very [ascertainment] is not established; how then could this [suspicion] be removed?
If this suspicion does not cease, what follows? To this he says:
"Then, because the suspicion has not been removed, it would be an inconclusive fallacy of the reason (hetvābhāsa). [1b7]

The meaning is that because there is doubt regarding the absence of the reason—characterized by its non-existence in the case of the [probandum's] absence—the reason would be a fallacy (*hetvābhāsa*) characterized by a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Why, then, is there a suspicion of non-exclusion even when [the reason] is not observed, given that such non-observation establishes its absence? To this he says: "Nor does exclusion from the absence of the probandum of the reason follow from mere non-observation" (1b7); the words to be supplied to complete the sentence are as follows.
The word "api" (also/even) has the sense of "because";
the inclusion of the term "mātra" (mere/only) is for the purpose of excluding [the non-perception of] that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility.
Why is this so?

If it is asked: "Since non-perception regarding objects that are remote—due to remoteness of place, time, or nature, such as China, the Daśārṇas, Piśācas, and so forth—proves their non-existence, what [specific] non-existence does it establish? [The answer is:
It is understood that it establishes the non-existence of those [objects] under discussion, namely, those that are remote.

[Objection: But surely he knows everything, including the objects of all compounds and so forth, and it is by his non-perception that he establishes the non-existence of even remote things; so why has this been said? [Response: He says, "of one who is not all-seeing" (asarvadarśinaḥ). This is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) with the word *sarva*, meaning "one whose nature is to see everything."
Why does the non-perception of that [object] not prove its non-existence?
Because for a person of limited vision, there is non-perception of certain existing objects that are remote;
this has been stated.

Here, the vision of the All-Seeing One does not encompass the existence of all things, such that its absence would exclude the existence of objects— just as the absence of a tree excludes a *śiṃśapā*— because they are distinct. Nor is it the cause of that [existence], such that its absence would exclude it— just as the absence of fire excludes smoke.
Regarding the statement, "Because it exists even in the absence of that [cause], there is a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) once again," and so forth,
some here raise the following prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

"What, then, is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) by the demonstration of which the cognition of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the fundamental reason (*maula-hetu*) occurs? To this he says, "Furthermore, the subverting [proof]," and so forth. [Objection: How does the demonstration of the subverting proof regarding the contrapositive (*viparyaye bādhaka-pramāṇopadarśana*) serve as the means of establishing the pervasion here? Since the meaning has already been stated previously in this very context with the words, "If everything that exists or is produced were not subject to momentary destruction," etc., the fault of redundancy (*punarukta-doṣa*) would result; thus, it must be considered by those very [critics] themselves. Enough of recounting the faults of others!
Therefore, the opponent objects otherwise: "In that case, how can this [reasoning] be free from fault for one who possesses a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)? To this he says:
"Furthermore, a subverting proof, when operating, brings about an incapacity"—this is the verb.
What is the characteristic of non-existence,

and how is it established as a valid means of cognition? It should be supplied that this refers to that entity for which there is an impossibility of causal efficiency, whether sequentially or simultaneously.
It has no capacity for any causal function whatsoever, just as, for example, [the capacity] of a lotus in the sky; this is the implied simile.

And since that [capacity] is impossible in a non-momentary entity due to the impossibility of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) through either succession or simultaneity—this being how [the argument] proceeds—if it is asked, "What follows from that?", he says:
For that reason, by means of which [reason] its occurrence—characterized as non-existent and lacking causal capacity—is drawn forth, it is established that whatever is produced is indeed impermanent.
Even so, what is established? To this he says:
And by that much—namely, by the mere presentation of a subverting proof—it follows that the concomitance with the probans-property alone is established.
To the question "By what [is this established]?", he says:
"This genitive case is to be understood as denoting the agent of the property to be proven."

The meaning of the sentence is established as follows: by means of that property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the mere probans-property (*sādhanadharmamātra*)—which does not require the operation of any other cause—is established. However, it should not be formulated thus: "the positive concomitance with the mere probans-property [occurs] in the property to be proven.

For if it were so, the property to be proven itself would become inseparably connected (*avinābhūta*) with the reason, rather than the reason [being connected to the probandum]; consequently, the reason would fail to be a signifier (*agamakatva*).
Then he states what benefit is obtained [by this]:

"And the definition of the essential-cause (*svabhāva-hetu*) is established. The phrase "by that much" (*tāvatā*) is understood to carry over. Furthermore, the definition of the essential-cause is that the nature of the subject (*dharmin*) exists by virtue of the mere presence of that [property], because even in the absence of conditions, it does not depend on further effort.

"Like the purification of the impurities of gold"—such are the reasons (*hetu*) which possess an excellence of established capacity. If these were to make known what is to be known even when they are not themselves established, then there would be no dispute at all with Jaimini and others.

Anticipating the objection—"But this is simply impossible: that one who is worthy of defeat (*nigrahārha*) should state a reason that is [only] nominally capable, though in reality it is incapable"—he reveals his own intention:
In reality, even if a capable reason (*hetu*) has been employed, its capacity has not been demonstrated; this is the meaning:

although he may have indeed employed a reason that is ultimately capable, nevertheless, because he has failed to establish the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*), his capacity has not been demonstrated by him. Thus, it is as if he were incapable;
for in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), the merits and defects of the actual object do not prevail.
Rather, it is because the speaker is censured by expressing a meaning that is not as it truly is.

For this very reason, even in cases where the merits and defects of the object are being deliberated, one must understand that this occurs precisely through the medium of speech. Otherwise, one would have to remain silent after merely stating the proposition: "Sound is momentary."
"Because the intended object is established simply by such a statement.
Having thus demonstrated the justification of the members of the proof regarding the essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*), he now states it regarding the effect as a reason (*kāryahetu*).

Regarding the logical reason of effect as well, he asks "What, then, is that? and replies with the words beginning "the effect-sign," etc.: that which is the effect-sign known by the name of smoke and so forth, which is employed for the purpose of proving a cause such as fire.

The meaning is that the very establishment of the causal relationship between the probans and the probandum—which consists in proving the relation of cause and effect between smoke and so forth and fire and so forth—is precisely what constitutes the validation of the member of proof in the case of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).
To the question, "By what means, then, is the causal relationship between those two established? he says:
"By the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish presence and absence. (2a3)

The etymological sequence is as follows: "existence and non-existence" (*bhāvābhāvau*) refers to the presence and absence of cause and effect; "their means of proof" (*tayoḥ sādhane*) refers to the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇe*) that establish them. Furthermore, the word "means of proof" (*sādhana*) is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, the means of proving existence and non-existence are perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), respectively.
To explain how the causal relationship is established by means of perception and non-apprehension, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "yathā" (2a3):

the ellipsis of the sentence must be supplied as follows: "This effect, designated by the name 'smoke' and so forth, exists when this fire is present; having previously been unperceived despite meeting the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), it is now perceived."

Otherwise, the operation of fire upon that smoke would not have been stated at all, because the suspicion could arise that "this [smoke] existed even prior to the presence of fire. However, when the non-perception as previously described is grasped, this suspicion does not occur. For this very reason, it has been stated in exactly the same way in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya* and other works.
And by this, the operation of the means of valid cognition consisting of direct perception (pratyakṣa) has been stated;
for it is through direct perception that it is understood: "When this exists, that comes to be.
Now, desiring to point out the operation of non-apprehension (anupalambha), he says:

Regarding the phrase "even though [others] exist" (satsvapītyādi): it means that even though others than that fire exist, and likewise even though its causes—such as fuel, wind, and so forth—are present and capable. The word "even though" (satsu) continues to apply here.
The word "ca" (and) is indicated here as being elided and should be understood [from the previous rule]; thus, [the phrase] "if [the causes] are capable" applies here as well,
and in the absence of that burning, "this" [effect] does not come to be—
this is what is governed by the context.
The word *iti* functions here in the sense of "thus" or as an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).
By this, it is established that cows, horses, and so forth—even though they are present in that same place and time—are not causes for the production of smoke;
for if those cows, horses, and so on were its cause, then even after the fire has passed away, smoke would necessarily arise because they remain present.
If it is argued that those [factors] such as fuel become its producers only by depending on other causes, and therefore this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) does not follow; [we reply:

if that were so, they too would be present right there, and thus the consequence would not be averted. If it is further argued that fire also produces that [smoke] by depending on auxiliary conditions (sahakārin), and therefore this [position] is not tenable; [we reply: in that case, it follows that fire itself is the cause for the production of smoke.
Therefore, this is said: "It is contradictory to claim that only the horse's hoof and so forth are its cause and not fire.
If it is argued, "In that case, let fire also be its cause, as well as the horse's hoof and so forth," we reply:
this is not tenable.
In that case, because the apprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is difficult to establish—
since even when cows and the like have departed, as long as there is fire and that collection of fuel and so forth, the production of the fire-cause indeed occurs;
for it is by relying upon a causal series and an effect-series that the relationship of cause and fruit is considered among entities, such that the effect-series is preceded by the causal series.
However,

for those who have attained the excellence of knowledge, there does not arise a cognition apprehending a distinction between moments such as "this is the preceding moment" and "this is the succeeding moment"; rather,
it is with reference to those of limited vision that the compassionate ones have formulated the definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
As it has been said: "This nature of conventional valid cognition (sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa) has been stated here; yet even in this regard, others, being deluded, cause confusion in the world.
If it is argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because smoke exists in places such as bedrooms even in the absence of fire, [we reply:
even for a fire that has already occurred, there is indeed the state of being preceded by a continuous series of fires.

The distinction, however, is one made by directness or indirectness. Those whose discerning intellects have become refined through the power of practicing the discrimination between the natures of diverse phenomena clearly perceive the difference between two series of smoke—one arising from a continuous stream of perception and the other from a broken stream—or between those occurring in a dwelling house and those occurring in the vicinity of a kitchen. Thus, inference based on distinction is not contradictory; for this very reason, it has been stated that in the case of an effect as a logical reason (*kāryahetu*) and in the perception of a contradictory effect, inference depends upon place, time, and so forth.
Indeed, dependence on place, time, and so forth is accepted even in the case of a contradictory effect.
"Otherwise, the means of proof would be inconclusive, like the [presence of] smoke at night"; thus,
even in the case of a contradictory effect, there is a dependence on place, time, and so forth.
Otherwise, the means of proof would be inconstant, like the movement of a crow. Even if someone,

by virtue of having the eye of wisdom opened by the excellence of skill in discerning the distinctions between various states of being, were to distinguish that "this smoke is produced from fire" and "this [other] smoke is produced from smoke," even then,
the inconstancy would not be any less.
For instance, smoke produced from fire does not arise from smoke, because that would entail the consequence of it being causeless;
and thus, as it has been said:
"Therefore, if smoke were to originate from what is not fire..."
"By whom could the arising of such a thing as Śakra’s head be prevented? and so forth;
therefore, if smoke were to arise from what is not fire, [it would follow that anything could arise from anything].
In the same way, who could prevent the arising of that [consciousness] from the head of Śakra?
Therefore, even if one disregards it as being without essence, the conclusion must be reached that those cows, horses, and so forth do not possess causality in that regard. Let this be settled.
Therefore, it is established that fire alone is its cause, and not horses and so forth;

thus, the causality of fire has been established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in the manner previously described. In this same way, the causality of the entire collection of conditions (*sāmagrī*), such as fuel and so on, should be established.
Or, it may be explained as a single coherent statement.
Therefore, even though other capable causes such as fuel and so forth are present, [the smoke] does not occur in their absence;

thus, the fact that cows, horses, and the like are not its causes should be understood through the aforementioned method by way of the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). If it is asked: "Is it not more appropriate to say simply that 'it occurs in their absence'? For what purpose is it stated that 'even though other capable causes of it are present'? he replies:
"Thus, indeed," and so forth:

because, by means of the statement beginning with "even when [the causes] exist," this smoke’s status as an effect of that—its being an effect of fire—is established and becomes certain and free from doubt;
otherwise, if it were not demonstrated in this way, [it would remain uncertain].

The overall meaning is as follows: when it is demonstrated that "it occurs solely through the absence of that [other cause]," and while such a demonstration is being made, since other things—such as cows, horses, or fuel—are also absent in that location on the ground devoid of fire, the capacity of this [specific] fire remains doubtful; therefore, how can there be certainty regarding the causal relationship?
For this very reason, he says:

For when those capable causes are present, the non-arising of the effect indicates a deficiency in some other cause; thus, its capacity is suspected to be otherwise. This very point is indicated by the phrase "something else is there" (anyattatra) and so forth.

In that case, regarding smoke as the effect of a horse, something else—namely the horse and so on—is required which is capable of fuel and the like; because of the absence of that, it does not occur in a place devoid of fire.
The meaning is: "How is this certainty established—that it was not produced from its own nature?

If one objects: "If there were something else capable [of producing it], then it was not produced due to the absence of that; but how can there be a cessation of this [effect] upon the cessation of that [cause]? he replies with the words beginning "Upon the cessation of this," etc. (2a5).

The meaning is that when this fire ceases, the cessation of smoke—which occurs—is a coincidence of chance (*kākatālīya-yoga*). However, when the phrase "even when they exist" (*satsu api*) is employed, then because all [the causes] are present there, one reaches the certainty that "upon the cessation of this [specific cause], this [smoke] ceases"; thus, the intention is that it is not a mere coincidence of chance.
"What does he say regarding the cessation of that [habitual practice]?
He says: "The mother’s marriage" (2a5) and so forth;
that is, the country in which the mother’s marriage is appropriate and customary is described as such.

Then, there is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) with the word "country" (*deśa*); in that context, because it is based on birth, it is used figuratively (*upacārāt*). That is to say, it refers to that which has its birth—its origin—in the Pārasīka country.

Just as in another country, such as the land of the Mālavakas, there is an absence [of a certain thing] due to the absence of a mother’s marriage, and yet there is a coincidental correspondence (*yadṛcchā-saṃvāda*), so it is here as well.

For instance, in another country, the absence of that [thing] is due to the absence of a specific type of clay, and not due to the absence of a mother’s marriage; thus, its absence when that is absent is merely a "crow-and-palmyra" coincidence (*kākatālīya*).
And this is the case here too.
Alternatively, it is explained otherwise:
just as this effect, such as smoke, arises when this collection of causes, such as fire and fuel, exists;
however, the ellipsis of the sentence must be supplied as before.

Its purpose is to be understood as that very thing: namely, the mention of the function of this perception by means of the phrase "even when [other causes] exist," etc., [which serves to distinguish it] from non-perception among those other than that; furthermore, [it distinguishes it] from that collection of causes such as fire.

In other cases— such as cows, horses, and so forth— which are capable [of producing smoke] despite the absence of this collection of causes consisting of fire and the like, [smoke] does not arise; and this has been stated with reference to the views of others,
for those [cows and horses] do not actually possess the status of being its causes.

If, on the other hand, those [individual causes] were its [the smoke's] causes, then there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that smoke would be produced even before the proximity of that collection, just as it is afterwards.
If it is argued that they are "produced by that" because they depend upon it,
then it follows that the collection itself is the cause.
If it is argued, "Let it be so for both; there is no harm to us," we reply:
No, because it has already been stated that [the relation] residing in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is difficult to establish in that case.

If it is argued that even when all those [causes] have departed, as long as that collection exists, its production certainly occurs, and thus it should simply be said that "it does not occur in the absence of that," for what purpose was it stated that "even when they exist" and so forth? To this he replies:
"For in this way... and so on.

Otherwise, if one were merely to demonstrate that [the effect] does not occur when that complex (kalāpa) is absent, then since other things such as cows and horses are also absent there, the causal capacity of this complex would remain doubtful. For it might be that some other thing, such as a cow or a horse, is capable there; and because of its absence, the [effect] did not arise. Thus, the cessation [of the effect] upon the cessation of this complex would be a mere accidental coincidence (yadṛcchā-saṃvāda). The rest is as before. Having thus explained the method for determining the relationship between cause and effect, he concludes the present topic.
By the passage beginning with "evam" (thus),

it is shown that in this manner— according to the method already described— that smoke and so forth is established as the effect of that fire and so forth; that which has been thus established and determined becomes proven, and that which is unproven and free from doubt is likewise established and ascertained.
Alternatively, if the effect of that whose existence has been established through perception and non-perception is indeed proven, then what follows? He says:
"Being established, [the effect] by its own occurrence—that is, by its own presence—establishes the occurrence of that cause, namely its presence. (2a6)
The phrase "in consideration of place, time, and so forth" is to be supplied [to the argument]. This is what is meant:

the determination of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established by the characteristic of "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*) for each individual thing. Wherever such [an effect] is perceived as being dissimilar [to its cause], it leads one to understand its own cause by its mere existence, in consideration of place, time, and so forth.
He asks, "For what reason? and replies, "Because the effect does not deviate from its cause" (2a6);
for otherwise, that would not be its effect at all.
Because of that deviation:

for it is not logical that something which exists even in the absence of another should be the effect of that [other], just as a bracelet cannot be the effect of an earring; such is the intended meaning.

Now, one might object: "Granted that smoke does not deviate from being the effect of fire, but why is it that another thing, such as a sprout, does not deviate from its own causes, such as the seed? To this he says:
"And if there is non-deviation," and so forth.

This is what is meant: when it is established that smoke does not deviate from its own cause because it arises from it, then the same principle of non-deviation applies to all effects, such as sprouts and the like, with respect to their own causes, such as seeds and so forth.
For these too, being established as effects of those [causes] through the aforementioned types of perception and non-perception, are proven to be non-deviating from them.

Demonstrating that this establishment of the members of the proof constitutes the probans based on the effect (*kāryahetu*), and that its opposite— its failure to establish— is the ground for the defeat of the proponent, he says:
"Thus," and so forth.

"Thus" means by means of perception and non-perception in the manner previously described; that is, not only in the case of the previously mentioned mode [of proof] regarding the essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*), but also in the case of the effect-reason (*kārya-hetu*), the proponent's failure to establish [the reason] is a ground for defeat.
As for the word "also" (*api*), why is it used? He says: "Thus."

"Unestablished" (asamarthita), etc.: when that causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) between the mark (liṅga) and the marked (liṅgin)—or the fact that the mark is an effect of that [cause]—is unestablished, there is a failure to prove the intended object (ārabdhārthāsiddhi). The verb "intended object" (ārabdho 'rthaḥ) refers to the proof of the existence of the cause.
The connection with the subject at hand is that because that [probans] is unestablished, it constitutes a ground for defeat (parājaya-sthāna).
Why is this so? He says:
because when another object such as smoke exists, there is no necessary rule (niyama) regarding the existence of that [other object], such as fire.
The inclusion of the term "restriction" (*niyama*) is for the purpose of excluding accidental coincidence;
for even in the case of another object, if its nature is connected to that [other's] existence, there is indeed a restriction regarding its existence. Therefore, he says:
"of that which has a nature not connected to its existence."
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that which has a nature that is unobstructed and non-contingent upon the existence of that [other thing], such as fire and so forth.
This should be understood as the reason for the statement that there is no necessity for the existence of one thing when another different thing exists;

furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is: whatever is a different thing and whose nature is not contingent upon another, there is no necessity for the existence of the latter when the former exists.

For example, just as when there is a foot-ornament (*nūpura*), there is a crown (*mukuṭa*) which is a different entity; so too, this smoke and so forth have a nature that is unconnected to that fire and so forth. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), or rather, it is established by the method of perceiving what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). As for how the logical reason (*hetu*) is conceived through its meaning, he asks: "Why is it that its very nature is unconnected to the existence of that [fire]? He says: [the following].

Regarding the statement "because the status of being an effect is unestablished" (2a7), it should be understood that this refers back to the fact that [the reason] has not been established. Furthermore, in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), you have not actually employed a reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*). Thus, even if that [reason] were indeed an effect, it has not been established by you; for how could such a person be defeated? To this he says:

In reality, even for an effect, there is the presentation of its material cause and so forth; this is the distinction regarding "the state of being that effect. Having thus stated the support for the members of the proof in the case of the reason of effect (*kāryahetu*), he speaks regarding non-perception (*anupalabdhi*):
The connection is that "there is also a justification for non-apprehension" (2a8); one must supply the words "of the members of the proof.
To the question "What, then, is that? he says:
He states that the means of proof through non-apprehension does not apply to just anything,
but rather to that which has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). 2a8.
The meaning is that there is no [perception] of anything other than the nature of the visible object.

"Perception" (upalabdhi) refers to cognition (*jñāna*), because the word *upalabdhi*—functioning as either an abstract noun (*bhāva-sādhana*) or an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*)—is a synonym for cognition; its "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is its cause.
Since the word *lakṣaṇa* functions as an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*), it denotes that which is produced;

and that [instrument] consists of the totality of other conditions (*pratyaya*) and a specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*), as well as the non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) of that which is pervaded by them.

If it is asked how there can be non-perception of such a thing, given that its "establishment" (*sādhana*) is defined by the etymological derivation as "demonstration" (*pratipādana*), we reply: no, for its demonstration occurs precisely there [in that specific case], whereas the demonstration of something belonging to that same class occurs elsewhere.
To whom, then, is the non-apprehension of such a thing established? He says:
"to the cognizer," that is, to the opponent (the respondent).

Furthermore, even if beings such as *piśācas* were to exist, provided they have reached the conditions for apprehension, or if there are others of that same class who possess supernatural power (*prabhāva*).
He says that for them as well, the means of proof is not the establishment of the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*), because it is [only] for the cognizer (*pratipattṛ*).
This is what is meant:
the means of proving non-perception applies only to that very object which is intended to be established and which meets the conditions for perceptibility, and not to anything else.
But what is the reason that the means of proving non-perception applies only to such a case?
He says it does not belong to anything else because the conventional usage of "non-existent" is established by precisely such a non-apprehension;
the point is that a non-apprehension which has not met the conditions for apprehensibility is a cause for doubt, and therefore lacks probative force.

The statement "because the conventional usage of 'non-existent' is established" is intended to demonstrate that by means of that [non-perception], only the conventional usage of non-existence is proven, and not non-existence itself; for non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is itself of the nature of non-existence.
Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "conventional usage of non-existent" is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*); by it, the cognition and the word "non-existent" are also to be understood.

If it is asked, "How is this further determined? he says: because even when there is no cessation of the perception of an object that has reached the conditions for apprehension (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), its non-existence is not established. (2a9) The mention of "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is an indication of the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), the word, and the cognition regarding non-existence.

And regarding the "characteristic of apprehension" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇa*), which is intended to exclude those things that are not cognized by being grasped through cognition—what, then, is this "attainment of the characteristic of apprehension," by virtue of which something is said to have "attained the characteristic of apprehension"?
To this he says, beginning with "In that regard" (*tatra*), etc. (2a9).
In that regard, for the purpose of introducing scriptural statements, [the question is asked]:
"Is the specific nature [of things] only this much?"
"No," he says;
"and there is the completeness of other causes.

Therefore, those other causes—namely, the sense faculties, mental attention (*manaskāra*), and so forth, which are distinct from that particular intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*)—are the "other causes" (*kāraṇāntara*). Of these...
"Sākalyam" means completeness; the word "ca" (and) has the sense of a conjunction with respect to a specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*).
[The author] asks: "What, then, is this specific intrinsic nature? and replies:
Regarding the passage beginning with "svabhāva" (2a9):

if this specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) is said not to be remote— unlike the forms of Mount Meru, Rāma, or the gods— due to the threefold remoteness characterized by distance in space, time, and intrinsic nature,
he clarifies that very point.
By the words "yadi" (if) and so forth, the meaning is as follows:

that which is not of the nature of self—that is, not of the nature of self, meaning it is of another nature—and which is also an appearance; the "separation" (*viveka*) of that [appearance] is its non-existence. That form (*rūpa*), that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which has the habit of not appearing in the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the cognizer with respect to that aspect, is described in that way.

Alternatively, a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) should be formed with the word "form" (*rūpa*), as in: "that which appears in its own cognition by way of an essence devoid of [other] similar and dissimilar [entities], provided that other conditions for perception are present. This means that when other causes are assembled, that which manifests in one's own cognition through an essence free from others of its own class or of a different class is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

"Such a thing" refers to an object characterized by being non-distant despite the three kinds of remoteness; that which is not perceived through the perception of the cognizer—by way of excluding the appearance of a form other than its own self—is the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent.
