The meaning is that it becomes fit for the cognition of the conventional usage of "non-existent.

If it is asked: "Even if it exists, it is not perceived due to the absence of the sense faculty, light, or attention; how then can such a thing be the object of the conventional usage of 'non-existent'? he says:
Regarding the phrase "even when other conditions for perception are present":

surely even an object such as a jar, though not distant and despite the presence of other causes for perception, is not perceived because it depends upon a transformation of the continuum (*saṃtānapariṇāma*).
For the mere proximity of other causes does not constitute a transformation of the cause that is conducive to the production of its own effect.

For instance, even when the causal complex of earth, seed, water, and so forth is present, the transformation of a *tāla* seed that is conducive to the arising of its own effect occurs only after a very long time, whereas for seeds such as those of hemp (*śaṇa*), it occurs immediately; the same will be the case here as well.

Furthermore, even when conjoined with something possessing power, such as one possessed of supernatural influence (*prabhāvavat*) like a sorcerer or a magician, when this entity is presided over by them, it is not perceived despite being present. How then can it be said that "such a thing, when other causes of perception are present, is the object of the conventional usage of non-existence because it is unperceived"?
Surely you have not exerted yourself in the *Nyāyabindu*;
for it is stated therein: "That which is its own nature (*svabhāva*) necessarily becomes perceptible when other conditions for perception are present.

Furthermore, that which depends upon a transformation of the continuum (*santāna-pariṇāma*), and that which is presided over by one possessing power (*prabhāvavat*), is not merely its own nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*).

Even when all other conditions for perception are present, because it does not produce a perception whose object is its own nature, such a thing—whose form is indistinguishable from that of a ghost or similar entity—is established as an object of the conventional usage of "non-existence.

If you object: "In that case, since the sense organs do indeed become perceptible when other conditions for perception are present, has their non-existence not been established in every respect? You are acting quite favorably toward our position.

For it was stated immediately prior that what is established as an object of conventional discourse is that very thing which comes within the range of vision when there is a completeness of unimpaired sense faculties and so forth, and its non-perception despite that same completeness; it is not, however, something whose nature is indistinguishable from that of a *piśāca* or similar entities.
Furthermore, it is not logical for such a thing to exist even when all other conditions for its perception are present, because its non-perception would then be impossible;
this is because there would be nothing else required for the production of its perception.
This point has indeed been made explicit in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*.

By this very [argument]—namely, "because there is no cognition of absence at the time of the effect," and so forth—it should be understood that everything raised by those clever critics who, failing to perceive even the slightest excellence in the mind of the wise, objected using such arguments as "just as a palm-seed undergoes transformation despite the completeness of its causal complex"—is entirely untenable; enough of these unstable prattle of fools, so we shall desist.

Therefore, it is established that only the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is the means of establishing the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*).

And since this is so, for that reason, when the mark (liṅga) is otherwise—that is, when a mark other than non-perception characterized by the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is employed as a means of establishing the conventional usage of non-existence (*asadvyavahāra*), consisting merely in non-perception—then, while that [other mark] exists, doubt arises; there is no certainty regarding the conventional usage of non-existence, because even upon the cessation of perception, the absence of the object is not established. This is the collective meaning.
Alternatively, it should be explained as: "When the mark is otherwise than from that mark of the non-perception of the perceptible, there is doubt."
Therefore, the word "therefore" (tasmāt) must be supplied from the preceding [text].

Alternatively, it should be explained as follows: when there is doubt regarding something other than that which has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), [the non-perception] is its mark (*liṅga*). He asks:
what, then, is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in this case of non-perception? He says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "atrāpi" (2b11), the phrase "of such a kind" refers to that which is perceptible yet not perceived; the inclusion of the term "all" is for the purpose of demonstrating pervasion through universal application.

In the second chapter of the *Nyāyabindu*, regarding one of the three types of logical marks (*liṅga*), [the author] says this: "Now, even if a certain thing such as a horn, which is unperceived despite meeting the conditions for perception, is the object of the linguistic convention of non-existence with respect to a rabbit's head and so forth, why is there this restriction that another thing—such as a universal, a particular, a whole, a substance, conjunction, or disjunction—must likewise be so [regarded] by some other [means of knowledge]? To this he replies:
Regarding the passage beginning with "kasyacid" (of some):

when it is accepted that something non-existent— such as a rabbit’s horn, which has not been perceived despite meeting the conditions for perceptibility— is the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent," then it is stated that "the object of the conventional usage of 'non-existent' is non-existent" because there is no difference in its defining characteristics (*tallakṣaṇāviśeṣāt*).

The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of that non-existent is the "sign" (*nimitta*), which is the aforementioned non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). Furthermore, the word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), because it is not distinct from that [non-apprehension]. The ellipsis of the sentence is: "[this applies] to the universal, the particular, the whole, substance, and so forth. What is meant by this is as follows: why is even a rabbit's horn accepted as an object of the conventional usage of "non-existent"?
If you say, "Because the aforementioned non-apprehension, which is the cause for that [usage], exists," [then we reply:]...

If it is thus the case that it possesses the nature of both universal and particular, why is it not accepted as the object of the conventional usage "existent" (*sad-vyavahāra*)? Otherwise, if you argue that such usage would apply there as well, we reply:
no, for a distinction between objects based on the whim of a person is not logically tenable regarding a cause.
By the words "not so" (na hi) and so forth, he clarifies this very point:
that when such a perceptible object exists, one cannot admit its non-existence because it is not perceived.

The meaning is that it is not admitted [as existing] because it is the object of conventional usage regarding non-existence (*asad-vyavahāra*) and so on; by the word "non-existence" (*asattva*), conventional usage regarding non-existence is indicated, which serves as a synecdoche for certainty (*viniścaya*).
If it is argued that "the non-perception of that very thing which is capable of being perceived is the cause of its negation," and so forth—[we reply:
in another case, such as the absence of a rabbit's horn, there is indeed the conjunction of a man with a staff; this is the meaning.
For such a perceptible object, when the causes of perception (such as the eyes) are absent, that non-perception does not occur [as a valid ground for negation].
Rather, it is simply perception that occurs; by means of this double negation, the sense is that there is an absence of any other requisite condition for perception to depend upon.
Thus, he clarifies the very subject at hand by this.

However, such a thing, being unperceived despite meeting the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), does not exist; therefore, the mere non-perception of what meets the conditions for perceptibility is the sole cause for this conventional designation of non-existence (*asadvyavahāra*). It is described as such because he states, by means of this, that the conventional designation of non-existence has no other cause.
He asks, "Why is this so? and replies with the words beginning "of anything else" (*anyasya*).
The meaning of the collective [argument] is that, setting aside the aforementioned non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), there is no other ground for the conventional usage of non-existence.
Now, one might object: whatever possesses no capacity whatsoever in a particular locus is the object of the conventional usage of non-existence, just as a lotus in the sky;

likewise, since the intended entity possesses no capacity whatsoever even in the intended place and so forth, the exclusion of all capacity (*sarvasāmarthyaviveka*) alone will be the ground for the conventional usage of non-existence.
One might occasionally say that this very unrelated [objection] is stated by those with their heads uncovered, because there is no other cause for it; thus, he anticipates that view, saying:
"If it be argued that the cause is the discernment of all capacities" (2b2).
Regarding this, he states the [author’s] position with the words "In this way" (evam) and so forth:

He thinks as follows: "It is well said that the exclusion of all causal capacity (*sarvasāmarthyaviveka*) is the cause [of non-existence]. However, how is this very thing—the exclusion of all causal capacity—cognized, if one sets aside the aforementioned non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), such that this exclusion of all causal capacity would become the cause for the linguistic usage of 'non-existent'?"
Nor can this [non-perception] be its cause while remaining unknown, because the context concerns a probative reason (*jñāpaka-hetu*).
Why? Because for one who is devoid of all causal capacity, cognition occurs precisely through the aforementioned non-perception; thus he says:
Because there is no other means for its apprehension;

however, when through the aforementioned non-apprehension there occurs the cognition of that [object] which is devoid of all causal capacity, then, upon that apprehension, the conventional usage of "non-existent" (asat) arises.
Thus, for this reason, this aforementioned non-perception is said to be the cause (*nimitta*) for the conventional usage of "non-existence.

However, fearing that another might again claim its untenability on the grounds that there is no other cause for such usage, [the author] raises an objection with the words "cognition, designation," etc.
His intention is this: the conventional usage of that [non-existence] arises from cognition, designation, and purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

For it is the intention [of the author] that when those [cognitions] occur, they establish the existence of a real entity (vastu-sattā) as well as its difference and non-difference, which correspond respectively to the difference and non-difference of the real entity;
and when they cease, they eliminate the conventional usage of "existence" which is their own cause, just as fire [eliminates] smoke.
And when that [cognition, etc. ceases, there is the linguistic usage of "non-existent";
for since the linguistic usages of "existent" and "non-existent" exist as mutually exclusive states, the abandonment of one is necessarily concomitant with the adoption of the other.
Therefore, it is not correct to say that [the cessation of cognition, etc.,] is the cause for the linguistic usage of "non-existent" for something else, and so forth.

Regarding this, he states the rebuttal beginning with "bhavati" (it exists) and so forth; the analysis of the compound is as follows: "the cognition of the appearance as described" refers to a cognition that manifests the form appearing to the direct perception of the perceiver, wherein the appearance is as previously stated.

And it has been stated [in the passage beginning with] "that which is non-self," etc., that from that [perception], the conventional usage of "existent" arises because of the direct apprehension of the object;
and since its opposite is non-existence, when that [non-existence] is present, the conventional usage of "non-existent" arises.
The completion of the sentence must be supplied as "when other causes of apprehension are present," because otherwise doubt would arise;
for it has already been explained by us previously that such doubt does not cease even when the object exists and all other conditions for its apprehension are complete. This is the intended meaning.
If such an understanding is indeed intended by you through this statement, then there is complete agreement between us; nevertheless, nothing undesirable has been said by us.
However, if it is otherwise, then there is a deviation (vyabhicāra). Demonstrating that very deviation, he says:
By the phrase "in the case of what is not an object of direct perception" (pratyakṣāviṣaye) and so forth,
[it is meant that] that which is born from a mark (liṅga) is "born from a mark" (liṅgaja);
the meaning is "inference" (anumāna).

From that [perception], there may be a correct conventional usage regarding an object even when it is not present; however, he says "also" (*api*) to indicate that this applies only to that which has the form just described as being graspable by itself.
Is this possible for every cognition born from a logical mark (*liṅga*)? No;
he says "from some [cause]" (*kutaścit*).
The meaning is: "those [cognitions] produced by the power of the two types of marks, namely essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*).
The intention is that non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) establishes both non-existence (*asattā*) and the conventional usage of "non-existent" (*asad-vyavahāra*).
If this is so, one might ask: "How, then, can there be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*)? To this, he says:

"But the conventional usage of 'non-existent,' etc."—the phrase "its opposite" means that when the aforementioned cognition produced by the logical mark ceases, [the reason] is inconclusive, that is, doubtful.

Why? Because even when the means of valid cognition consisting of the perceiver’s direct perception has ceased with respect to an object remote in space and so forth, there remains doubt as the cause [of uncertainty].
The word "of the object" (*arthābhāve*) is to be supplied;
"the perception of the cognizer" (*pratipattuḥ pratyakṣam*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
And this [statement] is employed in order to state that for one who has abandoned all obscurations to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), there is indeed no doubt once perception has ceased.
And this [argument] regarding another inference and scripture is stated while presupposing the authority of scripture;
however, that [scripture] possesses no such authority.
"Because there is no necessary connection (*nāntarīyakatā*) between words and things,
no object is established from them; for they [words] indicate the speaker’s intention," according to such statements.

This is his intended meaning: even if the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have ceased to function with respect to an imperceptible object, how can there be the certainty that "it does not exist"?

For instance, things such as the young shoots of *dūrvā* grass and leaves existing within the mountain thickets of Malaya maintain a form that transcends the scope of the three means of valid cognition, yet it cannot be asserted that they do not exist.
Since the absence of a means of valid cognition lacks the causal capacity to pervade the existence of all objects,

there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) resulting from the rule that the exclusion of one thing necessitates the exclusion of another when an object lacking that form is excluded; this has already been explained previously,
as it was said:

"How can there be non-existence through non-perception for those many things that are unrelated to the scope of the treatise, whose forms and sense-faculties are not manifest, and which lack any indicative mark? (5)
"Many objects are unrelated to the scope of the treatise, have forms that do not stimulate the senses, and lack inferential marks; how can their non-existence be established through non-perception?

(5) But surely, here [in this context], one has begun to refute the status of a cognition born from a mark as a cause for the conventional usage of 'non-existent,' by stating 'the opposite of that' and so forth."

If it is asked, "Why has there been an introduction of perception and scripture, which are indeed irrelevant here?"—the intention of this wise person appears to be as follows: this was stated to demonstrate that the absolute impossibility [of omniscience] is shown by pointing out that [omniscience] cannot be established even through the cessation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is what is understood to be his underlying purpose.

But has it not been stated that, since the conventional usage of "existent" and the conventional usage of "non-existent" are defined by their mutual exclusion, the absence of one necessarily entails the presence of the other? And since the causes for those usages are absent in the case of something remote, the conventional usage of "non-existent" follows from the cessation of the conventional usage of "existent"? True, this has indeed been stated; however, it is not tenable.

For instance, regarding an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), there is a cessation of the conventional usage of "existent. How is it that, even in the absence of the specific causes for those [usages], these two types of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) are equal in their result—the negation of the convention of existence—by virtue of the presence or absence of the cause of their respective opposites? If you argue that this is because of doubt in one case and error (*viparyaya*) in the other, as stated [in the text], then if that were so, how could the certain determination of the convention of "non-existent" (*asat-vyavahāra*) be logically applicable there?

However, where there is a definitive cessation of the conventional usage of "existent," there the conventional usage of "non-existent" is also entirely appropriate, because it has been stated that the other [usage] has the function of inducing [the former]. Furthermore, in the exclusion of the nature of non-existence, there is no necessary implication of existence; for in the case of things such as the son of a barren woman or a lotus in the sky, their status as non-existent does not imply a positive state of existence simply by virtue of negation. There would only be mere negation, since these two [existence and non-existence] abide through mutual exclusion.

Likewise here too, since there is a negation of the conventional usage of "existent" regarding that which is not perceived, there is no implication of a positive (vidhi) conventional usage of "existent"; rather, there would be merely its exclusion (vyavaccheda). This is because one state of being exists by way of mutual exclusion from the other state of being. And this very point was stated by Dharmakīrti himself—whose light of wisdom arose from the awakening to the reality of the stainless system of logic, thereby dispelling the darkness of all the doctrines of rival schools—when he said: "Even in the case of the exclusion of impermanence, selflessness, and so forth, that [positive entity] might exist," and so on; let us leave it at that for now.
Now, stating that even general mental designations do not serve as the cause for the conventional usage of "existent," he says "na ca" (and not) and so forth;
and there, the connection is to be understood according to the sequence.
All these designations by means of the intellect do not establish the existence of a real entity,
nor do their distinctions or non-distinctions establish the existence or presence of the distinctions or non-distinctions of real entities;
the inclusion of the word "all" is for the purpose of demonstrating that some [designations] indeed do establish them.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says:
"Because it functions even with respect to non-existent things such as the past and the future" (2b5). "Functioning" is the verbal action;
by the word "etc. (*ādi*), [non-existent things] such as sky-lotuses and the like are included.
If it is asked how their occurrence with respect to those [objects] is logical in the absence of an object, he says:
"How? By the power of the maturation of the latencies deposited by experience, which has the nature of consciousness" (2b6);
the meaning is that there is no necessary connection between them and a real entity. This is the intended sense.

By means of such modes as "the conch-shell universal emperor" (śaṅkhacakravartin) and so forth, he states the reason for the claim that [these arguments] establish the existence of a real entity (*vastusattā*): because they also occur in those things which do not have the nature of performing multiple or single purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*).
For what purpose is their occurrence within those [individuals]? It is for the sake of making known their state;

that is to say, it is for the purpose of explaining the state of those things which do not perform multiple functions, as well as for the purpose of describing both their performance of multiple functions and their performance of a single function.
If it is argued that there must therefore be a reality to that object, he says:

"Even in the absence of a nature consisting of both unity and plurality" (2b6)—the phrase "of that object" is to be supplied here. By this, he establishes that [cognition and designation] do not prove either the difference or non-difference of the object.
He makes this very illustration fruitful by demonstrating it:
"King Mahāsammata" (2b6); and the word "yathā" (as) should be supplied here as an example from past occurrences.

The phrase "conch, universal monarch," and so forth, refers to a term whose application has not yet arisen; whereas the phrase "horn" and so forth refers to a form that has already been acquired. It is "visible" because it generates visual consciousness, and it is "resistant" because it obstructs the arising of another [object] in its own location.
This serves as an illustration of the principle that a term applies to things that perform various distinct causal functions.

Since that visual consciousness and so forth, although uniform because it produces a single effect, is nevertheless made the object of various terms such as "visible" and so on, those [terms] are not capable of proving a difference in the entity. "And the jar"—this is the illustration for [the principle that] things perform a single purposeful action; for instance, many [qualities] such as color, smell, taste, and touch, being capable of accomplishing a specific effect such as holding water, are apprehended by themselves as objects through those [qualities] which are non-different from one another.
Therefore, those [cognitions] are not capable of establishing non-difference;
and it is well known that the cognition of such things as the past, the future, or a rabbit’s horn does not establish them as real entities.
Now, how is it understood that cognitions and words such as "visible" (*sanidarśana*) do not establish a difference in real entities? To this, he says:

"No," [he says], because of the application [of the definition] to this very subject, form and so forth; that is to say, it is because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "form is visible and possesses resistance. Otherwise, if they were not coreferential, there would be no coreferentiality at all—just as there is none between words such as *vakula*, *utpala*, *kamala*, *mālatī*, and *mallikā*, which refer to different substrata. This is the intended meaning.
However, those who follow the doctrines of Kaṇabhakṣa and Akṣapāda— whose inner vision is defiled by the impurity of false conceptual constructions born from an attachment to erroneous views—
declare: "Even if it is admitted that these [qualities] have different objects, their coalescence in a single [substratum] is not at all contradictory,
because their causes, such as 'visibility' and so forth, are inherent (*samavāya*) therein, in that [substratum] such as color."

Intending to show that all of this is a doctrine that provokes the laughter of wise men—because it is charming only so long as it is not investigated and cannot withstand the scrutiny of critical inquiry—he says, "Alas, for this effort," and so forth.
The word *vata* expresses compassion; he asks, "Compassion for what? and then replies:

The intention is that it is impossible for those [qualities] to have a relationship with that [universal] in the absence of assistance, since they do not assist the manifold related entities such as "visibility" and so forth.
By attributing to itself a manifold nature—such as visibility and so on—from those related entities, this [universal] falls into exhaustion;
for indeed, what are these distinct capacities through which it assists the manifold related entities by possessing their forms and so forth?
"Why does [the single cause] not produce multiple words such as 'intellect' (*buddhi*) and so forth by means of those very same distinct potencies?
If this were the case, what benefit would be gained? To this he says:
"In this way, indeed, the labor of following a succession [of causes] is avoided. (2b9)

The meaning is this: by means of various powers (*śakti*), [an entity] assists its related [effect], and from those [powers] words proceed; thus, this labor of following a causal chain is abandoned by this ascetic [who posits] form and so forth. Now, one might object: "Even though all entities possess specific causal powers, you too must necessarily accept this very point; otherwise, when challenged by an opponent as to why a rice seed produces only a rice sprout and not a barley sprout, what could you say except that it is due to the 'intrinsic nature' (*prakṛti*) of the entity?"
Therefore, for you, taking recourse to the very nature of word-meanings is the only refuge, since otherwise it would be impossible to avoid this fault.
And this [position] is not forbidden to me either by the royal court;
for it is possible for me as well to state that its capacity (*sāmarthya*) consists solely in assisting various related factors, and not in the production of multiple words. If [you object]: "..."
It is true that this is so;
however, it is thought that visibility and the other such qualities do not yet exist.
Since causal efficiency is not observed either successively or simultaneously,

and since things that have reached the conditions for perceptibility are not perceived, it cannot be asserted that something which has reached the conditions for perceptibility exists while remaining unperceived, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Alternatively,
if they do not reach the conditions for perceptibility, how could cognitions and designations based upon them proceed in the case of cows, gavayas, and so forth?

By this [argument], it follows that even for those things perceived, there is no perception of a universal as distinct from the individual, just as in the case of momentariness and so forth; for if a universal, though seen, is not perceived as distinct within the object in its entirety, then how could that application of words—which arises through the power of that [perception]—exist?

In the case of "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) and the like, since the cognition and the word do not exist when the basis [the staff] is not apprehended, that [universal] of yours cannot be established by reasoning in any way whatsoever.
Furthermore,
in your view, it follows that all entities would occupy the same location,
because they are non-different from existence (*sattā*) in every respect; or else, this [existence] would be excluded from a different location simultaneously.

Or, if it were to abide [in many], this [single entity] could not exist as one simultaneously in all ways; for in the case of fruits such as the palmyra palm, which possess multiple abodes that are manifold and diverse, there is no state of being one.
Or, even if they [the fruits] were to exist [as one], their capacity to produce cognition and sound would not be established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Precisely because it is not perceived, and because they exist even apart from it— as in the case of cooks and the like— this has been established in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (1.160).
"A word such as 'cook' (pācaka) is expressive [of its meaning] through a non-different [form], even without an external object;
because of this difference, action is not the cause of this [word], nor is the universal (jāti) residing in the action.
This and other such arguments are not stated here.
Furthermore, those [universals] cannot be recipients of assistance because, being eternal, they cannot have any excellence added to them.

Nor can they be brought into proximity by the manifestation [of their locus] independently of human intention, through the capacity of the universal—such as its resistance (sapratighatva) and so forth—which is assisted by that manifestation; for if such were the case, activity would result even when the speaker’s intention is not present.
Alternatively, let that very intention of the person be the regulator when it is present before one; what is the use of intervening universals?
For it is observed that universals conform precisely to the positive and negative concomitance residing in those [particulars], whereas eternal things do not, because they lack negative concomitance.
Therefore,
all this is merely a conceptual construction based upon a false view.

And that very conceptualization (kalpanā) should be adopted which cannot further be subjected to critical inquiry; for among the conceptualizations found therein, this one alone is appropriate because it is free from the defects of conceptualization and possesses positive qualities.
Thus, this conceptualization is indeed endowed with a rational nature.
"For a single [entity] does not have the capacity to produce various sounds, such as those of parrots;
if this is so, we say the same here," he says:
"If there is no capacity to produce various sounds, let there also be no assistance from various related factors."
The intention [of the author] is that it is accepted that there is a contradiction in one [entity] being the benefactor of many.
If it is argued that because [the universals] are eternal, it is indeed accepted that they do not benefit their correlates, he replies:

for if their lack of benefit is admitted—[that is,] if it is accepted that [properties such as] visibility and so forth do not benefit them, then their status as correlates of those [universals] is not established.
The meaning is this: for a cause that does not provide benefit to something cannot be considered related to it, just as the Himalayas are not related to the Malaya mountain.

Thus, by refuting the opposing view, it has been established with supporting examples that words such as "existent" (*san*) and "illustration" (*nidarśana*) have a non-distinct object; yet, carrying the weight of their own dullness, those same opponents challenge us once again.

Granted that words such as "visible" (*sanidarśana*) and so forth may indeed have a non-distinct object; however, how is it determined that words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*) and "cloth" (*paṭa*) have multiple things as their objects, given that there exists a distinct substance called a "whole" (*avayavin*) which is different from [its] form (*rūpa*) and other qualities?

And that very [reality] is made the object of words such as "pot" and "cloth. For instance, when brought under investigation, a cloth is distinct from its threads because it has a different maker, like a pot;
likewise, it is not the object of either collective or distributive cognition, like a cow or similar entities.
For the cognition of a cloth as "the threads" or "an aggregate of threads" is not erroneous,
because it is accomplished by other means— just like [the cognition] of a jar—
and because it is produced by [threads] situated in different locations.
Furthermore, because it possesses different dimensions (*parimāṇa*), like a jar and so forth, and like a *vakula* flower, an *āmalaka* fruit, or a mirror-image;
and because it exists at prior and subsequent times, like a seed and its sprout.
Alternatively, threads are distinct from the cloth because they are its cause, just as a shuttle and other such tools are;

or else, there is a difference between the thread and the cloth because they possess different potencies, like water and fire. Likewise, this other object under investigation—the blue lotus—is absolutely distinct from its fragrance and other qualities, because it serves as their delimiter.
Just as in the case of Caitra and others,

whatever here serves as the delimiter of something is distinct from that thing— just as Caitra is distinct from the body of a cow; since these are the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establish their mutual exclusion,
how could they possibly have different objects?

"This too is not a mere trifling manifestation of the darkness of those whose inner faculties are shrouded by the veil of dogmatic adherence to false views. Anticipating this, [the author] adds the qualification "kāryam" (as an effect), thinking: "Let even a jar, as well as color-form and so forth, which perform a single purposeful action, be denoted by a single word; what is the need for postulating a separate entity? 2b10.
The intention [of the opponent] is that for such a person, there is nothing at all [to be perceived], because nothing other than blue and so forth is observed.

As for those proofs stated to establish that [position], he considers them to be like "casting a shadow before those very people," because they are afflicted by defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*) and thus are not capable of proving its difference.
For instance, when this first proof is examined, it does not even withstand the preceding examination.
In this regard, two alternatives arise:
either the cloth's distinctness from the threads is established as being from threads existing in another state, or from those existing in a specific configuration.
Of these, the first alternative cannot withstand the weight of critical analysis.

Because of the consequence of the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*): since those whose pure intellects have been attained through the power of relying on the system of the Sugata’s doctrine— which has fully realized the true nature of all things— conceive that "all entities perish immediately after their production," and since you desire precisely their distinctness from those [entities], how is it that the demon of the impending fall into the fault of proving the already established does not seize you?
The second alternative, too, finds no foothold for its feet upon the surface of stone as if scorched by a fierce fire;
this is because the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the opponent.

For the fact that a cloth has different makers from those situated in specific locations does not enter the path of proof for the opponent. Indeed, how could one who does not even admit the distinctness of such types [of makers] due to their non-existence ever accept that there are different makers?
Even that which was stated immediately following is insufficient to fulfill the desired objective by means of valid cognition, because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For the cognition "cloth" occurs only with respect to threads situated in a particular configuration;
since a form distinct from those [threads] is not perceived even by one whose eyes are wide open, [the opponent might argue] that it is observed in the case of rock crystal and the like.

We shall refute this later. As for the argument that [the action] is distinct because it is accomplished by other means, because it is performed by those situated in different locations, because it possesses different dimensions, because it occurs at earlier and later times, and because it possesses different potencies— here, the opponent, like one whose eyes are averted by the intense gaze of a realization of the first fault stated in the proof, cannot endure the excellence of that [refutation].

"In the first case, there is the proving of what is already established; in the second, there is the unestablished nature of the reason, because the production of [entities] as qualified by momentariness is what is intended.
This is the summary verse (saṅgrahaśloka).
Furthermore, that which was stated— "the lotus is the object of investigation," and so forth—
is also not consistent,

because the fragrance and other qualities of the lotus are the very nature of the lotus; that is to say, these qualities such as fragrance are capable of producing effects such as the specific cultivation of honey.

Those things which are distinguished by a particularity known as "the accomplishment of a non-distinct effect"—a term well-known through words such as "smell" and so forth, which denote a general state of being the means for accomplishing a non-distinct effect—are described in this way.
However, there is no other substance here possessing the characteristics previously described; for it has already been stated that such a thing is not perceived.
Thus, in this manner, these [terms] serve to exclude that [substance].
Furthermore, that which excludes them is not absolutely distinct [from them]; thus, what contradiction could there be between these two?

Consequently, the reason (*hetu*) has an exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) that is doubtful; it is unestablished in its necessary connection (*pratibandha*), for there is no proof established by a mere example alone.
Furthermore, because it would entail the absurd consequence [of identity] for all things;

moreover, even in the case of the statement "the body of a stone statue is the nature of form," since there exists the exclusion of the nature of the body from both the stone statue and the form, a difference between those two would also follow from that [exclusion], yet no such difference exists.
Because it would entail the consequence of [all things] lacking intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*),
you must clearly state that this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by means of this very point.

Furthermore, why do these words— such as "the fragrance and so forth of a blue lotus"— proceed based solely on the actual reality of the object, independent of the operation of a person's intention, [as claimed] by those who are excessively discursive and whose intellects are possessed by the demon of passion for false views?

Or, do they express that object by means of non-existence (*asatkāra*) exactly as it is employed by them, regardless of the actual reality of the thing? If the first alternative is held, then there would be the consequence of always expressing what exists; furthermore, there could be no application [of words] to the past and so forth, nor to other things based on human will, and there would be no engagement with the meanings found in the various different scriptural traditions.

Furthermore, there would be no speech whatsoever that lacks a true referent; otherwise, for those [schools] for whom words possess a real object, they would not be dependent on the speaker’s intention.
This is logical for those who raise objections regarding the distinction of the genitive case and so forth,
as they have said:
"For those whose words are determined by the nature of things themselves, and do not depend on the speaker's intention."
The objections regarding the difference in the expression of the number six and so forth are logically consistent [with our position].
(9) In whatever way a word is employed by speakers as a designator, that speech is a designator of that very thing, regardless of its external referent. (10)

In that case, the true nature of the object would not be established by the force of words proceeding from the power of human intention; thus, the reason remains in a state where its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful.

By this, the following argument is also refuted: "We maintain that the color, taste, smell, touch, and qualities such as being fit for abandonment (in sandalwood) are other than the sandalwood that has become the subject of dispute, because they are designated [as such], like a stone, a scale, a *tulā*, a *āḍhaka*, or a *prasevikā*."
Therefore, it is established that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever to demonstrate its existence;
for us, however, this is the means of valid cognition that establishes the proof of its non-existence:
those things whose bodies are embraced by an abiding nature that excludes one another do not appropriate a distinct excellence of self in the form of a continuous substance consisting of parts.

Just as there are many things such as ashes, stones, and saliva, so too are threads and the like possessed of the nature (dharma) as it has been taught; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), there are things such as lotuses in the sky, because they lack that essential nature.

If one does not admit a single essential nature even for those things that are mutually distinct, then the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is that it is impossible for that [single nature] to subsist in them either in its entirety or in any other manner.

For how could that [entity]—which exists simultaneously in many places with its entire essence—be considered to have an undivided nature, given that it leads one to infer a plurality of selves, just as a supported object situated upon multiple supports is manifold? Furthermore, at the moment a single part is perceived, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of perceiving the whole, since the whole is entirely contained therein. If perception occurs through the perception of multiple parts, then even when only a few parts are seen, the whole would be perceived; yet if perception occurs only through the perception of all parts, there would be the undesirable consequence of never perceiving it at any time.
Furthermore, it must be stated that since its luminous middle parts are not perceived simultaneously,

and because if one part were to vibrate, it would follow that the whole vibrates and so forth; nor can it be [composed] of a single part, as that would entail the consequence of it having constituent parts.

Furthermore, because it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress regarding its parts—since those too would have parts, and for those parts residing in the hand, yet other parts would have to reside there, and so on—it follows that no single whole exists that is devoid of other constituent parts. Therefore, let it simply be a collection of atoms and the like; what is the insistence on [a whole] existing in its own constituent parts?

"Or rather, that [whole] does not exist anywhere at all, for the parts are not individually the whole; enough with these established false prattlings!"—having thus desisted, and considering that this position of the opponent, when thoroughly scrutinized, undergoes dissolution like a fragment of a rock on the Himalayas struck by the intense rays of the sun, he said:
"Why postulate another entity? (3a1).
Since it might be argued that for another [opponent], there is no such thing as multiple things performing a single purposeful action, he says:
"For even many... and so forth;
[the question being] "like what?"

The meaning is as follows: just as the eye and so forth—namely, form, light, mental attention, and the eye—produce a single visual consciousness, so too will form and the other factors perform a single purposeful action (arthakriyā), such as the specific act of holding water.

Since this is the case, we consider it logical that for the sake of indicating that capacity for a single purposeful action, there may be the application of a single term, such as "cloth," to those [factors] like form and the rest.
The word "also" (api) indicates that it is not only their performance of a single purposeful action [that establishes their identity].
If one asks, "How is this logical?

the following is intended: certain words are applied to certain things for some specific purpose; in that regard, whatever is manifold and yet serves a single function must necessarily be enjoined there as a single entity.
Furthermore, if there were a separate injunction for each [object], it would result in excessive prolixity;

nor is it possible to enjoin a form that is not shared by others, nor does this effort yield any fruit. Rather, by this [injunction], only those objects suitable for that [action] are to be enjoined, and whether they are enjoined by a single word or by many is a matter of the speaker’s autonomy in this regard.
Thus, this single word, being employed among many things according to the intention of the speaker, does not deserve censure;
nor is its employment impossible, because it is dependent upon the will [of the speaker].
For if there were no desire on the part of the user, how could this word function even with respect to a single object?
Or, even if there were a desire [to use multiple words], who would be capable of binding them all together?

Nor should it be suspected that there is no application because of a lack of purpose, for it has already been stated that the cognition from a single word may occur even with respect to distinct [individuals] according to the difference in those purposes. Therefore, we consider what we have said to be well-stated and appropriate.
If it is argued that this is not tenable because people employ words in some way or another even without a purpose, he says:
"And the employment of words by people toward objects is not without purpose. (3a1)

For this is not a calamity for the world that one does not employ [the word] "end" (*anta*) with respect to sound (*śabda*); rather, every undertaking of his is dependent upon a purpose (*prayojana*), and he considers that this very purpose has already been stated. In that regard, "by way of having a purpose" means that just as form, smell, taste, and so forth, when combined, have a single purpose and perform a single function.

Even when [causes] are assembled, there might arise the suspicion that at some time the operation toward the effect belongs to only one of them while another remains indifferent; therefore, he says "or separately" (pṛthak vā),
where the word "vā" has the sense of "and" (ca).
The meaning is that all [entities] indeed possess activity;
however, others explain it otherwise and refute that previous explanation.

In this regard, within the process of conveying meaning through words, there are objects such as form and so forth, which possess either a common purpose collectively or separate purposes individually. Regarding these combined forms and so forth, when they are arranged in a configuration with a broad base and a rounded belly, their single common purpose is the fetching of honey, water, and the like; or alternatively, their individual purposes consist in each one generating a cognition of its own specific form.

That single purpose observed in one instance does not exist elsewhere; thus, because even things existing together are sometimes seen to be indifferent (inactive), the phrase "or separately" is stated in order to demonstrate that all [factors] possess activity.
Others maintain that the word "or" (*vā*) implies a conjunction (*samuccaya*).

However, since they state that these [words] have only a single purpose here, the understanding that all of them possess that same nature certainly exists; thus, the phrase "or separately" (*pṛthak vā*) would be redundant. Furthermore, this is not the literal meaning of the word, so this argument is trivial.

For they have not grasped the context; for in this case, the intention was to explain how there is no contradiction in applying the singular number (*ekavacana*) to a collective term (*samudāya-śabda*).

In that case, what occasion is there for stating that [the word] is distinct? This word "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth is merely a genus-word (*jāti-śabda*); and in that regard, the grammatical operation will indeed be of a different kind.

As for the claim that because it is stated here that they have "only one purpose," there is indeed the perception of all [the gods] as being likewise [engaged], that too is not logically consistent; for instance, although those intent on defeating an enemy force may share a single purpose, not all of them are necessarily active therein—
so it would be in this case as well.
And for this very reason, it has been explained that the possibility of such a doubt arises;
however, when the phrase "or separately" (*pṛthak vā*) is stated in order to demonstrate that all [factors] possess activity, then the denial is removed.
By this very [explanation], the claim that [the word] lacks a meaning is also refuted; thus, this [objection] is quite trivial.

Or let this interpretation also stand, if it can somehow be established: if a single word such as "jar" were employed to indicate those various kinds of objects which perform that single purposeful action of that entity, then what would be the consequence? There would be no fault whatsoever; rather, only a benefit would be obtained. Thus he says:

There is no contradiction whatsoever with the use of the singular number for the collective term (*samudāya-śabda*) which is employed to indicate that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*) is non-different [among its members].
Why?
Because that single, non-different power belongs to them when they are combined; it does not belong to each one individually—that is to say, it does not belong to those things when they are separate.

Thus, in that case, when a collective entity such as a single jar or a collection [of jars] is to be expressed by that collective word, the singular number occurs—as in "jar" (ghaṭaḥ)—and the remaining verb would be "there would be" (syāt), or rather, the verbal action to be mentioned later [is "there would be"].
If it is asked: "But surely this word 'jar' and so forth is a genus-word (*jāti-śabda*) like the word 'cow' and others; how then can this [singular usage] be explained?"

This is not a fault, for the intention is that this term "genus" (*jāti*) is used with respect to its occurrence within a distinct collection, whereas it is also a term for a "collection" (*samudāya*) with respect to its constituent members such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
For indeed, there are only three ways [words function]: some words are exclusively genus-terms, such as the word "pleasure" (*sukha*) and the like, because pleasure and so forth lack parts.
Some, however, are exclusively collective terms, such as the words *Vindhya*, *Himavat*, and *Sumeru*, because there exists no other collection belonging to that same class;
others, moreover, are terms for both a genus and a collection.

Just as these very words such as "jar" and so forth [function] in relation to the constituents of another aggregate, thus has the non-contradiction regarding the application of number in the case of aggregate-words been explained; now, he asks: "How then [is it] in the case of genus-words? and says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "In the case of genus-words" (3a3):
because the capacity of objects such as jars exists both individually and collectively, there is both a manifold capacity and a single [capacity].
What is meant by this is that since even a single tree is capable of performing purposeful actions such as providing shelter, so too are many trees.

Furthermore, because those [atoms] are individually capable, there is a plurality of powers; yet, even when they are combined, they possess a single power. This is due to the metaphorical attribution of unity based on their being the cause of a single reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) and a single cognition.

Since this is so, then accordingly, when there is an intention to express multiple powers, the plural number is used—such as "trees" (*vṛkṣāḥ*)—because of the multiplicity of powers. However, when there is an intention to express a single power, the word takes the singular number because of its unity. Thus it should be understood.
Therefore, if this rule is maintained by you— whose minds are agitated by the possession of the demon of false attachment— that the plural number occurs only when many things are to be expressed,
and the singular number occurs only when one thing is to be expressed;

Therefore, by this [rule], even when this view is adopted— that "the plural occurs in the case of many" (Pāṇini 1.4.21) and "the dual and singular occur in the case of two and one" (Pāṇini 1.4.22)— [the following is established].
22. Thus, he shows that even then there is no fault whatsoever; and as for how it is for you [the opponent], he says "for us" (asmākam), etc. (3a4).

By the power of convention (*saṃketa*), words ending in the plural number—such as *dārāḥ* (wife), *sikatāḥ* (sand), *pādāḥ* (feet), and *guravaḥ* (teachers)—function even when there is no plurality in the referent; likewise, despite the absence of multiplicity, words ending in the singular—such as *ṣaṇṇagarī* (the six cities), *ṣaṭpūlī* (six bundles), and *vanam* (forest)—function. Thus, one should simply remain free from dogmatic insistence.
The sense is: what conscious person indeed would venture to insist upon words whose operation depends solely upon the mere intention of a speaker?

Thus, he treats the opponent's position as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), saying: "If it is argued that multiple [factors] such as color and so forth are not capable of producing a single word... (3a5).

The refutation begins with the words "For it is not logical for many [things] to have a connection with one," and so forth. The activity of persons is their desire; in that regard, being independent, do objects themselves produce words?
Alternatively, there is a twofold dilemma: are these [words] employed by persons for the sake of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) in relation to objects in whatever way they please?

In this regard, the point is that they are indeed employed by persons according to their own will; otherwise, there would be no application of past or born things to different philosophical systems or elsewhere. Consequently, if objects were to produce words independently of human intention, one might consider whether an entity possesses the capacity or lacks the capacity [to do so]; however, this is not the case, as shown by the verse beginning with "nāmaika... (name is one...).
If it is argued that there is indeed self-arising, [the author] says:
"And that is not tenable," because of the three reasons just mentioned; such is the intended meaning.

Therefore, since those persons have the power to assign those words to objects even without [grammatical categories] such as singularity and so forth, those persons may, according to their will, employ a word ending in the plural even for a single thing, or a word ending in the singular even for many things. What reproach, then, can there be against them regarding those words? [The objection that] "a non-unitary object such as color and so forth is not capable of producing a single word" is not valid at all; rather, one considers it to be merely the manifestation of excessive delusion.
One might ask: "Why would they assign a single word to many [objects]? To this he says:

Since the reason for the restriction has already been stated, [the author] provides further reinforcement at this juncture— beginning with "Moreover" (api ca)— in order to demonstrate its efficacy by showing that there might even be a restriction of a single word in that case.
By the phrase "by that which is accepted as the substratum," it is meant by the composite substance (*avayavidravya*), because they are connected to it through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).
How could there not be a connection? For it is accepted as a contradiction that a plurality [of things] should have a connection with a single [thing].
The opponent says: "Otherwise, it would follow that [the term] applies even to a single word"; his intention is this.
And we do not accept the application of a single word to color-form and the other [sensory objects], because of the contradiction in its connection with a single [referent]. This is the reason.

However, there is a contradiction regarding this manifold purposeful activity— such as holding water, covering, and so forth— which belongs to color and other qualities that are non-different and indistinguishable [from one another] in objects such as jars, blankets, and couches; for thus,
by the very fact of its manifestation through capacity, there is a contradiction with the word [which denotes them as identical].
And there is no difference between them because there is no difference in the substance that serves as their substratum.
He clarifies this very point:

those [factors] such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, being of a single nature, would perform that same purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*)—such as the specific capacity to hold water—which is impossible in another collection like a woolen blanket (*kambala*). For that reason, by the manifestation of that purposeful activity, these [factors] do not perform that other impossible purposeful activity.

Just as those very colors and so forth belonging to a woolen blanket are [distinguished] from their own kind, so too the colors and so forth belonging to a jar possess a nature no different from the colors and so forth belonging to the woolen blanket; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
This same logic should be applied elsewhere as well; such is the formulation of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
To this, he states the following reply beginning with "Let it be so" (bhavatu nāma) and so forth;
by this, he points out the unestablished nature (asiddhi) of the reason (hetu).

This is the meaning here: there is indeed no non-difference among color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory qualities] in things such as a blanket, because they are determined by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) precisely as being mutually distinct in their nature.
And this being so, why would this direct perception disregard either this [quality] or that?
In what sense? Is it as a question or as a censure? It certainly does not deserve to be endured, for [the opponent] refutes it.

Furthermore, what is undesirable here is this: that we [hold] form and the other qualities to be non-different from the pot, the blanket, and so forth. Why? Because, by the force of the reason [adduced] regarding the collection of form and the others, one must admit their own internal distinctions, even while disregarding the substance.
Thus, by means of this admission, he also points out the lack of proof (*asiddhatā*).
The distinction is that [the cognition occurs] through the door of direct perception as before;
yet again, another person, being envious, asks: "If the jar were indeed something other than its form and so forth, what would happen?"
The intention is that no fault would arise;
we do not refuse it out of stinginess,
but rather because there is this much that must be said here, he says:
Since that whole (avayavin), being perceptible, is admitted to be graspable by the sense organs of sight and touch,
it follows that it would lack the nature of color and so forth— that is, it would be devoid of the intrinsic nature of color, odor, and the rest—
because a distinction between qualities (guṇa) and substances (dravya) is admitted.

The meaning is that by means of its distinction from those [qualities], just as by the distinction from color and so forth, there is no obscuration whatsoever—no impediment—to its appearing in the cognition produced by the visual and tactile faculties. Furthermore, he thinks that even one who possesses unimpeded sense organs and investigates with great care is not able to perceive a substance such as a jar as having a distinct form apart from its blue, sweet, fragrant, or hard nature. Abhidharmakarṇa, however, says:

Even when color and other qualities are not perceived, the apprehension of the substance itself certainly exists; for in very dim light, a substance is perceived even while its color and other qualities remain unperceived, such that one cannot determine whether it is "a cow" or "a horse" due to its indeterminate form.
Now, is it not the case that in that instance too only the configuration (saṃsthāna) is perceived?
True, it is perceived, but it is not perceived as being identical in nature with color and the other qualities.
Alternatively, if it were of the nature of form and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving specific qualities such as blue or yellow;

likewise, in the case of a person inside an iron cage, even though the person's form and other qualities are not perceived, the cognition of a "person" is observed, and at night, even when the form and other qualities of a bird perched on a crane's beak are not perceived, the cognition of a "bird" is observed.
Just as there is a cognition of a crystal even when its own form is not apprehended— due to the crystal following the distinctions of adjuncts such as blue—
and just as a cognition of a cloth is observed even when the cloth's own form is not apprehended because its form is overwhelmed by a reddish dye,
all of this speech merely reveals the manifestation of a dullness of intellect born from the long-term habituation to false views.

For instance, regarding what was said—that even when there is very dim light at night and in the presence of a blue or other colored substrate, the substance is perceived even though its color and so forth are not grasped—it must be asked: what kind of substance is perceived there? If it is argued that "it is indeed seen exactly as it is perceived," [we reply: surely, in very dim light and at night, what is perceived there is the dark color of the substrate itself.
Nor does it possess that form,
because if it did, the faults of the positions just mentioned would follow,
and because it is not perceived as such by those standing nearby or at its side.

Nor can there be an apprehension of a real object by means of a cognition that does not possess its form; for if that were so, it would follow that any cognition whatsoever would be the determiner of all objects.

Therefore, this cognition is erroneous. Due to its own material cause—the seed of error existing from beginningless time—it arises as something appearing in such a way despite being entirely devoid of an object, like the perception of two moons.
Even though it is objectless, it occurs at specific places and times.
Because it depends upon an external dominant condition that awakens the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) of its own material cause,
there is no discrepancy with the object despite its being erroneous— just like the cognition of two moons— due to the presence of a specific dominant condition.
Just as there is an illusion of a jewel in the light of a jewel,

it is not logical that this [cognition] possesses an object merely because of its non-contradiction with reality, since there is a deviation by means of inference and by way of the illusion of a jewel.
If it is argued that the substance itself is apprehended in such a way that everything else becomes objectless, we reply:
indeed, it has already been stated that a substance is not of that nature, nor can a cognition permeated by one form be the determiner of another.
This being the case, even if there is dependence [on other factors], the state of having a real object (sadviṣayatva) certainly remains.

For it can be stated thus: those very [atoms] such as blue appear in that way, provided there is no cause for error or doubt, they are situated in a suitable location during the state of being illuminated, and they are in a state free from external adjuncts (*nirupadhāna*). That substance is not perceived at other times with an appearance of a nature other than its own, when distinguished [from others], except when there is a cause for error or doubt—such as when the eyes are covered by the darkness of night, when one is situated in a distant place, or when there is an external adjunct; in those cases, it appears with a distinction from the form of another. Who, then, more than a materialist (*bhautika*) would be able to say otherwise?
The cognition of a person within an iron casing is not perceptual;
rather,
it is inferential.

For instance, from the perception of a cloak situated in a specific configuration produced by the power residing in the parts of a human body, there arises immediately after the cognition—based on the mark of an effect and dependent upon the recollection of the relationship—the conviction that "this is a person" regarding such a causal individual.
For this very reason, that cognition possesses an indistinct form, and a doubt arises as to who this person might be.
Furthermore, since a cloak of such a configuration arises, the causes are simply the color and other qualities of the person, and not some other composite substance (*avayavidravya*).
Because that [entity] is unestablished, and it is impossible to accept the causal status of something unestablished;
whereas the causal relationship between form and so forth is established through perception and non-perception,
since they alone are perceived when arranged in such a manner.

In the case of a cloth, however, due to contact with substances such as *kaṣāya* or *mañjiṣṭhā*, that very [cloth] is seen to have become something entirely different; it is not, however, a perception resulting from the inseparable conjunction of two substances possessing distinct forms. Furthermore, the cessation of that [color-change] occurs through the severance of the causes for the persistence of the substance's configuration.
Furthermore, since water, fire, and so forth arise from other causes that depend upon their respective material bases (*upādāna-kāraṇa*),
this also clearly refutes the claim that "the cognition of that [fire] is observed even when the iron ball and its color are perceived.

Thus, since the perceptibility of a substance (*dravya*) is not established, the proclamation that "cows, horses, buffaloes, boars, and elephants— which have become the subjects of dispute— are distinct from color and the rest," is merely a hollow cry.
"Because, while being perceptible by the senses, it is not delimited by the sense-faculties that grasp all [objects] such as form—as in the case of pleasure and so forth"—this [argument] is refuted.
Furthermore, the formal arguments are as follows:
whatever is visible and is not perceived apart from existence (sat) must either be admitted not to be distinct from that [existence], or else it must be admitted not to exist at all.

Just as a horn is not perceived on a human head, so too—though it would be visible—universals, particulars, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and so forth are not perceived apart from blue and other such qualities; this is a non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
Its establishment is not [impossible], because its visibility is itself admitted.

Likewise, a substance (*dravya*) accepted as distinct from the five objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth cannot be determined by visual cognition; for, while it is accepted as meeting the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), it lacks the nature of entities such as blue and so on, just like sound, smell, or taste. Nor is this [substance] non-distinct from those [objects]; and in that case, this same fault [of imperceptibility] would follow. Having anticipated this objection, he says:

This excellence, characterized by exclusion, is non-concomitant with its substratum—the possessor of that excellence—since it is essentially identical to it; thus, while it necessarily ceases [in one state], because it lacks pervasiveness, how could it not, when it occurs [in another state], bring about a plurality of natures as surely as pleasure and pain do?
The meaning is that it certainly does bring it about.

Furthermore, the application (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which is the very essence (*ātmabhūta*) of something necessarily ceases when that thing ceases, and it proceeds only when that thing proceeds—just as the nature (*ātman*) of a particular excellence (*atiśaya*) is the possessor of that excellence (*atiśayavat*). This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Consequently, between those two states, there is a difference in the state-possessor (*avasthātṛ*), because they are occupied by mutually contradictory [attributes], just like pleasure and pain; this too is precisely a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

If it is argued that "an excellence (*atiśaya*) that is not accompanied by a causal continuity (*ananvaya*) neither proceeds nor ceases; therefore, in the former case [of the opponent's argument], the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*), while in the latter case, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*)," he replies:
"If the cessation and proceeding of an excellence are admitted to be accompanied by a causal continuity, then what is the cessation of what, or what is the proceeding of what? (4b4)

The intention is that no cessation or commencement whatsoever belongs to anything, because everything exists at all times; and thus, the previously mentioned fault— that everything would be applicable everywhere— does not apply.

He states the objection: "If you yourself admit that there is the occurrence or cessation of some intrinsic nature (svabhāva) called 'excellence' (atiśaya), because you assert that the distinction in conventional usage arises through the cessation of one excellence and the production of another excellence— then this very point is what the opponent, whose intellect has been purified by the repeated study of the Tathāgata’s words, is stating."

The "Noble-faced One" (Bhadramukha) does not agree, thinking: "If it were as I maintain—that activity and cessation are permitted—then by that [opponent] as well, because the arising and destruction of a substance are admitted to be without residue (*niranvaya*), it would not appear as distinct from those [qualities], just like light or blue, or because it is perceptible by the same sense faculty, it would be just like them. To this he says:

"And things are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as appearing with distinction, such as 'this is blue,' 'this is fragrant,' 'sweet,' or 'rough'"; and what are these [things], namely form (*rūpa*) and so forth, even though they do not occupy separate locations?
This was stated according to worldly convention, for they do not occupy the same location, as it is said in the *Abhidharmakośa* (1.29): "The ten material elements are characterized by resistance."

"Likewise, even though they are apprehended by non-distinct sense faculties, [there are] wind, sunlight, touch, and so forth"—this is the response in due order. By this, he demonstrates the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason (*hetu*).

Furthermore, having granted the connection with the subject (*dharmin*), the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of "being apprehended by non-distinct sense faculties" has been stated; however, that [reason] does not actually exist [in the subject], because it is unestablished in one part (*ekadeśāsiddhi*).
How so?
Because fragrant, sweet, and other such qualities are not perceivable by the sense organs that perceive substance,
for if they were, it would follow that a single substance is perceptible by all the senses.

However, in the case of light, blue, and so forth, there is indeed no difference; for, due to the proximity of a lamp or similar source, they arise as having the nature of illumination, their bodies being infused with such an intrinsic nature, and thus no distinction exists between them. Therefore, it is considered that the example is also devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikalpa*).

Consequently, those who accept its perceptibility must necessarily admit that it appears externally through a distinct separation from color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest; otherwise, its perceptibility would not be established.
As for the phrase "from which this very [object]," and so forth, it is easily understood.
Furthermore, this jar and so forth, which you accept as being distinct from form and the other [sensory qualities]— what is this thing that buys without paying its price?
By this, he explains that such a thing does not enter into the path of worldly convention.

He does not show his own nature through exaggeration, yet he wishes to accept its non-appearance and its imperceptibility, because of the reading in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "substance is both visible and tangible. This [point] should be supplied as: "friends who have internal love for the Self will believe this. The commentary states: "one who buys by paying a price" (*mūlyadānakrayī*) is not like that.
Alternatively, one who has the habit of buying is a buyer; a buyer is one who purchases by means of giving a price.
To explain how this is not so, he says:
"That which is perceptibility," and so forth.
And here, he mocks [the opponent] by stating that the "giving of the price" is actually the surrendering of one's own nature.
Now, if it is argued: "Surely that [universal] exists, because the cognition and designation 'one jar' exist, just like color and other qualities;
so how can it be non-existent?"—to this he replies with the words beginning, "The intellect, the word, and so forth have also been explained, and not all... and so on.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), its distinctions and non-distinctions are included;
if the establishment of its proof is accepted through those [factors] such as cognition and designation,
then it might be argued that even though a substance is manifesting, it is not perceived— just like the taste of sugar when the salty taste has been overcome.
Therefore, in order to establish that [point], a logical mark (*liṅga*) is stated; thus he says:
"And it is not reasonable for the form of an object that is directly perceived to be unobserved, provided it is not overwhelmed by another substance."
But in the case of overpowering, it is indeed appropriate,
as in the case of the taste of sugar-candy and the like;
however, in this instance, there is no overpowering by anything whatsoever.
If it is argued that [the object] exists by virtue of its blue color and so forth, [we reply:
perception occurs only when there is magnitude (*mahat*), possession of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattā*), and color (*rūpa*).
Thus, it has been stated that non-perception occurs due to the absence of the formation of such color.
And if that [whole] were not perceived, it would follow that those [parts] too would not be perceived;
and consequently, because all objects would remain unperceived, the very cessation of worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*) would result.
This is what is thought when a mark (*liṅga*) is stated for the sake of proving that whole by means of its non-perception.

If it were accepted that a logical mark (liṅga) exists which establishes its existence, then that would have to be stated; however, there is no such indicative mark whatsoever that makes it known, as was previously explained.
To the objection that "it certainly exists even in the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes it," he says:
Since it is improper to accept the existence of that which lacks a means of valid cognition even when it is not perceived,
by the phrase "of that which lacks a means of valid cognition," he states the absence of any means of valid cognition other than perception to establish it;
for one must admit that whatever lacks a means of valid cognition to prove its existence does not exist.

Just as one considers non-apprehension to have the result of negating the conventional usage of existence— thinking that there is no lotus in the sky and that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishing the existence of a whole (*avayavin*)—
so too, having demonstrated in detail the absence of a single substance, he concludes the present topic with the words "Therefore," and so forth.
He concludes the main treatise as well with the words "In this way, first... (evantāvad i) and so forth;
for this very reason, there is no reversal—meaning the non-existence—of those [properties] such as existence (*sattā*) due to a reversal of those [entities] such as cognition (*buddhi*).
The underlying intention is this: how can that which does not establish the very existence of something establish its absence while it is occurring?
Even if cognition and so forth do not establish existence, difference, or non-difference, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) will nonetheless establish them; therefore, he says:
"But the conventional usage of 'existence' would arise from causal efficiency," because existence is defined by that [causal efficiency]. This is the sense.
By this, he shows that there is indeed equality between the two of us in this matter;
however, he states that "there is disagreement elsewhere" regarding the conventional usage of difference and non-difference in existence (*sattā*).
How so? Because even a single thing is observed to perform multiple functions;
in that case, nothing exists that is produced by a single condition alone. Therefore, how can it be said [that there is no such thing]?
This is true; however, because a single entity exists within many causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), it is said to be a "performer of multiple functions."
As it has been said:
"Nothing arises from a single [cause]; rather, everything arises from a causal complex (sāmagrī).
Even for that which is single, [it arises] from two complexes; thus it is stated that [the cause] produces many. (11)
How is it so?

Just as in the case of a lamp—namely, the production of a modification of the wick, a subsequent flame, and other moments connected to its own and another's continuum—so too, in the absence of a conventional distinction between different entities, how can one cause produce multiple effects? This is the question.
