The masters of the *Nyāyatattva* maintain that because such a single entity produces multiple effects, its form is embraced by an excellence of power (*turyātiśaya*), since it has arisen from its own causes; likewise, since even multiple things such as the eyes and so forth are observed to perform the single action of cognition,
this is the reason for the absence of the conventional usage of non-difference.
Those whose intellects have been perverted by the doctrine of Kaṇabhuj (the Vaiśeṣika) say:

"We do not say [that there is a difference in existence based on the difference in the action of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)], but rather that there is a difference in existence due to the difference in the action of the unseen force. Thus they proceed.
He clarifies that very point:
the causal efficiency (arthakriyā) characterized by the fetching of honey and so forth, which was not observed in that [first] jar and the like, is seen again in another jar and the like.
In this manner, that very existence establishes the distinction among those things such as jars; by this, what kind of pervasion has been stated?

The connection with the subject at hand is as follows: just as the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyā), such as holding water, which is not observed in a cloth but is observed in a jar, establishes a difference in existence (sattābheda);

and this is stated by way of an example, showing that while the causal efficiency of covering and so forth is not observed in the threads, it is observed in the cloth—this constitutes the demonstration of the property of the subject (pakṣadharma).
Therefore, it follows that the difference in existence between the threads and the cloth is established;
by this, the result of the proof has been stated,
and this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), because the difference in existence is invariably concomitant with the performance of a distinct purposeful action.
By this, the Master, while establishing the difference of the cloth from the threads, intends to prove the existence of a composite whole (*avayavin*) as a distinct entity; however, he replies:
"In this way, a difference in their *sattā* (existence) between the threads and the cloth is indeed established," thus returning to the subject at hand.

Intending to show that the accomplishment of your desired object does not exist at all, he says: "Nevertheless, the whole (avayavin) is not established" (3b7). Why is this? Because, according to the conditions, within this continuum of formations (saṃskārasaṃtati), due to the arising of a difference in intrinsic nature (svabhāvabheda), there occurs a difference in causal efficiency (arthakriyā) characterized by such things as covering. What is meant is this: from the threads acting as the material cause (upādānakāraṇa) when they are gathered together, and through the presence of auxiliary conditions (sahakāripratyaya) such as the weaver and so forth, the threads themselves arise as delimited by a specific configuration (viśiṣṭasaṃniveśa).
We also certainly accept that the cloth is distinct from those preceding threads which are employed in performing functions such as providing a covering;

however, it is not distinct from those [threads] as delimited by a specific configuration. Therefore, let this hope for establishing the existence of a "whole" (avayavin) as a separate entity be abandoned.
Therefore, by this very [argument], it should be understood that the proof stated by Aviddhakarṇa— beginning with "because of occurring at prior and subsequent times," and so forth— is refuted;
for we have already set forth our own argument in detail previously, and thus it need not be restated here.
"How is it that there is a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) due to the arising of a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) based on conditions?
To this he says, "From the friction of the fire-drill," and so forth. Having presented the well-known example, he states the point to be illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*).
Likewise, regarding the passage beginning with "tathā yathā" (3b8),

by this very distinction of the intrinsic nature according to conditions (*yathā-pratyaya-svabhāva-bheda*), some raise the following objection: "But surely, because of the difference between cognition and designation, [the threads are not the cloth]."
With the intention of showing how its difference [from other things] does not exist and how that [objection] has been refuted, he says:
"By this, the distinction between cognition and designation is explained.

(3b8) This being the case, as for what was previously stated by you—that the conventional usage of "existent" is established through causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and conversely, when there is a cessation of causal efficiency, the opposite conventional usage of "non-existent" follows—this is true.
We say this much:
that very same [logical] reversal does not establish itself regarding those things that have reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).

For instance, if you do not accept this non-perception of what has reached the conditions for perception, then how have you understood that this [thing] lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*)?
Nor is it logical to say "not from mere non-perception," because that is fallacious; for in that case, [the consequence] follows for you even against your will.

If it is argued: "That which possesses this capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perception; therefore, it is the object of the conventional usage of non-existence (*asadvyavahāraviṣaya*).
Since existence is characterized by such capacity, let it be so—what is the fault? To this, he says:
Nevertheless, there would be a distinction between this non-perception of capacity—which you have postulated—and the previously described perception of what is perceptible;
for that was a non-perception of the very nature [of the object], whereas this is a non-perception of its capacity. To this, he says:
"Not indeed," and so forth;

likewise, the non-perception of that capacity is itself the non-perception of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, this non-perception of capacity is nothing other than the aforementioned non-perception of intrinsic nature.
Consequently, it is established that only the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is the means for establishing the conventional usage of non-existence.

And because this is so, the meaning is that this proponent, when accepting the conventional usage of "non-existent" in regard to something like a rabbit's horn, must accept it as being due to the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*), since there is no other means for its cognition.

Therefore, that non-perception applies without distinction to other such things as universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and composite substances (*avayavidravya*), provided they meet the conditions for perceptibility; thus, those universals and so forth also exist in that way, in the sense that they are objects of the conventional usage of "non-existent."

It might be argued that such things as universals and particulars are not perceived in that manner, and therefore they cannot be the objects of the conventional usage of "existent"; to this he replies:
nor should the conventional usage of "non-existent" be accepted in any case, such as with a rabbit's horn, because there is no distinction in the nature of non-perception.

The meaning here is as follows: even though the non-apprehension of two things is equal regarding their respective causes, if the conventional designation of "non-existent" does not arise with respect to a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth, then it should not be accepted in other cases either, because there is no distinguishing cause; by this, he reminds us of what was stated previously—that if one accepts something as non-existent, it is because there is no difference in its defining characteristic. Therefore, every such non-apprehension of the perceptible is the object of the conventional designation of "non-existent"; this is the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
The phrase "is established" is to be supplied when [the term] "non-perception" occurs; however,
the followers of Kapila say:

Everything indeed consists of everything; otherwise, if jars, curds, sprouts, and so forth did not exist even in the form of potentiality within a lump of clay, milk, a seed, and so on, then how could they ever arise from those?
For a non-existent rabbit’s horn does not emerge from there.

And this being the case, their position is that even if some object such as a jar is not perceived despite being visible, it does not become an object of the conventional usage of "non-existence" in any place or by any means, such as through a particular configuration. This is their view.
Who other than this Sāṅkhya beast would seek to say, with a sense of shame,
"There exists [something] never before seen— a hundred elephants on the tip of a blade of grass"? (Pramāṇavārttika, Chapter 2, Verse 12).
With this intention, he says "of everything" (sarvasya) and so forth;

the meaning is that if even that which is unperceived exists therein, then all things such as milk and the like would perform the purposeful action to be accomplished by them, because they would be endowed with all forms such as jars and so on.
Furthermore, this other point would not exist: that this effect, such as curd and so forth, arises from this cause, such as milk, and not from anything else, such as water;

or that this honey and so forth does not arise from this milk, and likewise this saffron and so forth occurs here in the land of Kashmir and not here in the land of Mālava; or that this sandalwood and so forth is not found here, and likewise this jasmine and so forth occurs now in the cold season and not at this time in the summer heat.

Alternatively, this should be explained as follows: "This is not a lotus and so forth; rather, this is a sugar-candy and the like, distinguished by qualities such as sweetness; it is not of such a form as bitter [pungent] things, or else, this is not a neem tree and so forth, but rather such [a thing]."

For what reason is this so? To this he says: "Of nothing whatsoever," and so forth. This means that because there is an absence—the discernment (*viveka*)—that this kind of form does not exist for it at present, there is an absence of the cause for that [form].
The view is that [the universal] persists at all times in all forms of everything.

If it is asked: "But was this not already stated in substance immediately prior, in the passage 'everything would be applicable everywhere and at all times'? Why, then, is this being chewed over again?"—it is true; however, there is no fault, because the former [statement] described the operation residing in the cause, whereas the present one describes that residing in the effect; thus, due to this distinction, there is no defect.
Furthermore, this statement of refutation is made by way of one of these alternatives for the sake of instructing the disciple;
consequently, the analysis is: "that in which, due to the absence of difference, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) do not exist.
Here, "this exists here" and so forth constitutes positive concomitance, while "this does not exist" constitutes negative concomitance.
The opponent says with the words beginning "avasthā" (state),
etc.; this is what is meant:

"Where something is manifested, it is conventionally expressed as 'it exists there,' and where it is not manifested at all, it is expressed as 'it does not exist there'; therefore, this is not a fault.
To this, the Master [Dharmakīrti] replies:
"In your view, those very distinctions between the cessation and the occurrence of states are impossible."
Why? Because there is an absence of the conventional usage of "non-existent" regarding all objects.
Furthermore, if the conventional usage of "non-existent" is nevertheless accepted in some particular case, then you must state its cause; thus he says, "In some cases," and so forth.

If, indeed, one must necessarily accept the conventional usage of "non-existent" regarding some imagined entity such as a distinct whole (*avayavin*) and so forth, that [usage] is not tenable for him because of the absence of a reason; thus he says,
"In some cases," and so on.
Why?

Because there is no means of proof other than non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) that establishes exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), which is to say absence (*abhāva*); and the implication is that such a means is not accepted by you.

Why is this so? Because, according to the formal rule (*vidhi*), when non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) alone is always the means of proof—whether in the case of the apprehension of what is contradictory to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalambha*) for a negation, or in the case of the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) for an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) as the probandum—if you say, "I too shall prove the exclusion from this very same non-apprehension," we reply to that as follows: it must be stated that "whenever that non-apprehension exists, all such things are objects of the conventional usage of non-existence (*asadvyavahāraviṣaya*)."
Why? Because there is no distinction;

for in that case, even a jar or the like is established as an object of the conventional usage of "non-existent" in certain specific locations, since such a non-perception exists here as well. So why do you say this?
The intention is that nothing whatsoever has ever been observed to be the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent.
Otherwise, the opponent [argues] that even in this case—such as with a distinct whole (*avayavin*) and so forth—the conventional usage of "non-existent" would not occur;
thus, there would be a cessation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and so on.
And thus it has been stated incorrectly that there is no cause for exclusion other than non-perception;

for if this were the case, even a jar would not be an object of the conventional usage of "non-existent" anywhere, because all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) would be absent due to the absence of both scripture and inference. This is what [the opponent] intends.
He mocks him by way of an objection, asking, "From where have you acquired such extraordinary skill in wisdom?
with the words, "O one of tender intellect," and so forth;
the reason for his being of tender intellect is that he is unable to endure the hardship of investigating the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

"Now, what is it that we have said here that is improper for you to mock? To this he says, "For indeed... and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of scripture (*āgama*) is intended.
And the fallacy [of the reason] has already been established.
To the objection that "the cessation of perception by all living beings will then lead to the inference [of non-existence]," he replies:
"Not the cessation of perception by all. (4a8)
The meaning is: "From what [is it unestablished]? Because neither oneself nor another perceives it.
For there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever here that allows for the certainty that [the object] has ceased from the perception of all people.
If it is argued that "the cessation of one's own perception alone, then, leads to the understanding [of non-existence]," he replies:
"The cessation of the specific [object] is not even perceived by oneself" (4a8).
The word "even" (*api*) implies that it is not only the previously mentioned [cessation of perception] that does so.

The analysis of the compound *aviśeṣanivṛtti* is as follows: "cessation without distinction" (*aviśeṣanivṛtti*) means the cessation of the perception of self (*ātmapratyakṣa*) without distinction; thus, it is the "cessation of the perception of self without distinction. Now, the cessation of the perception of self—which has all other proximate causes present—necessarily implies the non-existence (*abhāva*) of that which is not separated by the three types of distance (*trividhaviprakarṣa*). Therefore, the expression "not separated by distinction" (*aviśeṣaviprakṛṣṭa*) must be explained [in this way].

Since the cessation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not the cause for the conventional usage of non-existence, therefore, that specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*)— an entity whose form is not remote due to the three types of remoteness— which, through perception (*pratyakṣa*), necessarily attains or acquires the conventional usage of existence because of that perception being present and all other causes for its action and so forth being absent, it is precisely the cessation of that aforementioned means of valid cognition which establishes the conventional usage of non-existence for that specific nature; this restriction is for the purpose of excluding the cessation of inference, verbal testimony, and so on.
What is the reason? Because that specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) is pervaded by the existence of that aforementioned means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for wherever such an object exists, it must necessarily be accompanied by that means of valid cognition as well, since a capable cause does not deviate from its effect.

And thus, this means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), by its absence, excludes that [tree-ness] as well—just as the absence of a tree excludes the śiṃśapā—thereby concluding what was stated previously with the words "from the aforementioned non-perception" and so forth. It might be argued: "Even though curd and the like have reached the conditions for perception, they are not perceived by direct perception (pratyakṣa) in milk and the like; rather, their non-arising from the incapable [cause] is known through inference. Therefore, even by their absence, those [curds, etc. do not become objects of the conventional usage of 'non-existent'. To this, he says:

"If not," and so forth. [The author asks: "By what means would there be the apprehension of this through inference by way of the apprehension of another? Furthermore, why is the apprehension of another not tenable? To this he says:
And so forth;
the word "ca" (and) has the sense of "because.

The remainder of the sentence is: "The transformation—that is, the departure from the state of that form which has reached the conditions for perception—is not possible without that [transformation]; therefore, it is not logical for that entity to be imperceptible."
By this, he establishes that its perception is indeed perceptual (*pratyakṣa*), because there is no other required cause [for it] to exist; the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
whatever has all its causes present and whose capacity is unimpeded necessarily exists at that time, and it does not fail to act immediately.

Just as a sprout arises from a collection of causes whose capacities are complete and unimpeded, so too, in states such as milk and the like, there exists a cognition directed toward curds and the like that possesses the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) as previously taught; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
With respect to the second probandum, it is an observation of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

If it is argued that otherwise this reason would indeed be unestablished (*asiddha*), he replies: if a change in state (*anyathābhāva*) is admitted, then that very curd and so forth, having reached the conditions for perception, would not exist, because it has fallen away from its prior form; and thus, if it were to possess that [new] form, there would follow the consequence of destruction without residue (*niranvayavināśa*). This is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, with the words "api ca" and so forth, he states the accumulation;
the analysis of the compound is: "that which is this entity (bhāva) whose excellence of form (rūpātiśaya) is both unborn and undestroyed."

Since [the self] is eternal and of a unitary nature, perceptibility, imperceptibility, and so forth might still occur even when there is an intervention by another substance or when [the object] is situated at a distance; therefore, he says "without intervention or being situated at a distance" (avyavadhānadūrasthāna).
The analysis of the compound is: "that for which intervention and distance do not exist."
In some places, "situated at a distance" (*dūrasthāna*) is read as "without intervention" (*avyavadhānāt*).

In that case, one should first form a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) with each of the words "intervention" (*vyavadhāna*) and "situated at a distance" (*dūrasthāna*), and subsequently apply a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇa-samāsa*).
He states that there is no contradiction because something may be perceptible relative to one person while being imperceptible relative to another.

He says that there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that for that very same person, [the object] is perceptible during states such as having one's eyes open, and non-perceptible at other times; for the analysis of the compound is: "one whose sense organ (*indriya*) remains in that state—that is, unaltered—is *tadavasthendriya*."
The inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi) is intended to imply mental attention (*manaskāra*) and so forth;

for [the substance] is sometimes perceived at the time of its manifestation, and sometimes unperceived at times when it is unmanifest, such as in the case of milk and the like. It is by virtue of this perceptibility and imperceptibility that, at certain times, the apprehension of inference is impossible due to the non-arising [of the effect] from an incapable [cause], whereas at other times, during the state of manifestation, it is perceived.
If it is asked, "What is it that is illogical here, such that you speak thus? he replies:
"Because there is a contradiction among these various modes—such as being perceptible and imperceptible—with respect to a single thing like curd, which lacks any distinction [between its states]. 4b2
Those things which are mutually contradictory cannot possibly exist together in a single substrate where there is no distinction [of locus],
just as, for example, cold and hot sensations and so forth;
and [in this case] perceptibility and imperceptibility and so forth are mutually contradictory.
Thus, the opponent considers this to be the perception of a contradictory pervader; he says:
"There is no excellence" (4b3).

Since the conventional usage "milk becomes curd" is accepted through the cessation of one excellence characterized by an unmanifest state and the arising of another excellence characterized by a manifest state, [the opponent] states by this that the claim "an excellence whose form is neither born nor destroyed" is unproven.
For you do not admit that this excellence is distinct from the entity possessing the excellence; otherwise, the fault just mentioned would remain as before.

Therefore, having anticipated the objection that "this [distinction] is indeed non-different from that, and thus this fault remains," he says: "This excellence (*atiśaya*), characterized as a state (*avasthā*), being identical with the nature of its possessor (*avasthātṛ*), does not persist [throughout]. Since it ceases absolutely while arising from a pervasive nature, how is it not the case that there is a plurality of natures (*svabhāvanānātva*) in what is actually non-existent?"

The meaning is that it draws [the result] toward itself and indeed draws it along, just as one does with pleasure and pain. Furthermore, that which is the very essence (ātmabhūta) of something necessarily ceases when that thing ceases, and it proceeds only when that thing proceeds, just as the self of that very excellence (atiśaya) does.
Because that which possesses excellence (*atiśayavat*) is identical with the excellence itself, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Consequently, the substratum (*avasthātṛ*) of those two states must be distinct, because it is superimposed with mutually contradictory properties, just like pleasure and pain; thus, this too is a reason based on essential nature.
Therefore, that excellence does not proceed or cease without a causal continuity (*ananvaya*); hence, in the former proof, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
If it is argued that the reason is unestablished later on, he replies:
"And if an excellence [is admitted] to have both cessation and occurrence, then what is the cessation or occurrence of what?
(4b3) There is no cessation or occurrence of anything whatsoever.
The intention is that because everything exists at all times,
the fault previously mentioned— namely, that one would have to employ everything everywhere— is not applicable; thus he states the reinforcement.
And if you yourself admit that there is the occurrence or cessation of some intrinsic nature (svabhāva) called "excellence" (atiśaya)—
since you accept a distinction in conventional usage through the cessation of one excellence and the arising of another—
then it is precisely this [point] that the opponent, whose mind has been purified by the repeated study of the Tathāgata’s words, is stating.
[The opponent] does not agree, thinking: "If it were as I maintain—that both engagement and withdrawal are authorized—then it would be so;

however, since he accepts that for this [entity] there is arising and destruction without any substrate (niranvaya), whereas for me there is merely manifestation and disappearance, how could he possibly agree? Thus, anticipating the thought of the opponent, [the author] addresses it with the words beginning "tasya" (4b4).
"Always, you who are empty-hearted proclaim this 'succession' (anvaya); regarding that, it must be asked:
what is this so-called succession? Is it [the continuity] of an entity between its birth and destruction? To this, the opponent replies: "That is true."
What is there to be said here? For it is established that the power (*śakti*) of an entity (*bhāva*) persists through its birth and destruction.

But how is that power persistent? He says: because that power, characterized by its continued existence, exists even prior to birth and even after cessation. By this very fact, he indicates through the inclusion of the term "in every way" (*sarvathā*) that this entity does not arise as something entirely new, having previously been non-existent; rather, it was already established previously in the form of power and merely becomes manifest.
Likewise, the preceding [entity] does not perish absolutely, but rather becomes concealed; that is to say,
there is no arising of the non-existent, nor is there destruction of the existent— so says the Teacher.
If that power is always of a single nature— meaning it is devoid of any increase or decrease during the times of its concealment and manifestation—

then what is there now that possesses an excellence (*atiśaya*) such that this distinction in worldly usage (*vyavahāra-vibhāga*), such as "milk," "curd," or "buttermilk," could arise? From what source would this differentiation come?
The Sāṃkhya says: "The states possess excellence," and so forth;
this is the view of the Master [Vasubandhu].

And since no other alternative is possible, two alternatives are established: [is it] a non-distinct entity or not? A theory of external objects is not tenable because "self" and "otherness" are characterized by mutual exclusion and thus exclude a third category.
If it is asked, "What is the fault in [their] being one? he says:

If [the self] were one, then how could this [distinction between states] be consistent within that which is undivided in itself and undivided in its essential nature? He says: "It might exist through mutual dependence," but then he asks: "What then is that which is non-sequential? He replies: "Birth, because of the incapacity of states to remain [simultaneously]."
Likewise, there is the application of states toward causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), whereas there is no application for that which lacks capacity;
furthermore, there is the arising even of capacity.
Because it is not distinct from its states, [the power] lacks origination,
just like the nature of the states themselves;
or else, because the states are not distinct from the power, they likewise lack origination.
The perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory of a nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*), like the nature of power itself;

in this very same manner, the perceptions of what is pervaded by the contradictory of a nature-reason are to be applied to cases such as the cessation or non-cessation of the utility of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), falling and non-falling are also included; furthermore, he anticipates the Sāṃkhya position with the words beginning with "it exists" (asti).

"By some interpretation, there is non-difference between state (*avasthā*) and power (*śakti*), yet in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*) there is indeed difference; therefore, there is no contradiction regarding birth and the other [marks].
With the underlying intention that "surely you have forgotten even yourself, whose intellect is so unskilled at defending its own position," he said:
"Prone to forgetfulness" (4b8), etc.:

since we have stated this fault in the case of non-difference, [the opponent argues that] in the case of difference there will be an entirely different one; he begins to demonstrate what that other [fault] is.
Furthermore, if there were a distinction or even a difference between these two states of potentiality (*śakti*), then there would be no contradiction;
however, it would simply follow that the birth and destruction of an entity are not identical with it.
What is the reason for this?
Because that which possesses continuity is not subject to birth and destruction— since it remains eternally established in one and the same nature—
and because that which is held to possess those [states] of arising and destruction is not possessed of continuity—
since its form is not stable due to the emergence and disappearance of successive states.
The follower of Kapila (the Kāpila) says that there is no fault because of the non-difference between those two, power (*śakti*) and manifestation (*vyakti*).
To this, the Teacher replies with "anuttaram" (no answer) and so forth, asking: "What here is inconsistent, such that you speak in this manner?"
For non-difference (*abheda*) is indeed said to be identity.

These two—the difference between power (*śakti*) and manifestation (*vyakti*)—are a conventional usage based on difference and grounded in otherness; this is considered real because that which is constructed by conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is not rejected.
Furthermore, when there is cessation and appearance, there would be no cessation and no appearance [of the other]; likewise, while stability exists, there would be instability.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," [the cases of] "going" and "not going" and so forth are to be applied.
How is this definition of difference to be applied by you?
For indeed, you do not accept that there is non-difference between a power that possesses cessation and manifestation and the states of cessation and manifestation themselves.
Likewise, even though the power remains present, it is not the case that the states remain [as separate entities], nor is it accepted that the power is distinct from those states;
therefore, he says that such is the nature of their diversity.
For this is the distinction [between entities]: the non-cessation and non-appearance of one when there is the cessation and appearance of another, and so forth.

To explain: that whose cessation and so forth do not occur through the cessation and so forth of another is distinct from that other, just as a *tāla* tree is distinct from a *tamāla* tree; this is extremely well-known.
Furthermore, the absence of this [distinction] constitutes non-difference, such that the cessation of one occurs through the cessation of another, and so forth.

But surely, this [distinction] exists for the primary elements (bhūta), their derivatives (bhautika), and the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta), which have specific, simultaneous arising, ceasing, and abiding;
yet there is no non-difference among them. So how can it be said that "non-difference is the absence of this"? If you ask this, it is not so, because they possess distinct arising and so forth.
He states two examples in their respective order,
beginning with "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth,
and [the second] with "otherwise" (*anyathā*).

If the previously mentioned definition of difference and non-difference is not accepted, then, due to the absence of a defining characteristic for the two types of difference, there would be no established distinction between difference and non-difference anywhere; thus,

there would be non-difference between pleasure and the like on one hand and consciousnesses on the other, as well as between various consciousnesses themselves and from those consciousnesses to the pleasures and so forth.
The meaning is that there would be no distinction for each of pleasure and the other [qualities].
With the words "in that nature" (*tadātmani*) and so forth, the opponent states the definitions of difference and non-difference as they are understood in his own system;
therefore, there is no contradiction regarding birth, non-birth, and so forth.

Alternatively, [the author] rejects the relationship of container and contained between the lump of clay and the jar by means of the previously mentioned passage beginning with "Certainly not in the nature of the clay," etc.;
rather, it is maintained that the very essence of the clay itself, when delimited by a particular configuration such as a neck and so forth, is designated as a "jar."
[Objection: But surely the substance of clay (*mṛd-dravya*) is one and the same everywhere; how then can this be stated? To this he says:
"For there is not one [substance] whose nature is the clay of the three worlds.

Why? The connection is: because of the difference in the appearances of each respective representation (*prativijñapti-pratibhāsa*), there is a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the substance.
The meaning is that substances appear in cognition only as mutually distinct;
likewise, because they exist in states differentiated by differences in their conditions (*pratyavasthā*),
and by relying on the difference in their causal efficiency toward respective objects (*pratyarthakriyābheda*), there is a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the substances.

The phrase "because of the mutual impossibility of cause and effect" means that even for the opponent, this very reason is appropriate for accepting the distinction among *sattva*, *rajas*, *tamas*, and consciousness; explaining this, he says, "For thus... (5a4).

If a distinction among cognitions is maintained on the basis of differences in their respective manifestations and so forth— and since it is a tenet that there are many persons, as indicated by the plural form "among cognitions" (*caitanyeṣu*)— then,
if this is the case, [the distinction] is due to differences in the manifestations of each individual cognition.
Furthermore, he [the opponent] says:

"Even though there is this distinction between the various manifestations of individual cognitions and so forth, there is oneness of the states because of the persistence of the power of some self (*ātman*).
To this, the Teacher says:
If this is so, then the same undesirable consequence of non-difference applies to pleasure and the rest, as well as to the conscious selves (caitanya).

For [the opponent might argue that] pleasure and the rest, being qualities (guṇatva), are followed by such properties as being enjoyers (bhoktṛtva) and agents (kartṛtva), while in the conscious selves there is likewise the presence of being non-enjoyers, non-agents, and non-qualities; and similarly, pleasure and the rest, along with the conscious selves, are followed by such properties as existence (sattva) and knowability (jñeyatva). The formal argument (prayoga), however, is as follows: the conscious selves and pleasure and the rest are non-different from one another, because they participate in a mutual relationship of pervasion (anvaya-anvayabhāktva).

Just as power and its manifestation [are distinct], so too, if power and its manifestation were distinct, there would be no concomitance; this is because of the very absence of concomitance, just like pleasure and consciousness. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Now, it might be argued: "Where there is a concomitance (anvaya) by way of the entire essence, there is non-difference; but where there is concomitance by way of some form [only], as in the case of jars and so forth, this fault does not apply. To this he says:

"And even in the case of jars and so forth, there is no concomitance by way of the entire essence, but rather by way of some form"; the word "even" (api) implies that this is not only the case with pleasure and so forth.

Why? Because it would entail the consequence of lacking diverse forms and arising simultaneously; for if all states were connected in every respect, they would attain identity, and consequently, there would be an absence of specific form, taste, smell, potency, and post-digestive transformation.

The meaning is that there would be no variety [of phenomena], and furthermore, it would follow that the five elements do not exist, as well as the consequence of contradicting direct perception and other means of valid cognition; moreover,
it follows that all states would arise simultaneously.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), non-cessation, causal efficiency, activity, transformation, and so forth are included;

furthermore, the formal arguments (prayoga) are as follows: whatever does not exist in various ways through specific forms, tastes, smells, sounds, and so on, does not possess manifoldness (vaiśvarūpya).

Just as it is for a single entity whose nature is pleasure and so forth, so it is in this case: the property just mentioned does not exist even in the various states [of the mind], nor is the reason unestablished. For, if something is not distinct from another, it cannot be manifold through specific forms and so forth, just as the self of that very thing is not; and yet the states are held to be non-distinct from it. Thus, there is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

Likewise, if something is not distinct from another, it possesses the arising and so forth of that other through its own arising and so forth, just as its own essential nature (svarūpa) does; and since the states under discussion are admitted to be non-distinct from that [entity], this is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu).

Otherwise, if one accepts a difference in meaning, it would be illogical for the expression "this is a jar" to imply non-difference, or else it would be a mere change of name; thus, he states an objection.

Furthermore, no one—even with eyes wide open—perceives the jar and its clay-nature through such a distinction as "this is the jar" and "this is the clay-nature," whereby it might be said, "this has appeared here. Therefore, by this [argument], he states that the definition of non-difference is utterly incoherent.
If it is argued: "But surely there is indeed a distinct perception of the jar from the clay-nature in the form of a lump; why then was it stated thus?"

There is truth, yet there is no fault because the intention is that the other does not perceive it as distinct from the jar; for even if those two are indeed not perceived as distinct, one might ask, "Why should it not be so? To this, he says:

For it is not the case that [one can say] "this has appeared here" only when there is no perception of the distinction between the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the located (*adhiṣṭhānin*), or between the support (*ādhāra*) and the supported (*ādheya*), as in the case of a bowl and a jujube fruit.

Therefore, by this [argument], he considers that the relation of support and supported does not exist between the jar and its nature as clay, because their distinction is not perceived while they exist; rather, it exists only between an entity and its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Now, wishing to demonstrate the lack of pervasion (*avyāpitā*) of the definition of non-difference—namely, that "whatever appears in something is non-different from that"—he says:
Furthermore, there can be no manifestation within the essence of power, because it is admitted that power abides eternally;
otherwise, it would be nothing but a state [of that essence],
and thus its non-difference from its own self— which has been admitted— would not exist.

This is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*), because the characteristic of non-difference (*abheda-lakṣaṇa*) is absent; for this same fault applies equally to individuals, to pleasure and so forth, and to persons.
However, some Sāṃkhyas—whose intellects are defiled by the error of their own system—assert as follows:
"Whatever is the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of something, that is non-different from it."

If it is argued that— just as, for example, there are specific states such as a bracelet and so forth of gold— their [the Vaiśeṣika] position is also refuted by this very demonstration of the non-pervasion of the previously mentioned definition of non-difference, [the author], having placed this in his mind,
says "by this very [argument]" and so forth, making an objection with the intention that even the transformation in your [Vaiśeṣika] view is not tenable.

Regarding the passage beginning with "kiñcedam" (what is this?), the author intends to show that even the opponent has nothing further to say here, since this has been clearly stated by the Blessed One Kapila; thus he says:
"Just as there is the cessation of another property, such as a bracelet, while the substance remains constant, such as gold..."
And as for the claim that "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) is the manifestation of a different property (*dharmāntara*), such as a earring and so forth—
how has this kind of intellectual lapse occurred to the Teacher himself? With a mind filled with both wonder and compassion,
one wonders how even others repeat this, whereby darkness, having mercilessly overwhelmed the world, spreads across all directions.
Thinking that what desire for the welfare of living beings might be an offense, he said:

"Indeed, even if it was spoken thus by him, you must examine this: when that other property, such as the bowl and so forth, ceases and another appears, is it the same gold substance that remains, or is it something different from it?"
If it is asked why only two alternatives were formulated, he says:
"Because there is no other alternative," the underlying intention being that the doctrine of the Nirgranthas is untenable.
If it is asked, "What fault is there if the first alternative is accepted? [the author] says:

If that other property (*dharmāntara*) is that very substance (*dravya*) remaining as it was, then because of its persistence, there would be no disappearance and appearance characterized by manifestation and concealment; therefore, you must state to what those two belong.

Furthermore, the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: that which possesses persistence does not undergo cessation or manifestation, just like a substance that persists; and such is the case with another property that possesses persistence. This is an observation of what is incompatible with the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi).
Nor is the reason unestablished, because that which is not different from the persisting entity must itself persist, just like its own essential nature;

and since this other property is not different [from it], this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Furthermore, if the substance remains exactly as it was while that other property arises, then the statement "an other property of the persisting substance" is established.
He asks: "What is the reason? and says:

"For that very thing does not become a different property (*dharmāntara*) of itself. [The opponent objects: "That very thing indeed becomes a different property of itself, just as 'producedness' (*kṛtakatva*), although it is non-distinct from sound, [is nevertheless its property]. To this he replies: "[This is so] provided one does not rely on a distinction based on dependence."

This is what is meant: for in that case, the very same sound, because it is excluded from non-produced things and so forth, is not designated as a property (*dharma*) by means of another word whose distinctions have been set aside, when there is an inquiry into its mere essence with reference to that exclusion. But here, moreover, there is not even a distinction of expectation; so how could that very thing become a different property of itself? He states the fault [that arises] if one holds the position that a property is a distinct entity from the substance: [The text continues: "In that case, what is the fault if a property is a separate entity from the substance? He says:
Now, as for the passage beginning with "athetyā" (5a9):

why is it that the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of a substance does not occur through the disappearance and appearance of [distinct] dharmas? Because the transformation of one thing does not occur through the disappearance and appearance of things belonging to a different category (*arthāntara*).
Why is that? Because otherwise, it would follow that everything would be subject to transformation.

Furthermore, the transformation of consciousness is not admitted, because of the statement: "Otherwise, there would be the consequence of the identity of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, and [consciousness] would be a non-agent.
The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows:

If a thing does not undergo transformation through the cessation and emergence [of states] belonging to something else—that is, just as consciousness does not transform through the cessation and emergence of a sprout whose nature is distinct from consciousness—and since a separate property [cannot arise] from a substance, this would be the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). This would be so; however, why should there be a transformation of one thing through the cessation and emergence of some other unrelated object? For how could there be a transformation of one thing from that which is simply unrelated?

If it is argued that, just as in the case of that very sprout connected to its seed, when the seed is established by means of that [sprout] through its general property (*sāmānya*) via its disappearance and appearance, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because a property (*dharma*) is related to a substance (*dravya*); whereas if it were established by means of its specific property (*viśeṣa*), the example would lack the probans (*sādhanavikalatā*), because the sprout has no connection with consciousness (*caitanya*). To this, he says:
The designation "the property of a substance" is not established;
why? Because of the very absence of a relationship.
One thinks thus: this very thing—that "this property is related to the substance"—does not exist.
"How then can there be the consequence of exclusion?

[If one asks this, the opponent replies: "In that case, there certainly exists a relationship between the substance and its property characterized by the relation of locus and located; and consequently, even when the reason is accompanied by a qualification, it remains unestablished.
To this, [the author] says: "For there is no real, substantial relationship other than the relationship of cause and effect."
The relationship of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) is also established solely as a particular instance of the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

This is the intended meaning: as was determined in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya* within the section concerning the nature of the locus, such is the case for the self that has arisen from its basis, and such is the case for its effect.
If it is argued, "In that case, let there be a causal relationship between those two," he replies:
Furthermore, there is no causal relationship between these two substantial entities;
for how could that which is not itself of that nature be the cause of it?
For whatever does not possess the nature of something else should not be accepted by you as its cause, just as [the qualities of] *rajas* and *tamas* are not the causes of one another.

If this intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were likewise a property of a substance (*dravyadharma*), then how could it possibly be accepted as its cause? Thus, one considers this to be a consequence of the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Nor should it be thought that this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because the present context consists precisely in stating the fault by relying on the position that the object does not exist.
As for what was said— that dharma would be a distinct entity from substance—
nevertheless, even if our [argument] were to fail, it would still surpass the earlier followers of Kapila; for the Sāṅkhyas [hold that dharma is a quality], like Śaka and Mādhava.
Even if the cause of a property is admitted to be distinct from the substance, we reply as follows; thus he says:

"Even if the substance is a distinct entity, if its status as the cause of a property is accepted, then because a distinct effect is produced, the transformation of the substance would have to be accepted by you. What follows from that? he asks.

Even for one who follows the Tathāgata, though this [position] is contrary to that [view], what is the reason? Because even he accepts a distinction in conventional usage, such that when the substance of the effect—the jar—arises from the preceding substance of the cause—the lump of clay—through the continuity of cause and effect, it is designated as "the substance of clay has undergone transformation. For this reason, it might be thought [that there is no fault].
If transformation is indeed untenable even in these two ways, one might think that it will nonetheless occur by some other way; to this he says, "And not... and so forth.
Therefore, the conclusion is that there is no transformation in either case.

The ultimate [reality] is not a substance that is devoid of distinction or devoid of differentiation; nor is it absolutely something other than the substance. Rather, it is a particular arrangement of the substance, a different state (*avasthāntara*), and nothing else. Just as a fist is a particular arrangement of fingers—a different state—so too a fist is an indescribable state of the fingers in terms of being either identical to or different from them. For what reason? Because the fingers themselves, when undifferentiated, do not constitute a fist; for how could there be a fist when they are extended?

Otherwise, since there would be no distinction even when [the fingers] are extended, it would follow that they possess the nature of a fist even in the state of being open, just as they do in the state of being clenched.
Thus, at the time when the cause is absent, what form could there be?
Nor is the fist a separate entity distinct from the fingers, because even by one possessing effort, the fist is not perceived as something apart from the fingers, given that its cause is unimpeded.
Lest the followers of Kapila should say this, he anticipates their view with the words "not without discrimination" (*na nirvivekam*), etc.;
this has already been explained.

He refutes [the objection] by stating that a fist is not something distinct from its fingers; and by saying that a fist is merely the fingers themselves when they are held together without distinction, he points out the inapplicability of the example.
For this reason also:
The claim that "because extended things lack the nature of a fist" is likewise untenable; for what reason?
Because it is only certain fingers that, arising in such a manner through the power of specific causes and conditions, constitute a fist, whereas not all [fingers] do so.
He asks, "Why is that so? and says:
"Fingers that are extended do not possess the nature of discrimination, nor do fingers that are in a fist"; one should understand that the word "ca" (and) is used here as an elided reference.
Alternatively, it should be explained that the fingers, which constitute the fist, do not possess an undifferentiated form when they are extended;
why?
Because even in both states, the forms are respectively extended and unextended.
Because it would follow that there would be a cognition of both states— the extended and the non-extended— respectively;
furthermore,
the formal argument is that there would be a cognition of the non-extended state even in the extended state, because there is no separation of the fingers.
Just as in the state of being unextended there is a causal factor by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-hetu*),
so too, it should be applied that in the state of being unextended and in the state of being extended, there would be the cognition of that [extension];
furthermore, regarding the phrase "of both," the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) should be applied.

Furthermore, even if some kind of distinction were to exist between the two states while they remain [in that condition], there would be a twofold dilemma as to whether that distinction is inherent to the nature of those fingers or not.
Regarding the first case, he states the fault:
"That very distinction which is indeed inherent to the nature..."
He states this very point regarding the second [position] as well: "The characteristic of its own differentiation is like pleasure and pain";

and he says that even when there is the production of a distinction consisting of something else, the fingers would be perceived as being extended even in the state of a fist—the word "even" (api) being understood.
Why is this?

Because for that which has not fallen away from its own nature (*svabhāva*), there can be no perception of it as otherwise when another entity arises; for if it were so, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
One must state the over-extension: even when a different entity, such as a young elephant (*kalabha*), arises from a camel, there would have to be a perception of the camel as otherwise.
The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows:
where something has not fallen away from its own essential nature (ātmabhāva), there is no perception of it otherwise even when another object arises,
just as in the case of a camel when a young camel appears.

Furthermore, even when the distinction [of the fingers] arises, they do not fall away from their own intrinsic nature; thus, when formulating the reason through both affirmation and negation, the opponent [states] "nanu" and so forth, referring to the non-perception of a cause that is contradictory to the cause [of the perceived state].
The meaning of the sentence is that it has been stated that this [distinction] is indefinable in terms of being either identical to or different from [the fingers].
The Master [Dharmakīrti] states that although this has been said, it is not logical;
and explaining how it is illogical, he says:

"For there is no other possible mode for an existing entity apart from its being identical to or different from itself. This mention of an "existing entity" is intended to demonstrate that [entities such as] "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) and the like cannot possibly exist apart from conceptual construction (kalpanā).
To the question "Why?", he says:
"Of those two," and so forth;
this is the formal argument (*prayoga*).
When two things are defined by the characteristic of existing through mutual exclusion, the abandonment of one is inseparable from the adoption of the other,
and the adoption of one is inseparable from the abandonment of the other— just as, for example, existence and non-existence;
and since the two modes of identity and difference possess the aforementioned properties, this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).
[Objection: Surely, apart from the two modes of identity and difference, another mode is indeed possible between the fingers and the fist;

for the fingers themselves are not the fist, since when they are extended they are not a fist, yet it is not a separate entity either, because no distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is perceived. To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, in the fingers" (aṅgulīṣu) and so forth, the analysis [of the compound] is: those [fingers] in which destruction exists at every moment;
the meaning is that because they are momentary, they arise in such a manner that they become denotable by terms such as "fist" and the like.

This point, although already stated in the passage "In reality, [the fist] is not [distinct] from the particular fingers," is stated here again for the sake of the present context; it should be understood that it was rightly said. Otherwise, what would be the purpose of this? If this is so, then how is there a difference in designation such as "fist" and "fingers"?
To this he says: "In that regard, words such as 'fist' have specific objects, because they denote fingers only when they are in a specific state."
The word "finger," however, is a general term because it denotes them in all their states;
thus he provides two examples in sequence:
"like the words 'seed,' 'sprout,' and so forth, and like the words 'rice,' and so forth. (5b9)
Having thus shattered all opposing positions, and desiring to refute every remaining objection raised by others, he presents an objection through the mouth of another,
beginning with the words "If that... (tadyadi).
This is his intention: just as clarified butter does not exist in sesame seeds, so too does oil;
therefore, if an effect that was previously non-existent arises from a cause, then clarified butter would likewise arise from sesame seeds.
Because it is non-existent, it is not like oil;
nor is oil [non-existent] for that very reason, just like clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

For there is no distinction whatsoever regarding what is unreal. This is the method for establishing the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) by means of what are intended as the "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) and the "essential reason" (*svabhāvahetu*).
Having fully considered all this, thinking that the production of an effect belongs to you [the opponent], he says:

"But surely, even if everything were non-existent everywhere, this same fault would apply; for there is no distinction whatsoever in the case of existence. Thus, by reversing the reason (*hetu*) from those two very same formal arguments (*prayoga*)—namely, "because of existence"—one should formulate the two [syllogisms].

If it is argued that there is some specific distinction (viśeṣa) by which, even though [the cause] exists, not everything arises from everything—and therefore the exclusion [of the reason] from the counter-example is doubtful regarding the two means of valid cognition—the author replies: If such a distinction is admitted, then that which possesses the distinction would have to be different from the "Three Qualities" (triguṇya), consisting of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Why? Because, despite the presence of those Three Qualities, the distinction does not persist; for that reason.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which does not persist even when something else exists is absolutely distinct from it, just as consciousness (*caitanya*) does not persist in sound, touch, form, taste, or smell; and yet, the particularity (*viśeṣa*) does not persist even when the three qualities (*triguṇya*) exist. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
This has been stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position];
now, he says "And if [the effect] exists," etc., to show that even in the theory of the pre-existent effect (satkāryavāda), birth itself is not logically tenable.
There is no arising whatsoever for that which is intended to be non-existent, because it exists,
just as in the state of being already accomplished; thus, the perception of a property pervaded by the contradictory [of the probandum] occurs in his mind.
Otherwise, for that which has already been born, there would follow the birth of what is already born, resulting in an infinite regress;
as it has been said: "If there were birth for that which exists, there would be birth even for what is already born. (13)
If birth were to exist for one who already exists, then existence would also exist for one who is already born.

Furthermore, it would follow that the means—the causes such as seed, heat, water, and so forth—would be rendered futile, because there would be no form of the "thing to be accomplished" (sādhya) to be produced; this is the formal argument.
Wherever there is nothing whatsoever to be accomplished, there the efficacy of the means is found, as in the case of the sky, which cannot be further augmented.
Furthermore, when a cause is established, there is no effect whatsoever that could be proven [to exist]; this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Nor should it be thought that this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), because if some excellence (*atiśaya*) were to be postulated as arising in some way within the effect while that cause remains present, how could that excellence—which was non-existent there—be produced? It could not be produced at all, because it was non-existent.

If the non-perception of its pervader—the notion that "it is like a sky-lotus in milk"—resides in his mind, then if a particular excellence (*atiśaya*) were to arise even though it is non-existent, the same objection would apply: since it is non-existent, every excellence of that [entity] would arise from everything. Thus, the logical challenge is equal.
Even for you, an excellence of ghee would arise from sesame seeds because of their non-existence [in them]; thus, the meaning is that it would possess that excellence.
This is a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) based on an essential nature (svabhāvahetu).
He anticipates the opponent's view with the words "nātiśayastatra" (6a2) and so forth,
and raises the objection: "Since that [excellence] does not exist there, how could that non-existent mode arise?"
The intention is that the previously mentioned fault—that "everything would arise from everything" because the objection is equal—is not applicable.
If it is argued that there is nevertheless a distinction in the form of the produced [effect] in every respect, he says:
"And not," and so forth.

Thus, it has been demonstrated that the fault of everything arising from everything is equal for both proponents of the existence of the effect (satkāryavāda) and the non-existence of the effect (asatkāryavāda). Furthermore, it is not the case that the same objection applies equally to both such that one alone would be unable to answer it;
for in the doctrine of the existence of the effect, it has been established that there is no purpose whatsoever for "birth," and thus this constitutes an additional fault.
Thus, at some point, an opponent might say: "Well now, friend, even if this has not been refuted by me, you must certainly state something for the sake of defending your own position;
for one who merely attacks the opponent's position does not thereby attain an irreproachable standing for their own position.
Sound is not eternal, because it possesses form."

Regarding the objection that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth—as if it were already established that [pleasure] is impermanent—the author says:

"Even for an effect that is non-existent, when it arises from a cause, there is a rule (*niyama*) that its birth is from that alone which has the nature of producing it, and not from anything else. Here, the word *api* (even) expresses possibility (*sambhāvanā*).

The reality here is this: although oil does not exist [within them], it is produced from sesame seeds alone because the sesame seeds possess the power to produce it, and not from anything else because that other thing lacks the capacity to generate it; and when questioned as to how this restriction of power comes about, the answer must be given in terms of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of things.

Whether it be thus or otherwise, if the Great Principle (mahat) alone were produced from the Primal Nature (pradhāna) and not the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), or if the ego-principle were produced from the Great Principle and not the five subtle elements (tanmātras), and so forth— regarding such a process,
your only recourse would be to rely on the specific determination of potencies (śakti-pratiniyama), since there is no other means of avoiding this contradiction.

Furthermore, this point— which was stated by him [the opponent], namely that "there is no distinction whatsoever regarding non-existence"— has not even been swallowed by a crow; it is illogical because the production or non-production of an effect is determined by the presence or absence of causal efficacy.

Therefore, since the two aforementioned means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are subject to the stain of proving that the exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful, this [objection] might arise: "From what source does the restriction of the nature of that cause to produce its effect (*tajjananasvabhāvaniyama*) originate? To this, he says:
If it is asked, "Whence does even that [nature] have its restriction to its own nature by way of its own cause? he says:

Thus, there is no restriction regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena as being beginningless; the analysis of the compound is "that which has no beginning" (*anādi*). Because the beginninglessness [of the causal sequence] is accepted, the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*)—which pertains to the succession of cause and effect—is not capable of bringing even the slightest injury. Otherwise, if a beginning were postulated, it would follow that such a beginning would be causeless. Therefore, the point is that this doubt of yours is misplaced. Alternatively, the text may be explained in another way:
"In that case, excellence (*atiśaya*) arises as something immediate and not through a sequence;

and it is not to be questioned why everything does not arise from everything, for the production of excellence occurs only from that which has the nature of producing it, by relying on the restriction of causal power (*śakti-niyama*). Anticipating this objection, the opponent might sometimes state his own position while disregarding [the author's] established tenets; having resolved that "this reliance on the restriction of power is not prevented by anyone with any stick," he says:

Regarding the analysis of the phrase "even from the non-existent" (*asato 'pi*) and so forth, it is as before. Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever has a cause capable of producing it is necessarily produced even if it is non-existent, just like a specific excellence (*atiśaya-viśeṣa*).
There exists a cause capable of producing that specific effect; this is a *svabhāvahetu*.

Likewise, whatever lacks a cause capable of producing it does not arise even when its conditions are present, just as there is no excellence of ghee in sesame seeds. Similarly, a specific effect lacks a cause capable of producing it, because it is a specific cause; this is a *vyāpakānupalabdhi* (non-perception of the pervader).
Another formulation of the proof through the mark (liṅga) is:
because of the apprehension of material causes, because of being existent, and because of the absence of the possibility of everything arising from everything.
The [Sāṃkhya] arguments such as "the effect exists because that which is capable produces what is capable" and "because of the nature of the cause" (sāṃkhyakārikā 9) would thus be rendered futile.

Because there is an absence of the elimination of doubt and error regarding any object to be established or accomplished, and because there is no arising of a cognition of certainty, every means of proof (*sādhana*) sustains its name by removing doubt and error concerning a subject of dispute and producing a cognition of certainty regarding that object. However, neither of these two functions is possible in the system of Kapila, because it is impossible for an effect that exists eternally to undergo either loss or production.

Now, if it is thought that although this certainty already exists, it was previously unmanifest and attains manifestation through the statement of the proof—and therefore there is no futility—then [the author] says:

if some excellence characterized by manifestation were to arise in that certainty which is the nature of the probandum, how could that excellence, being non-existent therein, be produced from the proof? For [an effect] that was non-existent cannot be produced from a cause.

Or, if [the effect] were already produced, then the excellence consisting in the manifestation of the certainty regarding all things to be accomplished would arise from every other means of proof or from a fallacious means of proof; thus the same undesirable consequence follows.

The meaning is that smoke and other signs, which are the causes for the cognition of fire and so forth, would likewise produce the manifestation of the certainty regarding the pre-existence of the effect (*satkārya*).
This is said with reference to origination and manifestation;

however, this [manifestation] does not find a footing in things whose nature is unchanging. For that [manifestation] would have to be characterized either by the thing's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), or by the cognition having that as its object, or by the appearance of a different form (*rūpāntara*). Since the essential nature itself is immutable, it cannot be produced by means or by anything else.

Alternatively, if there is a manifestation of a prior form within a modification—as if it possessed its former nature—then the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*) is precisely what has been established, because a modification is characterized by the abandonment of a prior form and the acquisition of a subsequent one. Furthermore, since consciousness is a single unity, no other cognition can have it as its object; thus, the manifestation of that [consciousness] in another is untenable. Moreover, if there were a manifestation of a different form, nothing at all would arise for the other [subject], because they are distinct; therefore, a third kind of manifestation is also impossible. This same defect remains unavoidable even in the second case.

Even when a cognition arises having that as its object, it is impossible for there to be a manifestation of another entity—a non-existent state or its opposite—because that which does not provide assistance cannot possibly be the object of a cognition.
Alternatively, if it were to provide assistance, the cognition would arise from that very [assistance] alone; thus, there would be no dependence on a logical mark (*liṅga*).
It follows that its manifestation is the ascertainment of the probandum (*sādhya*) by itself alone;

however, since the ascertainment of the probandum arises precisely from dependence upon the means of proof (*sādhana*), it has been demonstrated that the production of a cognition of its own object—which is characterized by the arising of an excellence of dependence—is established only among unstable things. Alternatively, it would have to exist at all times, because the form of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is also always present.
Even if there were a dependence upon the cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*), the same [objection] would apply,
because for the proponent that [effect] exists at all times; furthermore,
with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth, he states another reason for the refutation of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).

If it is argued that in that state— that is, in the state of the lump of clay— there is no such causal efficiency (arthakriyā) as there is later in the state of manifestation; for instance, the specific causal efficiency consisting of holding water, which is to be accomplished by the jar, does not appear because the manifestation has not yet emerged, despite the configuration being indistinguishable [from the later state].
Regarding the rebuttal beginning with "only for that which is free from fear of the highest [reality]," etc.,
this is what is meant:
a certain modification of clay, delimited by a specific arrangement such as a neck and so forth, which performs a specific purposeful action (arthakriyā), is called a "jar," and nothing else.
If that [capacity] were present even earlier—in the state of the clay lump—just as it is in its unmanifest state, then that causal efficiency would be perceived;
yet it is not so for you. Therefore, the certainty should be reached that "this [capacity] simply does not exist"; why this false persistence?
If it is argued that it does exist because the substratum exists, he says:
For when one form exists, another form does not exist—just as blue does not exist when yellow is present; thus, what is intended is the perception of a pervader of the contradictory.
Nor should it be clamored that the reason is unestablished because there is no difference between the state and the possessor of the state.
Because a difference in the object is not logical even when there is a difference in the appearance of form— since that would lead to an over-extension—
the mention of a difference in the appearance of form is intended as an illustration;
therefore, a difference in causal efficiency must also be admitted.
He thinks as follows:
if cognition appearing as distinct establishes difference, then there would be a non-confused determination of the difference between pleasure, pain, and delusion, and not otherwise;
and thus we maintain that even between a lump of clay and a jar, there is an absolute mutual difference.

Because they are distinguishable by cognitions of distinct forms and because they produce effects that are mutually incompatible— just like pleasure and so forth— these are reasons based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*);
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even pleasure and so forth are not mutually distinct, just as [the distinction between] power and its manifestation is not.
Or rather, a specific distinction must be stated;

therefore, the conclusion is "from that," for it is not logical that there should be non-perception of that jar or other object while its nature remains present and has attained the conditions for perception.

Moreover, in that case, there would be non-existence within that intrinsic nature; since it is not that [nature], it follows that its being that intrinsic nature is an absolute difference from an intrinsic nature that has met the conditions for perception.

Having thus explained in detail the justification of the members of the proof regarding the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), he says "In the case of the non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalabdhau*) and so forth, wishing to explain the remaining types of non-perception.

Just as, having established by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the relationship of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between two properties—such as *śiṃśapā*-ness and tree-ness—the establishment of the absence of the pervader, such as tree-ness, is the "justification" (*samarthana*); [here] the term "of the member of proof" (*sādhanāṅgasya*) is to be supplied.
For example: "There is no *śiṃśapā* here, because of the absence of trees.
Now, one might object: "In that case, the absence of that [tree] is established by the non-perception of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) alone; what then is the use of this [justification]?"

For an instrument (*sādhana*) that does not produce a new excellence (*viśeṣa*) in an action whose function has already been accomplished cannot be a "most effective means" (*sādhakatama*); thus says Pāṇini [in Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.42].
From the statement that "valid cognition is that which consists in the apprehension of an object not yet apprehended," or "the illumination of an unknown object," this is indeed true;
for it is not applicable in all cases.

Rather, this [non-perception] is employed only where there is a mere absence of concealment by the sky, such that there is no determination of the specific distinctions among trees like the *sāla*, *sarala*, *palāśa*, or *śiṃśapā*.
It is used precisely where the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) cannot be ascertained in any way due to some cause of error.
Non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) likewise should be employed only where the absence of the effect (*kārya*) cannot be ascertained, and not elsewhere, because it would be futile.

Just as, in deep darkness, when the absence of smoke is not certain, one might say "there is no smoke here because of the absence of fire," there is doubt regarding the absence of the effect (smoke) but certainty regarding the absence of the cause (fire).

The perception of what is incompatible with the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) should also be employed only in cases where the object is situated within a range accessible to the senses, such as when one's body is touched by a mass of hair or licked by fire; it cannot be applied to things existing solely in space and so forth. Furthermore, the perception of what is incompatible with the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*) can only be used when the ground is occupied by a person standing nearby—someone from whom the presence or absence of specific effects, such as goosebumps, teeth-chattering, or horripilation, is impossible to perceive; otherwise, its application elsewhere would be futile. In this manner, the scope of application for all other types of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) should be understood accordingly.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "the perceptions of those [factors] which are opposed to their respective natures, pervaders, and causes.
Among the two types of opposition, this is the presentation of one.

Furthermore, there are two types of contradiction: the presence [of one thing] when the cause is unimpaired but another [contradictory thing] is absent, and that characterized by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇa*).

Following this same method, the justification of the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) in cases such as the perception of an effect contradictory to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*) is likewise easy to understand; therefore, it has not been explicitly stated.
