Nevertheless, it should be understood that even in cases other than the eleven types of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), the justification of the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) has been stated for such [reasonings] as the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory of the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory of the effect (*kāryaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), the perception of the effect of the contradictory of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*), and the perception of the effect of the contradictory of the effect (*kāryaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*).
Furthermore, their examples are, in due order:
"There is no smoke here because of the touch of frost."
"There are no causes of fire here whose capacity is unimpeded, because of the sensation of frost;
there is no sensation of frost here, because of smoke;
therefore, there are no causes of cold here whose capacity is unimpeded, because of smoke."

The presence of a cause, an effect, or something incompatible [with the negandum], as well as the presence of a pervader or an effect— these, along with another [type of evidence], namely the presence of something incompatible with the effect, are the means for establishing a negation.
(15) "There is no smoke here because of the sensation of cold," or "there is no efficient cause of fire here."
"Here, from smoke, the touch of snow is not [inferred], nor is it possible [to infer] the cause of cold"—
these are summary verses.
Thus, first of all, the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) has been established in one manner as consisting in the statement of what is not a constituent of proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*).

He establishes that very point by another method as well, beginning with "Alternatively" (athavā) and so forth. The compound "na ca" here functions, through repetition (*āvṛtti*), to conjoin a different meaning while abandoning the previously stated sense;

it does not, however, function like "either the *dhava* tree or the *khadira* tree," where there is an intended expression of an alternative meaning involving the abandonment of the prior sense. This is because [in the present case], the intention is not to express a disjunctive or similar type of meaning.

In this context, the word *sādhana* (means of proof) is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*), whereas the word *aṅga* (member) in the former [verse] refers to a cause (*kāraṇa-vacana*). This is the distinction.

By employing the term "collection" (*samudāya*) for the statement of the three-featured reason (*trirūpa-hetu*), [the author] subordinates the status of being a means of proof to the statements of the definition and other such elements within that collection.
It might be thought: "In the formulation based on similarity (sādharmya), the absence of the reason in the dissimilar instance (asapakṣa) is stated;
and in the formulation based on difference (vaidharmya), its presence in the similar instance (sapakṣa) is not [stated], because it is precisely what is about to be negated immediately thereafter.

Therefore, how could the failure to state even one of these two constitute 'the statement of a non-essential member of the proof' (asādhanāṅgavacana)? This [objection] is not contradicted by what is about to be said."
And this is not explained in that way alone;

for the three-featured reason exists as an objective reality (*arthātmaka*) in the ultimate sense. Regarding its verbal expression, those two illuminating factors—the statement of the presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmavacana*) and either the statement of its existence in similar instances (*sapakṣasattvavacana*) or the statement of its non-existence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣāsattvavacana*)—constitute a collection. Of that collection of two statements, the statement of the presence in the subject and so forth is a constituent part. Thus, the statement of the presence in the subject is necessarily constant, while each of the other two is merely occasional.

Therefore, since the whole (the composite) consists of a collection of two statements, its parts are always only of two kinds. Now, the non-statement of even one of these two parts is a non-statement of a probative member (*asādhana-aṅga-vacana*);
this applies not only to both [parts] according to the first explanation, as indicated by the word "also" (*api*), for the non-statement of both is indeed silence (*tūṣṇīmbhāva*).
Having stated that [the opponent] is silenced by his inability to respond, he provides another synonym, beginning with "Alternatively" (athavā).
"Of that very [statement]" refers to the collection of statements possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*); "that which is not a limb" means that which is not a constituent part (*avayava*).
If it is asked, "How then is it that the thesis and so forth are not members of the proof? it is said: the statement of the thesis is not the proof.

Because its establishment does not arise either directly or indirectly; for it is the object (*artha*) itself that leads one to understand the connection, and not the verbal expression (*abhidhāna*), since the latter lacks a connection with the object. Therefore, neither the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) nor the statement of the reason (*hetu*) is a direct means of proof for the establishment of the object.
Furthermore, from the statement of the subject (*pakṣa*), doubt regarding the object is observed, not certainty; for that reason as well, it is not a direct means of proof.

It might be thought: "The doubt itself is unestablished, because the proponent and the opponent have ascertained [the matter] from the statement of the thesis; however, for others it does indeed exist.
This being so, even upon hearing the statement of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, doubt arises in those who are unlearned; thus, [your reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
This is irrelevant.

For the certainty of the proponent and the opponent must exist regarding either a single property, such as impermanence and so forth, when one begins to cause [the other] to understand it, or regarding two opposing properties; however, it cannot be in the case of a single [property], because there would be no dispute,
which would entail the futility of employing a proof.
Nor [can it be established] by means of two opposing properties, because that would entail the superimposition of two contradictory properties upon a single entity.

For when two contradictory properties are ascertained with respect to a single entity by the proponent and the opponent through the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then that entity would necessarily become dual-natured.

Alternatively, if those two are not ascertained through the power of valid cognition, but rather from their respective scriptural traditions (*āgama*), [then they cannot establish the nature of the entity].
Even so, since the two properties are ascertained by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it must be explained why doubt does not arise from the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*).

Therefore, the statement of the thesis is neither a direct proof nor an indirect one; for, by merely expressing the thing to be proven (*sādhya*), it indicates what is impossible—just like the statement of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) when [the probandum] is unestablished (*asiddha*).

The statement of the reason (*hetu*), however, because it indicates what is possible, is said to be established by its capacity as being grounded in the means of proof (*sādhana*). Being a member of the means of proof while being the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*), it assists the proof of the proposition because it aids the means of proof, just like the statement of the reason; furthermore, it favors the proof of the proposition by way of illuminating the object of that proof.
Otherwise, that proof would proceed without an object.
Since the contact between the self, the mind, and cognition, and so forth, also serve as auxiliaries to the means of proof, the qualification "being a statement" [is necessary].

Furthermore, [the opponent argues] that because it illuminates the subject, the probandum, and the means of proof—which are the components of the proof—just like the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), [this definition is valid].
However, this too is utterly devoid of substance.

Since it has been requested that one "prove sound to be impermanent," the external statement—which, while being speech, assists the proof and reveals the opposite of what proves the probandum—is not an internal factor for the establishment of the probandum.

What utility, then, is there in pointing out the subject (*viṣaya*)? For if the establishment of the probandum could not occur without it, everyone would agree; however, [the establishment occurs] even without this, as long as...

Whatever is produced is entirely impermanent, such as a jar and so forth; and since sound is produced, even if the word "subject" (*pakṣa*) were not explicitly stated, it would be understood solely from the sense that "sound is impermanent. Therefore, its explicit mention would be entirely purposeless. This would be a reversal [of the proper order] if a statement like the subject were not employed to demonstrate the scope of the operation of the reason (*hetu*); for in that case, how could [the reason] receive the designation derived from its dependence upon the subject?

It is also untenable to claim that the properties such as being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) are established because they depend on those [other factors] which have acquired their own capacity, or that the movement toward the subject is impossible without the capacity [of those factors], and that the properties such as being a property of the subject are established by the force of the subject obtained through capacity.
If those [other factors] do not exist, the very subject (pakṣa), which is obtained through the force of [the other members], would be impossible; furthermore,

this would result in mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya), for the property-of-the-subject (pakṣadharmatva) and so forth are established by virtue of the subject, while the subject is established by the force of the property-of-the-subject and so forth.
To this it is replied:

indeed, at the time of the formal proof (*sādhana*), there is no conceptualization of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth; rather, it is simply that in whichever substratum (*dharmin*)—be it sound and the like whose specific nature is sought to be known, or a pot and the like whose light is obscured by a wall—the property characterized as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), "smokiness" (*dhūmatva*), and so on, is either cognized through inference or made known through perception.

When another object, such as a jar or a kitchen, has been determined through its connection with that specific property, it is remembered as being present; or when an object such as the sky or the ocean lacks that specific property, it is remembered precisely as being absent.

That [property], by virtue of being an inherent characteristic of the thing itself—even without the formal designation of "being a property of the subject" (pakṣadharmatva)—conveys the subject as qualified by the property sought to be known through its own power alone.
And that which is the object of this power is called the "subject" (pakṣa).

Thereafter, for the sake of conventional usage in the treatises, designations such as "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth—which arise based upon that [subject]—are elaborated according to one's preference;
or rather, by the force of the context of reflective consideration, let these conceptualizations of "property of the subject" and so on occur even at the time of the formal proof (*sādhana*).

For, whatever property of a real entity (*vastu*) is intended by the proponent to be proven as being qualified by a subject that is the locus of dispute—that is the "subject" (*pakṣa*); and whatever other property belongs to it is the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*).
And a "similar instance" (sapakṣa) is an object that possesses the general property of the probandum under discussion, while a "dissimilar instance" (asapakṣa) is one that lacks it;
for even for one who employs the "subject" (pakṣa) at the time of the formal proof, the subject is not merely the initial statement by the proponent, such as "sound is impermanent."
But even if one were to speak of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth by the force of the context alone, even within a different introductory discussion,
that [force] would be the same for one who objects to the formulation of the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Therefore, the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is not a constituent of the proof (*sādhana*).
As for the statement regarding the application (*upanaya*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*), it is explained how they are not members of the proof (*sādhana*).
In that regard, the application (*upanaya*) of the proof is the subsumption [of the subject] as "so" (*tathā*) or "not so" (*na tathā*), depending upon the example (*udāharaṇa*). (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.38)
Just as for the purpose of providing a reflection [of that],
what more is there to say here once it is established that the property belonging to the example in the reflection is non-deviant?
Therefore, the meaning of the application (*upanaya*) is the existence of that which possesses the same property as residing in the probandum (*sādhya*), namely, "and this [sound] is produced";
for its existence together with the probandum has not yet been stated by the [reason] "because it is produced."
It is not stated [as a fallacy], because there is merely an indication of the property to be proven and the proving property;
for there is merely an indication of the property to be proven and the proving property, as in: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced."

Furthermore, whether that property of being produced exists or does not exist in sound is understood through the application (*upanaya*); and it is established that the property of being produced does indeed exist in sound.

And thus, it can be inferred that the application (*upanaya*) conveys a meaning distinct from the statement of the reason (*hetu*), because—while possessing a non-different form and being distinct from well-known synonyms—it is employed after the statement of the reason, just like the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
[As stated in the *Nyāya-sūtra* 1.1.39: "The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the citation of the reason. (*nyāyasūtra* 1.1.39).

"The restatement of the proposition" means that once the subject matter of the proposition has been established through all available means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the subsequent statement made for the purpose of negating any contrary consequence is the conclusion (*nigamana*);
it is not merely a repetition of the proposition itself.

What is the reason? Because the statement of the thesis is the indication of what is to be proven, and the conclusion is the indication of what is established; furthermore, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is observed in cases of multiplicity, as in the expression:
"Again, this radiance of lightning flashes forth."

Furthermore, in the statement "this city of Gandharvas is seen again," by implication, what is understood is the presentation of the reason (*hetvapadeśa*) occurring immediately after the application (*upanaya*),
and not that which occurs immediately after the proposition (*pratijñā*).
Because it is impossible;
for no one, after stating the proposition, employs the conclusion immediately following the statement of the reason, as in:
"Sound is impermanent because it is produced."
Therefore, the statement "sound is impermanent" has a meaning distinct from the sentence stating the proposition (*pratijñā*); for,
while possessing a form distinct from the propositional sentence, it is uttered after the statement of the reason (*hetu*), just like the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Furthermore, the conclusion (*nigamana*) does not establish the probandum (*sādhya*), because it functions as a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) upon that which has already been conveyed by other words—
just as when someone says, "This person who is coming here has horns," another might say, "Therefore, he is not a horse," and so forth.
Therefore, a sentence accompanied by a word does not convey a meaning that has been established for the purpose of investigation,
because it is employed after the instruction of the cause;
the example is as before.

This is refuted: indeed, the formal argument is not stated in this way— "Sound is impermanent because it is produced"— because such a formulation of the proposition (*pratijñā*) has already been rejected immediately following [the previous discussion].
Furthermore, sound is produced;
and thus, whatever is produced is impermanent, such as a jar and so forth;
or rather, whatever is produced is entirely impermanent, such as a pot and so forth.
And thus, the formulation "sound is produced" may be employed in either way as desired, because the proof of the probandum exists in both cases.

In that regard, having stated, "Sound is produced; and whatever is such is entirely impermanent, like a jar or the like," the statement of the application (*upanaya*) is then uttered for the purpose of reflection: "In this same way, sound is produced."
Therefore, this [application] is useless, because comprehension occurs merely through the previously mentioned formal argument even without this reflection;

and that which is useless as a means of proof (*sādhana*) should not be adopted by the learned in a syllogistic statement, just as the sentence "ten pomegranates" and so forth; and thus the statement of the application (*upanaya*) for the sake of reflection is useless—this is established by the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*).

This same principle is observed even in inference for oneself (*svārthānumiti*); for no conscious person, having apprehended the existence of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) in sound and recalled its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*), proceeds to form a mental reflection such as, "and so, sound is produced.
Nevertheless, the statement of application (*upanaya*) is uttered for the purpose of demonstrating possibility: "Whatever is produced is all impermanent, like a jar; and so, sound is produced."
We accept both of these points; however,

we do not accept the mere statement of the proof occurring immediately after the proposition, such as "sound is impermanent because it is produced," because there is no formal employment of the proposition [in that specific manner].

Furthermore, the reason stated to demonstrate that *upanaya* is a distinct member [of the syllogism] is incapable of its purpose, because it is bitten by the serpent of the "unestablished" (*asiddha*) fallacy.

Moreover, as for this *nigamana*, which is described as having the characteristic of restating a proven object (*siddhārtha*) in order to avoid redundancy—that is simply untenable. For one who maintains that the proof consists of five members cannot logically exist without a *nigamana*, since the establishment of the object would already have occurred prior to the *nigamana*; thus, being redundant, the *nigamana* would not qualify as a member of the proof.
Consequently, this [reiteration] should not be included in the proof-statement, as it is not a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) of something already established.

If there were confusion on the part of one who has reached a conclusion, it would follow that there is no dependence on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, the impermanence is established.

However, the conclusion (*nigamana*) functions for the sake of ascertainment by referring to all the constituent members once the object of each respective [member] has been validated by all the means of valid cognition, thinking "it is indeed impermanent.
If, then, there is no dependence on other means of valid cognition, then the probandum (*sādhya*) is already ascertained through the force of the argument itself.

For instance, since that which is unproduced is necessarily impermanent—just as a pot or the like—and sound is produced, the statement "sound is produced" makes known the presence of "being produced," which is invariably concomitant with impermanence; by the very force of this, the certainty arises that "sound is impermanent. Therefore, this statement is redundant because it conveys a meaning already understood, and it is unfit to be employed.
Nor is even a trace of the possibility of a contrary conclusion (viparyaya-prasaṅga) suspected here,
such that the inclusion of this [term] would be fruitful for the purpose of excluding it;
for the pervasion (vyāpti) of "being produced" by "impermanence" has already been established.
As for the application:
a wise person should not utter a statement that is already understood through the force of implication;

such a statement would be redundant. For example, when it is said, "The boy is not in the house, yet he lives," the statement regarding his being outside—which is understood through the force of that [previous] implication—is redundant.

And it is understood through the force of the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—namely, "therefore, it is indeed impermanent," and so forth. Thus, the object intended to be proven is, with respect to the first probandum, an observation of something incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), and with respect to the second probandum, an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
For this very reason, the reasons stated in order to demonstrate that the conclusion (*nigamana*) is a separate member [of the syllogism] are unestablished (*asiddha*);
that too has been refuted by this very [argument].
As it has been said:

"When the conclusion (nigamana) is stated for the sake of comprehending the meaning of the sentence after the proposition (pratijñā) and the other members have been examined, it does not constitute a mere repetition. (17)
Since multiple meanings are not established by scattered statements,
the conclusion (nigamana) must be stated separately for the purpose of establishing the connection. Enough with this overly prolix discussion.
"Or [it is] positive and negative concomitance"— this is another way of stating what was called "appropriation" (upādāna) in Nyāya Sūtra 2.1.1.
12. There occurs the incapacity of the second [cognition], because that which has already arisen as a proof cannot be produced again.
However, the commentators on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* say: "Now, [the objection] beginning with 'nanu'... and so forth;
this is the response beginning with "na" and so forth.

If the member of the proof called the "accumulative reason" (*upacaya-hetu*) were necessarily to result in the thesis (*pratijñā*), because it is the cause for the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*), just like the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth;
if it is argued that [then] the reason would have a doubtful exclusion (*sandigdha-vyatireka*), he says:

If it is argued that the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is not [the means of proof] either— because the contradictory (*viruddha*) and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reasons, despite the presence of the property of the subject, lack probative force and give rise to doubt for that very reason; and therefore the statement of the property of the subject is not the proof, just like the statement of a common (*sādhāraṇa*) reason and so forth— the author replies:
By this [passage] beginning with "that which is similar to that" (tattulyam), the arising of doubt is refuted;
he clarifies this very point by stating "even from the statement of the property of the subject" (pakṣadharmavacanāt).
By this, he declares the deviation (vyabhicāra) of the immediately preceding reason.

But one might think: "Since a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), such as audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) and the like, functions as a member of the proof (*sādhanāvayava*) only when its relation [to the probandum] has not yet been demonstrated, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because there is no counter-example (*vipakṣa*) at that time.

However, once the relation has been demonstrated, it then functions as a member of the proof; and since there is then no doubt arising from that [property], there is all the more no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). This is what is being considered.

That [objection] applies equally to the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*); therefore, that too would be a proof (*sādhana*). Now, if you were to think: "It would be true if it were the probandum (*sādhya*)," [we reply: there is no establishment of the probandum from anything else.
Furthermore, once the action has been accomplished, axes and other tools do not serve any further purpose for the wood.

However, since it is stated that "because doubt arises when the relationship has not been demonstrated," and that "doubt arises from that very [non-demonstration]," if this were the case, then the probandum could not be established without its formulation; thus, its formulation would be entirely useless. Otherwise, who would be capable of excluding the statement of the subject (*pakṣavacana*) from the proof?
Furthermore, the words of the Teacher—such as "inference for others is the communication of the three-featured mark" (*trirūpaliṅgākhyāna*)—would be contradicted.
How then is it that it was stated:

"The exclusion of other [members] follows from the statement of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva), the connection (sambandha), and the probandum (sādhya)"? There is no contradiction, because the explanation is as follows: the "statement" (ukti) is the manifestation of the probandum through the property of the subject and the connection; this constitutes an "implication" (ākṣepa). Therefore, there is an exclusion of other members—such as the statement of the thesis (pakṣa), the application (upanaya), and so forth—from the syllogistic argument (sādhanavākya) insofar as they are not to be employed.

In the *Vivaraṇa* as well, this is the meaning: since it is logical that only the statement of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and the relation [between the reason and the probandum], through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), is the cause for establishing the intended object, and nothing else;

therefore, the statement of the subject (*pakṣavacana*) is to be employed for the purpose of indicating and establishing the inferable (*anumeya*), and not anything else—this is the supplement (*upaskāra*).

It is called the "subject" (*pakṣa*) because by means of it, [the object] is projected (*ākṣipyate*) and revealed (*prakāśyate*); thus, the "statement of the subject" is the three-fold indicative mark (*liṅga*).
For it has been stated that "suggestion (ākṣepa) is indeed equivalent to direct expression (abhidhāna)," or [it may be so called] because the root *vac* has multiple meanings;
however, for us, in that context, the mention of the object of inference is intended to have the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) as its scope. 19
Even this statement is contradicted,
because the connection of the science of logic (*tarka-śāstra*) is here stated to be "therein."
But if there were a connection with the application (*prayoga*), there would be much that is inconsistent and discordant.

This has been stated specifically regarding the very nature (*prakṛti*) of that [word], and within its own definition (*lakṣaṇa*), for the purpose of refuting the various opposing views of others. (20–21)
Thus, enough of this digression;
that means of proof, which consists in its positive existence, is a property of the subject by virtue of being its object.
When a certain matter under discussion is the very limb of the proof, its manifestation by means of the subsequent two words—

whereby the opponent does not desire to know it through such means as taking recourse to non-scriptural sources or using pretexts— and the inclusion of irrelevant digressions indicated by the word "etcetera," constitutes what is called "interpolation" (*prakṣepa*), which is a proclamation at length merely by name.

Just as the Naiyāyikas, when desiring to know only whether a self exists or does not exist as distinct from the aggregate of the intellect, the senses, and the body, offer proof as follows: "My perceptions and other cognitions, which have existence and so forth as their common objects and have knowable objects as their domain, are perceived by a cognizer distinct from my own body and so forth, because they possess birth dependent upon their own causes, like the cognitions of another person. Thereafter, through great elaboration, they explain at length that there is no distinction between substance, quality, and action, based on the commonality of existence and so forth, according to the categories: "It [the self] is existent, non-eternal, a substance, characterized by cause and effect, and possesses universals and particulars."

For here, the qualification of the property (*dharma-viśeṣaṇa*)—namely, that its object is not a particular such as "that" (*sa*), but rather that its object is the knowable (*jñeya*)—does not in any way assist in establishing the probandum under discussion; this is because it serves as a reason for [the opponent's] inability to mislead others, to repeat [the argument], or to obstruct the capacity for understanding the response—the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "obstruction of the capacity for understanding the response" includes this latter point. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has a consequence (*prasaṅga*) [as its result]. What does the example of the proponent of selflessness (*nairātmyavādin*) indicate?

In this case, even for the Sugata’s Dharma and Vinaya—which prescribe and prohibit [certain actions]—there is an effort directed toward washing away all the impurities of pride, conceit, and so forth; yet, in establishing that very point, there is the consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [allowing] dancing, singing, and the like for those who profess a self (*ātmavādin*).
If such is the case, what need is there to mention others?
Now, one might object: "We are Buddhists, so how can we say this?"—for surely you have stated a negation accompanied by a qualification (*saviśeṣaṇa*).

One must say, "I am a Buddhist, I speak," just as one says, "I, Gārgya, speak" or "I, Paṭu, speak. And Pāṇini [states in Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.59] that this plural form occurs only when there are many [speakers].

It cannot be said that [the example] applies to anyone at all, because of the statement "not indeed," since he employed it in such a manner with respect to himself, to others of his own school, and to many others as well;
and it should be understood that this example was stated regarding precisely this intention (*vivakṣā*) of the proponent, and not regarding any other.
Alternatively, this was stated in this manner to dispel the stubborn adherence of dull-witted grammarians; accordingly, he will demonstrate the futility of the science of grammar.
For this very reason, it has been employed by another great poet as well:
"You are a king, and we too are elevated by the pride of wisdom cultivated through service to our gurus."
"Thus you are the king, and we too are elevated by the pride of wisdom gained from serving our gurus;
we are the members of the assembly approved by the virtuous"— in this way he mocks them.
The word "aho" (oh! is supplied here [as an exclamation]:

for the purpose of illuminating the expansion—that is, the detailed exposition—of the twelve characteristics beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is the treatise known as Mīmāṃsā; its author is Jaimini. That which was propounded by him is the reality consisting of the declaration of eternality; the locus of that [reality] is the word "sound" (*śabda*). Between that [word] and the pot, one or the other is taken—namely, "that second pot. Having thus formulated the proposition (*pratijñā*), he proceeds to provide the commentary on the twelve characteristics and so forth.
First, he explains a single definition of the means of valid cognition over a long period of time: "Dharma is that which is characterized by Vedic injunction" (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.1.2).

2. "Injunction" (codanā) they say is a statement that impels one toward action; for an injunction is capable of making known an object that is past, present, future, subtle, concealed, or remote—nothing else can do so. For instance, when there is contact with an existing object, the arising of cognition in a person through the sense organs is perception (pratyakṣa).
The signless (animitta) consists in the apprehension of what is actually existing, as stated in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.1.4 and following.

Without establishing the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), impermanence cannot be established, because that which has not arisen dependently cannot possess momentariness.
To the objection that such a phenomenon must then be stated separately,
he replies with the words "But such a one," and so forth.

Even though such a factor is invariably concomitant with the property to be proven under discussion, if it is not desired by the opponent, why would this statement—which is neither a reason nor an example and thus lacks a part of the proof—be considered a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) as previously described? To this he says: when the opponent has demonstrated that it is not a part of the proof, but the proponent does not so demonstrate it, then neither of the two parties wins or loses; for since the proponent has failed to state the proof, he does not win.
Furthermore, because the opponent has not established that such a state exists, there is no defeat for him either, since defeat depends upon what has been established;
for this very reason, both of these [defeats] are likewise absent in the case of the opponent.
Mīmāṃsā-Śabara-Bhāṣya 1.1.4
Now, concerning the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the opponent, he says: "The non-utterance of a fault," and so forth. 7b6.
The intention is that there is no fault when a point is not raised as a defect, provided that the subject matter was either intended to be investigated or was not intended to be investigated at all.
As for what those defects of the proof (*sādhana*) are, he says: deficiency is of six kinds, occurring from the non-statement of one, two, or both [of the members] of each [type].

It might be thought: "If there is no simultaneous employment of the presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the absence from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), how can a deficiency in the mode [of proof] be stated? For when there is no implication [of these] through universal inclusion by means of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), then this [deficiency] is established. To this it is replied: even then, there occurs the fault of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) consisting in the failure to demonstrate positive and negative concomitance, and so forth.

"Let this be another fault of his; for proofs are not always beset by only a single defect. The three fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) and the eighteen fallacies of the example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), along with their illustrations, are to be seen in detail in the third chapter of the *Nyāyabindu*.
He explains the failure to point these out using two synonymous terms, and states that such failure occurs due to three causes."

Furthermore, [the opponent objects]: "Since the proof (*sādhana*) is faultless, etc., it is indeed logical that the opponent should suffer defeat for failing to point out a fault when the proof is faultless; however, in the case of a faulty proof, even if the fault is not pointed out due to ignorance or incapacity, defeat is logically appropriate for the proponent alone, because he employed a defective proof, and not for the opponent."
To this, he says:
"For even when a faulty means of proof (*sādhana*) is stated" (7b8).
If this is so, since the proponent has defeated the opponent even by means of a faulty proof, why does the victory not belong to him? To this, he replies:
Regarding the passage beginning with "only" (kevalam) and so forth:
if this is so, why is there no defeat?
This objection arises from the thought that there would be a loss of the establishment of reality (tattva).

The response beginning with "not because of non-refutation" and so forth means that the misconception of the wicked is an ignoble practice; therefore, there is no such thing as a "disputation for victory" (*vijigīṣuvāda*) prescribed by logic (*yoga*) that is conducted through quibbles (*chala*) and the like—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
For if the principle has been stated and the opponent, seeking the truth, should understand that matter endowed with logic, [then the purpose is achieved].

Now, if— due to the greater force of attachment to one's own position— one should not understand the meaning of the stated reasoning even when it has been explained, then, considering that the assembly of people nearby who know themselves should not fall into error because of that opponent's failure to understand the meaning of that reasoning, the pursuit of reasoning alone constitutes the debate of the virtuous; this is for the sake of protecting the truth, so says the opponent.

As it has been said: "Sophistry (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) are for the purpose of protecting the determination of reality, just as the covering of thorny branches is for the purpose of protecting the growth of seeds" (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.50).
"No," says the Teacher; the meaning is that reality (tattva) remains thus well-guarded by the absolute uprooting of its opposite.
"In the absence of that" means in the absence of both the demonstration of the proof and the refutation of fallacious proofs;
"even otherwise" means even in the absence of false chatter and the like.
He explains how this is not a fault of the proof:
"Even when that which is intended as a fault is present, there is no obstruction to the establishment [of the thesis];

for instance, when one intends to prove merely the impermanence of sound by means of its being an effect—despite the fact that some followers of Kaṇāda, ignorant of logic, raise an objection regarding the undesired property of being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*) and so forth."
Because of the acceptance of a treatise (*śāstra*), everything intended therein would have to be the probandum (*sādhya*);

and since the reason (*hetu*) and the thesis (*pratijñā*) would then be subject to faults regarding that [entirety], that is untenable. Even when relying on a treatise, only that which has been [previously] abandoned is the probandum;
otherwise, in the case of proving the opposite of "earth possesses the quality of smell," this very same reason would result in being contradictory (*viruddha*) with respect to that very same thesis.
Likewise, this is another demonstration of a fault,

as Bhāradvāja stated: "There is a mutual contradiction between the two terms of the proposition, namely 'the self' and 'it does not exist,'" because the word "self" denotes a real entity, while "does not exist" is its negation.

This too is incorrect, because it is intended to refute the fact that the referent of a word—which consists of a distinction appearing as established through conceptual constructions of a self arising from beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*)—has for its material cause the existence of a specific character such as "eternal," "mental," and so forth, as desired by others.

For it is precisely regarding this subject (*dharmin*) that wise people investigate its existence or non-existence, [asking]: "Does this object appearing in the conceptual construction of a self have as its material cause an entity as it is asserted, or not?"

However, it is not the case that the object appearing here as a conceptual reflection is being denied; for words are employed precisely to bring that very [object] to mind, and because it is personally experienced (*pratyātmavedya*).

But the external particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is distinct from the conceptual reflection, is certainly not the meaning of a word; therefore, there can be neither its affirmation nor its negation, otherwise—
Furthermore, if words were restricted solely to their own forms, there would be no application of them toward objects that differ according to various philosophical systems;
nor would there be any falsehood regarding past or future things. (23)
"Of some speech whatsoever"—this [statement] is considered to have the conceptual object (*bauddhārtha*) as its domain.

And this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is intended to be refuted on the grounds that it has a real entity (*bhāva*) as its material cause, does not lack an object because its very nature is to have the reflection of a conceptual construction as its domain; for the word "self" (*ātman*) does not lack an object.
Consequently, whatever is negated in whatever place exists elsewhere than that.
Just as the word "jar," which does not exist without a common substratum (*asamānādhikaraṇa*), is unable to convey the non-existence of the jar itself,
but rather conveys a negation with respect to a particular place and time—
such as "the jar does not exist" being a negation with respect to a particular place, or "it does not exist in the house"— [so too is the case here].
Or the prohibition refers to a specific time:
"it does not exist now," or "it did not exist previously."
"There is nothing above" is a negation of everything; it is not logical for this to apply to the existence of a jar that has never been experienced.
Likewise, when it is said "the self does not exist," what specific location is being negated?
Regarding the phrase "a distinction of subsequent time":
if this refers to the negation of a distinction of place, that is not tenable in the case of the self, because the self is non-spatial.
Nor does the negation of a specific location imply that the self is negated; nor is it your intention [to claim] that "the body is not the self. If you say this...
Or to whom does the body belong as its self, such that there is this negation regarding the body, namely, "the self does not exist in the body"? If it is asked,
"To whom does the self belong in the body, such that there is this negation?"
Where, then, is the self?
Nowhere is there a self;
does this mean it simply does not exist?
It is not that it does not exist, because of the negation of specific [locations]; what kind of verbal logic is this, that it is neither in the body nor elsewhere,
yet it is not non-existent?
This is indeed the proper method of speech:
that things are described exactly as they are; and since this self does not exist anywhere at all, it is therefore described in that very manner.
Furthermore, a prohibition regarding a specific time is not tenable,

because the three times are not manifested in the self; moreover, one who seeks to negate the self must state the referent of the word "self," for we do not observe a single word that is devoid of meaning.
Furthermore, even if you were to accept the word "self" (ātman) as referring to the body and so forth, there would still be a contradiction because [the self] has not been excluded. How so?
At that time, the meaning of the statement "there is no self" would be that "the body and so forth do not exist."

Such extensive [objections] as these are set aside by the fact that [the reason] is a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*); yet even this is incorrect, because there is no such thing as a "particular universal" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*).

Alternatively, the property of "being immediately subsequent to effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is not a part of the meaning of the proposition, because it ceases once the locus (*dharmin*) has been characterized.
For that which serves as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaka*) of something else cannot be a part of that thing; just as a crow is not a part of a vulture.
2. Refutation of the Nyāya view: Furthermore, what was stated by Akṣapāda regarding the twenty-two types of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is not tenable. 8b5.
Abandonment of the proposition,
shifting the proposition,
and contradiction of the proposition.

The points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are: abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāsaṃnyāsa*), shifting the reason (*hetvantara*), the irrelevant (*arthāntara*), the meaningless (*nirarthaka*), the unintelligible (*avijñātārtha*), the incoherent (*apārthaka*), the mistimed (*aprāptakāla*), the deficient (*nyūna*), the redundant (*adhika*), the repetitive (*punarukta*), failure to restate (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), lack of understanding (*ajñāna*), lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), admission of the opponent's position (*matānujñā*), overlooking a censurable point (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*), censuring one who is not censurable (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), deviation from a tenet (*apasiddhānta*), and fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). (Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.1)
These twenty-two types will now be explained in detail:
"Granting the property of the counter-example [to one's own example] constitutes the abandonment of one's own proposition" (Nyāyasūtra 5.2.4).
Having refuted the view of the Bhāṣyakāra, this Vārttikakāra states his own established position, saying: "We shall explain that very point."
The sense is that since the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra has already been refuted by Bhāradvāja himself, our burden is now half-finished.
In this regard, the view of the Bhāṣyakāra is as follows:

when one who has countered [the opponent] with a property contrary to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) fails to acknowledge the property of the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭāntadharma*) in his own example, he abandons his proposition; this is "abandonment of the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*).

In the demonstration "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses, like a jar," when the opponent objects, "The universal (sāmānya) is seen to be perceptible by the senses and yet is eternal; why then is sound not likewise [eternal]?"—and thus stands in opposition—the proponent says, "If the universal is perceptible by the senses, then let the jar also be eternal. This person, indeed, by attributing eternality to the example used in the proof, abandons his own position immediately after the conclusion (*nigamana*). And for one who abandons the position, it is called "abandonment of the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*).
Because the thesis (pakṣa) is the locus of the proposition (pratijñā),
this has been refuted by the author of the Vārttika in this manner; however,
we do not understand how the proposition is here abandoned, since the opponent merely objects that the reason (hetu) is inconclusive (anaikāntika) by means of a general example.

Without having stated the removal of the fault of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) regarding that [reason], he attempts to establish permanence in his own example; and because of this attempt to establish permanence, the fault of the example becomes one of being unestablished (*asiddha*). Thus, this is a defeat (*nigraha*) either by way of a fault in the example or a fault in the reason, and not a "relinquishment of the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*).
Nevertheless, it is designated as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) in a figurative sense, on the grounds that by relinquishing the example, he relinquishes the proposition.

Since a metaphorical usage cannot be established when the primary sense is impossible, one must state the primary object of the proposition; thus, fearing the abandonment of his thesis, the author now presents the view of the Vārttikakāra himself with the words "of the counter-example," and so forth. But what is intended here as an example? If it is that wherein there is a consensus of understanding between ordinary people and experts, then that is the example according to the *Nyāya-sūtra* (1.1.25).
1.25 Thus, if [the term] were technical, there would be no difference from the view of the Bhāṣyakāra; and in that regard, [the objection] has been countered.
Then he says: "But if it is something else, that is not perceived."

In this context, that which is "seen" (dṛṣṭa) is established at the end of the five-membered proof as the conclusion (*nigamana*); thus, it is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Together with the word *pakṣa*, there is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).
That which is the opposite of this is the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*).

For example, when a proponent states, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," and the opponent objects generally that this reason is inconclusive because it also exists in the counter-example—since universals (*sāmānya*) and the like are perceptible by the senses yet eternal—the proponent replies, "If that is so, let sound be likewise [eternal]. This is the point of defeat called "abandoning the thesis" (*pratijñāhāni*). Why? Because it involves relinquishing the original proposition.

Because of the abandonment of the previously asserted impermanence of sound, [the opponent] objects to this by means of the term "pratijñāhāni" (retraction of the proposition), wherein the word *dharma* refers to the property that serves as the qualification of the subject (*dharmī*), since it is a constituent part of the whole complex.
In this regard, according to the view of Bhāradvāja, since the abandonment of a thesis that has been accepted constitutes the reason for "abandonment of the thesis" (*pratijñāhāni*),
what determines the specific restriction of that [definition]?
By what means is it established that "abandonment of the thesis" consists in this manner— namely, the admission of a property belonging to the opposing side within one's own position?
It might be thought: "This very abandonment of the thesis (*prati-jñā-hāni*) is the [only] method; there is no other. Therefore, it is stated for the sake of restriction.
For it is possible that [the abandonment could occur] by another means as well.
Or, it might be thought: "This is the primary cause; therefore, when this has been demonstrated, the other [methods] are also effectively revealed."
Regarding this, he says here as well:

"And this very reason is the cause for the exposure of defects in the logical reason (*hetu*) and so forth; because when the opponent has thus established [the refutation] by exposing the defects in the reason and so on, the proponent must abandon the thesis due to the statement of a valid refutation.
And as for what was stated—that when it is said "the universal is eternal and perceptible," one might reply "let sound be likewise"—to this he provides the following response:

This, moreover, is entirely irrelevant, because what person of sound mind, upon the mere presentation of a general property (*sāmānya*), would— without investigating whether that [property] exists and whether it is perceptible by the senses and eternal— accept that the word is eternal? At most, one might become doubtful, since even an eternal general property is perceptible by the senses, yet that same perceptibility is observed in a jar, which is non-eternal.
Moreover, he states that in this case, the mere admission of the property of the counter-example is not appropriate:

"Nor is that property [of the example] [the same as] the property of that universal, namely eternality, such that by saying 'sound is non-eternal,' one would clearly have a direct counter-thesis in the form 'some sound is eternal'; for the universal is a different substratum (dharmin). For indeed, there is a contradiction between eternality and non-eternality only when they reside in the same locus, not when they reside in different loci."

The inclusion of the term "directly" (*āñjasā*) is for the purpose of indicating that this [opposing position] is a counter-thesis because it possesses contradictory properties, yet it is not as closely proximate as the example "sound is eternal.
It does not mean that one is subject to defeat on account of abandoning the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*) in this manner; to the question "by what means? he says:
Either by the admission of the counter-position’s property, or by this statement of a non-probative member [of the syllogism],
it is shown that this very [admission] is the primary cause, as previously stated.
In the Nyāya-bhāṣya of Vātsyāyana, 5.2.1.
In that very place, 5.2.2.
Nyāyavārttika 5.2.2

"Shifting the thesis (*pratijñāntara*) is the statement of another meaning for that same purpose, due to a modification of the property (*dharma*), when the original meaning is refuted. (Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.3) This is the second definition-sūtra.

The term "point of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*) applies throughout [the following]. Its meaning is as follows: when there is a refutation and a statement of the presence of the reason (*hetu*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), one makes a different proposition (*pratijñāntara*) for the sake of establishing the meaning of the previous proposition by means of a distinction between the properties of the similar example (*sapakṣa*) and the counter-example. For instance: "Just as a jar is non-omnipresent, so too is sound non-omnipresent; like a jar, sound is likewise impermanent. The rest is easily understood.
This [text] refutes that with the words "atrāpi" (9a8) and so forth;
for Abhidhakarṇa, in his *Bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, having raised this objection, desires to avoid it by saying:
"But surely, [the condition is] 'if there were non-omnipresence'."

However, since that which was stated with a qualification— the reason being qualified— is absent from the counter-example (vipakṣa), this is not the point of defeat known as "shifting the thesis" (pratijñāntara);
for it is not the case that one has introduced a new thesis by saying, "Sound is thus non-omnipresent."
The claim that "the inclusion of a qualification of the reason constitutes the ground for defeat known as *hetvantara* (shifting the reason)" is far too crude;

for a person of such refined intellect would merely qualify the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) itself, rather than introducing a new proposition (*pratijñāntara*), since [the original thesis] has already been established.

As for what was asserted— that the introduction of a qualification to the reason constitutes a different reason and is thus a point of defeat— that too is utterly trivial, because in that case let it simply be called "another proposition" (*pratijñāntara*),
as it is connected with [the definition of] "another proposition" through its similarity to the example and so forth.

Because of the absence of the definition of the proposition (*pratijñā*)— namely, "the statement of the probandum" (*sādhyānirdeśaḥ pratijñā*)— which [is required] for the definition of the reason (*hetu*) as "the means of proving the probandum through similarity with the example" (Nyāya-sūtra 1.1.34).
Furthermore, since this person, desiring to establish his proposition through mere assertion devoid of reasoning, does not accept that proof is achieved by the proposition alone,
he would not have stated the reason "because it is perceptible" even immediately after the first proposition.

Therefore, because it is impossible to enumerate such childish ravings as these— wherein another proposition is stated for the sake of proving a proposition— the restriction of definitions is entirely incoherent.
What is this "proposition-shifting" (pratijñāntara) that is called a point of defeat?

Is it not the case that there is no such restrictive definition as this, since [the definition] was formulated as: "When the meaning of the proposition is refuted, the restatement of that same meaning through a modification of the property"?
There is no fault, because that very same point is being stated through a different formulation.

Now, it might be argued: "Just as the learned do not state a proposition (*pratijñā*) by means of a proof for the proposition, so too they employ unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reasons for the sake of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*); therefore, you too should not have said [in the definition] 'the statement of what is not a member of the proof' (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) and so forth. To this, he says:
"Even for the learned... (9b6).
The meaning is that in my own system (*tantra*), the acceptance of a treatise (*śāstrābhyupagama*) is not established as being without authority (*apramāṇaka*) merely because it is a general rule;

for those heroes who are courageous in their determination to perceive reality do not respect the obstruction of the conventions of other systems when their minds have emerged [from meditative equipoise].
This is because the speech of one who lacks authority cannot override the acceptance of one who possesses valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since such an acceptance is inviolable by the wise.

And this would be the case because, by stating a proof that is not established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the proponent does not become a victor even though he has refuted the opposing position. [This is] "contradiction between the thesis and the reason," which is "contradiction of the thesis" according to Nyāya Sūtra 5.1.4.
The ninth point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) called "Nāma" is the proposition that substance (dravya) is distinct from its qualities (guṇa).
The reason "because no object distinct from color and so forth is perceived" constitutes a contradiction between the proposition and the reason;
for if substance were distinct from its qualities, the non-perception of an object distinct from color and so forth would be untenable.
Now, since no entity distinct from color and the other [sensory qualities] is perceived, it is not tenable that substance exists as something separate from its qualities.

By this very [point], the contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) has been explained by the author of the Sūtras as a contradiction with one's own words; this was stated by him for the purpose of illustration.
O Śramaṇas, [you claim] that there is an absence of sexual union with men, yet a fetus does not exist without sexual union with a man; thus, there is a contradiction of your own words.
By this, it is stated that there is a contradiction of the reason (*hetuvirodha*).
This applies to the entire [argument]: "separate," "distinct," "not one"—that is to say, no single entity exists.
The meaning is that because the word "entity" (*bhāva*) is applied to a collection— that is, because it is denotable by words such as "pot" which denote a collection—
since one who says "it is a collection" necessarily accepts a unity, for a collection is indeed a unification of many.

For instance, by one who perceives substances such as cows and the like as aggregated, a "collection" (samūha) must be admitted; yet this collection—namely, these substances existing in the form of cows and so forth—is not established [as a single entity]. Furthermore, since differentiation exists in degrees of being more or less minute, that which is there most extremely minute and indivisible is what remains after differentiation has ceased. And that from which this differentiation ceases is the One.

Now, if you think that which you consider to be an indivisible atom is also a collection of form and the other [sensory qualities], then according to this view, those form and other qualities which are collected together constitute the atom; it must therefore be stated: "In the atom there is form—of what is that a collection?
The same applies to the remaining qualities.
Now, if you do not accept that collection [as the atom], then the treatise stating that "an atom consists of eight substances gathered together" would be contradicted;
for the *Abhidharmakośa* (2.22) says: "In the desire realm, an atom that is without sound consists of eight substances."
Therefore, to claim that because one [mode of] arising is untenable, many modes of arising must exist, is extreme folly;
furthermore, this reason is unestablished.

Since a single entity is established as being connected with various characteristics such as odor and other qualities, as well as with parts such as the base, therefore, when a single object is apprehended from a word, the remaining associated meaning is understood.
But is this not also a contradiction between the proposition and the reason? Indeed, it is no different from the first [case].

It is not so; for Bhāradvāja has stated that since contradiction depends upon both [terms], the mention of either one may be intended according to the speaker's wish. Thus, there is no contradiction with the example in the proposition: "The manifest is of a single primordial nature because it is limited, like a bowl and so forth. In this case, the example—the bowl and so forth—actually subverts the property of having a single primordial nature.

Because the material cause (*prakṛti*), which serves as the illustrative example, is itself a distinct material cause, it would follow that there is no single material cause; or, if there were a single material cause, the examples such as the clay bowl and so forth would be inappropriate.

Furthermore, there is a contradiction between the reason and the examples and other factors, as in the case: "Substance is distinct from its qualities, because it is not perceived as a separate entity."
The example "like a jar and so forth" contradicts the reason, because jars and the like are perceived as distinct;
by the inclusion of the word "and so forth," the contradiction of the reason with the application (*upanaya*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*) is also understood.
An example of these two is as follows: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced;

whatever is produced is impermanent, like space; and sound is likewise produced. Here, there is a contradiction with the reason (*hetu*) due to the application (*upanaya*). For, according to the *Nyāya Sūtra* (1.2.43), the conclusion is an application based on the example, expressed either as "so it is" (*tathā*) or "not so it is" (*na tathā*). In this case, the application contradicts the reason.

1.38: The application (upanaya) was stated [in the previous section] as that which conforms to the probandum (sādhya), whereas here the example (udāharaṇa) is the opposite; thus, there is a contradiction of the reason (hetu) by virtue of this [contrary] application.

And in such an application, when the conclusion is summarized as "therefore, [sound] is impermanent," there is a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of the final restatement (*nigamana*); for example, the thesis and reason— "fire is not hot because it is a substance, like water"— contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and so forth regarding the opponent's position.

And this—namely, "that which does not depend on its own position," and so forth—is also included by the very [category] of "contradiction between the proposition and the reason"; thus, he shows that it should not be stated as a separate ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). In the phrase "the opponent's position," when the opponent has established a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), Kaṇāda points out that it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Regarding the phrase "and independent of its own side," the distinction is that the Vaiśeṣika alone provides the proof, while the opponent demonstrates its fallibility (*vyabhicāra*).

If, then, a contradictory response is given when fallibility has been established by means of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, [the opponent] says: "In that case, the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason would be without a subject."

"Both" (ubhaya) refers to that which is established for both the proponent and the opponent, and is agreed upon by both parties; because it has that as its object, it is "inconclusive" (anaikāntika) by way of metaphorical designation, and thus the term "inconclusive" is applied to it. Regarding the phrase "here too," etc.: * **Inconclusive (anaikāntika):** A reason is called "inconclusive" when it is present in both the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), thereby failing to establish a necessary connection with the probandum. * **Metaphorical designation (upacāra):** The term "inconclusive" is applied to the subject of the debate (the *pakṣa*) because it is the locus of that inconclusive reason. * **Agreed upon by both (ubhayapakṣasaṃpratipanna):** This indicates that the reason must be acknowledged by both sides of the dispute to be valid in this context. * **The phrase "here too" (atrāpi):** This introduces the subsequent discussion regarding how such a reason functions within the logical framework.

Nor does this refute that [contradiction], for that contradiction has as its basis that very thesis; it is "based on that" (tad-āśraya), meaning it has that thesis as its basis, or "produced by that" (tat-kṛta), meaning it is produced by that thesis.
The remainder is exceedingly clear.

Even in the case of entities distinct [from the locus], such as piśācas and the like, which are remote from something like a mountain, this very thing—the formulation of the proposition—is the ground for defeat (*nigrahādhikaraṇa*);
it does not follow that contradiction of the proposition is the ground for defeat. This is what is understood.
What is meant by this? It means because that [the thesis] is its locus, that is, because it is the substratum of the proposition (*pratijñā*).
If that locus [of the thesis] were not present, it would constitute a ground for defeat;
thus he says "yadi" (if) and so forth.
The conclusion or completion of the discourse—that is, the debate—is its termination, and the formal statement of the proposition (*pratijñāprayoga*) is the cause of that [termination].
It is recited that because the proponent suffers defeat by stating a non-essential member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*) with that alone,

there is an occasion for the conclusion of the discussion at some point; even in that case, the meaning is that there is an "occasion" or "authority" (*adhikāra*) when the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) has been employed, since the debate has not yet reached its completion.

Now, just as you establish a single property of an object—such as its momentariness—by means of many reasons, such as existence, having an origin, and being differentiated by the diversity of cognitions, so too is a single thesis (*pakṣa*) that has been put forward by another to be refuted, whether by way of restating the proposition (*pratijñā*), by way of contradicting it, or otherwise.
And thus, this is not a fault, because there is no defeating of one who has already been defeated.
To this, he says:

However, as for those which are called "reasons" (hetu), they possess efficacy because they function toward the establishment of the probandum (sādhya) through conceptualization— either by disregarding the preceding reason or by thinking, "I shall establish this in this way, or otherwise."
What, then, is the reason why there is neither a conjunction nor an application [of another reason]? He says:

otherwise, if in the case of conjunction no application of another distinct reason is intended, then because the second would be redundant—referring here to the phrase "the universal by way of option"—he demonstrates that it is indeed redundant.
For if, even in that case, the employment of one were not possible without the employment of the other— since the determination of the rule would result from the negation of both—
the meaning is that if, upon the employment of one, the employment of the other were possible through conjunction (samuccaya).
In that case, there would be no purpose for a second [reason], because there is no need to demonstrate what has already been understood;

since it would be occupied solely with the very object already established by the first reason, it would lack the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), just as an axe or similar tool has no such status once its function on the wood has already been accomplished.
Now, one might object: "But surely, just as with the proof (*sādhana*), the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) will also proceed by way of the same alternatives."
He thinks thus:
"The opponent will not accept it in this way;
for in that case, he would have himself admitted that the [reason] is not a constituent part of the proof for the proposition."
And consequently, this [definition] is contradicted:
"The thesis, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion are the members" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.32).

32. Thus, by means of these other reasons—which negate the existence of a composite substance (*avayavidravya*)—it has been established that words such as "jar" do not denote specific composite substances characterized as a single jar and so forth; rather, they denote the generality (*sāmānya*) of multiple objects such as color-form (*rūpa*), which consists in the capacity for a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyāsāmarthya*). Furthermore, it has been shown that every word-referent, such as color-form, which is capable of a single purposeful action, possesses a manifold nature (*nānārtharūpatā*) by virtue of its being the instrument [of that action].

It is a single entity, and its nature is that of a specific thing, namely the form of a composite substance (*avayavidravya*). Demonstrating the absence of this state—its being a single specific thing—the Buddhist might say, "There is no single entity. However, he would not be rejecting the forms (*rūpa*) that are the objects of the senses, because [the capacity] is not distinct from form and so forth. Furthermore, since that capacity is itself manifold, how can it be said to be one? Or else, how could it be the referent of a word?
For it is never said that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the referent of a word.

Even though things are diverse, because they do not exclude one another and produce a single effect through their capacity, they act as the cause for a single unifying cognition (*ekapratyavamarśa*); thus, they are called "one" in a figurative sense.
As it has been said:
"Because it is the cause of a single unifying cognition, the intellect is non-different."
In one way, there is also non-difference among individuals by virtue of their causal nature.
(25) As long as the person’s determination (*adhyavasāya*) is not suspended, that [universal] is established as the meaning of a word.

For the person, through the power of the ripening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from beginningless false habitual practice, projects an internal form onto external objects and perceives the identity between the perceived and the conceptualized. In ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, words are indeed devoid of any [external] object.
Because the form of consciousness in individual instances lacks any conformity with an external object, it is beyond the scope of verbal expression; yet,
since the form exists according to its cognitive determination (*adhyavasāya*),
as it is stated in the Sūtra.

"For by whatever name each phenomenon is expressed, that [phenomenon] does not exist therein; for that is the true nature (dharmatā) of phenomena. (26) Thus, the summarized meaning here is as follows: form and so forth, as well as the jar, possess respectively multiplicity and unity, because they are denoted by plural and singular grammatical endings.

For example, by means of fallacious inferences such as "the stars are the moon," the opponent's accepted object of the word "pot" and so forth—which is a single entity designated as a "whole" (avayavin)—is precisely what is being refuted;
however, color, taste, and the like, which are of the nature of atoms, are not [refuted], for it is indeed admitted that they each possess a singular nature individually.
It is simply that, like seeds that have been singed, they do not form a collection [on their own]; thus, it was stated [in the verse] in order to illustrate their fixed simultaneous arising.

In the *Abhidharmakośa*, Chapter 2, verse 27, it is stated: "A subtle atom (paramāṇu) in the realm of desire consists of eight substances and is devoid of sound; it is beyond the senses. One possessing the body-faculty consists of nine substances, and one possessing another faculty consists of ten substances."
For by whatever name any phenomenon is expressed,
that [phenomenon] does not exist therein; for such is the true nature of phenomena.
An atom in the realm of desire consists of eight substances and is devoid of sound; it is supersensible.

An atom possessing the body-faculty consists of nine substances, and one possessing another faculty consists of ten substances. However, the manner in which atoms are perceptible by the senses and their impermanence has been explained by us in detail elsewhere.
As for the argument that [the self is manifold] because it is denoted by both plural and singular number, that is inconclusive;

for instance, when there is the conventional usage "wife" (*dārāḥ*), "waters" (*āpaḥ*), or "sands" (*sikatāḥ*) even with respect to a single woman, water, or a mass of sand, what plurality is there in those cases by which such usage occurs? If you say it is due to a difference in capacities (*śakti-bheda*), [we reply: so be it.
If it is argued that the singular number is now abolished everywhere due to the absence of a single power,
whereas the singular number occurs elsewhere because of the non-difference of the object, then let it be so here as well.
Thus, this groundless restriction being imposed reveals the autonomy of desire in the employment of words;
by this, that which Kumārila said is also refuted:
"In that regard, if a word such as *dāra* is employed for both the individual and the genus..."
Or does it function by taking the number of the individual parts?
How then can there be the singular number in "ṣaṇṇagarī" (the six cities), for the cities themselves are not some single entity; how then could there be a collection of them?

Since there is no production of heterogeneous entities such as palaces and persons, how could their collection be a substance? Furthermore, it cannot be a conjunction, because there is no mutual conjunction among the palace and its parts;
moreover, since the palace itself consists of conjunction, it lacks further qualities and thus cannot be conjoined with anything else.
And for that very reason, number would be non-existent.

If it is argued that "city" is existence (*sattā*) qualified by its conjunction with persons, then what qualification could there be for this undifferentiated existence? Furthermore, since existence is a single entity, even when there is a plurality of cities, the plural form "cities" (*nagarāṇi*) would still occur.
If it is argued that [the city] is the mutual accompaniment of these two, then what kind of assistance can there be between two things that do not benefit one another?
Furthermore, since the person (puruṣa), the conjunction (saṃyoga), and existence (sattā) are plural, how can the word "city" be used in the singular?
If it is argued that the power (*śakti*) of things existing in such a state is sometimes non-distinct [from the thing itself] and serves as the cause, we say no;
for power is not distinct from the nature of the entity (*vastu*).
If it were distinct, then that which is not benefited by another could not logically possess dependence upon it.

Alternatively, if there is a distinction [between the power and the possessor of power] even when the power is capable of assisting, then because of that persistence, there would be a failure of cognition;
if there were no distinction from it, the same consequence would apply to other powers as well—thus, this [argument] is trivial.
He states another alternative as well:

This is an illustration of what has been seen; furthermore, he says "the produced, the impermanent, and so forth" (10b7) to show that it is indeed an example even when expressed in the ablative case (*pañcamyanta*), just as it was stated by him.

Where the concomitance of the probandum with the reason is stated, as well as its absence in the case of its absence, by means of the fifth [case-ending], that is the example; the reason, however, consists of the application (*upanaya*). (29)

When there is a dispute regarding a certain object, such as a substance like a jar—concerning whether it exists or does not exist apart from its color and other qualities—he points to the well-known application of words for a universal (*sāmānya*) such as "Ṣaṇṇagarī" (the City of Six), which is superimposed by the intellect upon various mutually exclusive objects like cities. By means of this subsequent application (*upanaya*), having intended to conclude with the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), he demonstrates that the application of a term denoting an entity (*bhāva-śabda*) occurs toward a collection formed by the intellect out of things that are mutually exclusive yet follow into a single conceptual unity; thus, having established the point of dispute, he concludes by way of a generalization.
The analysis of the compound is: "that by which all [things] are established as distinct is the locus of practice.
This is what is meant.

While there is a dispute as to whether or not the whole (avayavin) exists apart from the skull-bones and other parts, this example is presented to indicate a reason possessing the three characteristics;
however, the formal syllogism (prayoga) is formulated here as follows:
those things which are mutually distinct do not possess a form that is permeated by a single, separate substance that is the whole.
Just as the six cities and so forth, and likewise the skull-bones and so forth which are mutually distinct,
if a word such as *dāra* (wife/consort) is applied there to both the individual and the genus;
It functions by taking up either the number of the individuals or the number of their parts.

(28) Where the positive concomitance of the reason with the probandum is stated, as well as its absence when [the probandum] is absent, by means of the fifth case-ending—that is the example; the reason, however, consists of the application (upanaya). (29)

Now, if this application of the example were not stated by that very straightforward sequence of its formal application— as in "whatever is existent is momentary, like a jar" and so forth— then what is the purpose of the indication using the ablative case (pañcamī),
and why is the object of the dispute not shown as being characterized by the negation of the whole (avayavin) with respect to the shards and so on?

Just as elsewhere [it is said], "Sound is impermanent because it is produced and impermanent," why is the reason clearly shown here to be concomitant with the probandum?
