For in this case, since the word "collection" (samūha) is applied to things that are mutually excluded and not concomitant with a single object once they have been mentally unified, the completion of the sentence must be inferred [as follows]: "Because [the word 'collection'] is applied to a state of collection when [individuals] have been mentally brought together."
To this, the reply is: "No, because it is a concise indication," meaning because it is a brief statement.

Even so, since such usage is observed—as in "because of being produced" and "because of being impermanent"—this sentence is not a proof (*asādhana*), but rather a statement indicating the conceptualization of the application of a proof (*sādhanaprayoga*) due to its being a [complete] sentence.
The meaning is that this is not a statement of a proof (*sādhana-vākya*).
"For this very reason" means precisely because it is a statement of an example (*dṛṣṭānta-vākya*).
And as for this logical reason (*hetu*): "The forms of the threads and the cloth have distinct causes, because they possess specific qualities, like color and touch."

This [reason] is also unestablished because its substratum is unestablished; for since the difference between the thread and the cloth has not been proven, the quality residing therein is likewise not proven to be distinct. Thus, it is insufficient for establishing the desired conclusion.
For others explain that "possessing particularity" consists either in inherence in substances of subtle and gross dimensions, or in inherence in substances produced at different times.

[Objection: "But surely there are speakers with diverse intentions; among them, we state that the thesis contradicts the reason only in the case of those who employ words solely with the intention of providing a reason, and not in the case of those who take pride in their examples. To this, he says: "And not... (10b9), and so forth.

The summary meaning is this: the contradiction raised by you, the followers of Ākṣapāda (the Naiyāyikas), against those who rely on the view of the Blessed Tathāgata, does not exist for us even in our dreams. There certainly exists the Yogācāra position—that through simultaneous conjunction with [other] atoms, an atom attains the state of a mote of dust.

By stating, "Because the six [atoms] occupy the same location, the aggregate would be the size of a single atom," and so forth, it is said that even one who does not accept the unity of the atom nevertheless accepts the aggregate—which is synonymous with a collection—as real; this is expressed by the words "even he" (yo 'pi) and so on. However, what is actually intended to be proven by this method is the non-existence of the atom itself.
How is unity refuted by the negation of being one or many?
First, unity is refuted through such arguments as its lack of connection with mud.
Since that [entity] does not exist, its nature as a composite— that is, its multiplicity— also does not exist,
as it has been stated: "Indeed,
whatever entity is examined, that very thing lacks unity."

"Therefore, there are not even many, since not even one is found" (31). Now, how is unity refuted by means of [the analysis of] connection with parts and so forth, given that in that case its state of having parts was established?

Furthermore, those very parts of it are the smallest atoms (*paramāṇu*), because atoms are characterized by having their division come to an end. Now, if one were to apply this same method to show that even those limbs possess parts, then the same answer would apply there as well; thus, in this manner, it is impossible to deny the oneness of the atom.

Since division is dependent upon that which is divided, how can one who does not accept atoms accept their conjunction with mud and so forth? Therefore, all the reasons for proving their non-existence are inherently unestablished in their substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*).

But this is not so; for competent disputants call that entity which has reached its minimum limit—devoid of any further division of parts—an "atom" (*aṇu*), and it is the unity of that [entity] which is being refuted by its conjunction with mud and so forth.

And if, having been thus refuted, they nevertheless accept that the object under consideration possesses parts, then they would fall away from their own thesis; for those who do not admit that it has parts are not entitled to respond in such a manner. Let those very parts themselves be the atoms.
Furthermore, it is precisely by those [means] that its definition must be established and by the Yogācāra that it must be negated; thus they are refuted.
For this very reason, there is no consequence of infinite regress, and because it is a proof by means of a prasanga, the fault of being unestablished (asiddha) does not exist either—enough of this.
Now, it is said: "We do not say this to you; rather, we say it to whoever—be they a venerable one or a disputant—who speaks thus.

That [objection] is incorrect, because all things possess distinct characteristics due to their separateness (*pṛthaktva*). This is because a single entity cannot be established by means of multiple characteristics, as was stated in the section concerning Bhāradvāja when our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*) was introduced against us with the words, "O Kāmeṣṭadravyaka, who [is there]? and so forth.
Nevertheless, having provisionally accepted [the opponent's position], he states another fault.

Nor is this [type of contradiction] distinct from the previously mentioned contradictions indicated by the words "distinct from the quality" (*guṇavyatirikta*) and so forth; for there is no difference in meaning between the two examples of contradiction—whether they relate to the connection between the reason and the thesis or are presented separately—though there is merely a difference in wording. Furthermore, if such [separate] examples were to be given, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), whereby one would have to provide examples such as: "Sound is unproduced because it is produced."
In some recensions, the reading is "saha vā pṛthak vā" (together or separately).
In that case, the meaning is as follows: "saha" means simultaneously, as in the first instance; "pṛthak" means individually, as in this instance.
Alternatively, he states that even the consideration of contradiction is inappropriate here.
Furthermore,

the reason— "because the term 'existent' (bhāva) is applied to each individual as well as to the collection"— is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is not a property of the subject (*dharmin*) in its entirety, but rather a property of words (*śabdadharmatvāt*).

And thus, because of the lack of a common locus (*vyadhikaraṇatva*), the very fault of being unestablished (*asiddhatā*) remains—just as in the case [of the fallacious argument]: "Sugar is sweet because a crow is black.

In that instance, there would be no contradiction because the reason and the meaning of the thesis have different loci; however, this is not the case here, because of the usage by Bhāvivikta in his *Bhāṣya-ṭīkā*: "Because it is denotable by a word expressing a collection (*samūha*). Thus, there is no lack of a common locus.

He thinks as follows: "This fault was not initiated by us against Uddyotakara for having employed [the reason] in this manner; even for those who employ it differently at present, let this fault remain if it does not apply.
However, the fault just mentioned and that which is about to be stated cannot be avoided even by Brahmā himself.
And it was with the admission that the contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) constitutes a separate point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) that I stated this.
But that [defeat] is not applicable to him; rather, fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). (Nyāyasūtra 5.2.24)
Desiring to state that [the faults] are included by this very [definition], he says:
"Moreover," and so forth.
That class of faults—that type of defect—consists of two members; thus, it is "twofold" (*dvayī*).
To what does he refer?
To contradiction (*viruddhatā*) and unestablishedness (*asiddhatā*).
Furthermore, as to how there is contradiction, he says:
Regarding "contradiction" (*viruddhatā*) and so forth,
this is the summary of the meaning here:
in whatever application of a thesis (*pratijñā*) and a reason (*hetu*) contradiction is alleged, there must necessarily be an established subject (*dharmin*).
And when that [locus] is established, there would be the existence of either the property of the subject (*dharmin*) or the probandum-property (*sādhyadharma*),
or both; however, in this case, there is not the existence of both, because they are mutually contradictory like cold and heat, and thus lack a common locus.

Otherwise, because they would exist together in one place, there would be no contradiction at all— just as between taste and form— and thus a contradiction between the proposition and the reason would follow most certainly;
for he will state later that "since two contradictory natures cannot exist in one place, there is no contradiction otherwise."

Furthermore, even if the reason exists there, if the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) does not exist where the reason is present, while its opposite does exist, then its contradictory nature is evident,
just as in the case [of the fallacious argument]: "Sound is eternal because it is produced."
Thus it is said:
"The contradiction [of the reason] consists in its presence in the subject (*dharmī*) despite the establishment [of the opposite].

When, however, the existence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in that subject has been ascertained by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the reason does not occur there, because it is encompassed by its contradictory.

Therefore, the reason "sound is produced because it is not an effect" is unestablished (*asiddha*); just as in the case of [the argument] "those two are produced from that," there is again non-establishment regarding the subject (*dharmin*), and so forth.

Now, you might think: "The contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) is established only when the subject (*dharmin*), such as substance (*dravya*), is already established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as distinct from its qualities (*guṇa*); therefore, this fault does not apply. To this, he raises the following objection with the words "unestablished" (*asiddha*, 11b8) and so forth:

even if, in this way, the charge of being contradictory (*viruddhatva*) is avoided because the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is impossible due to the non-existence of the subject (*dharmyabhāva*).
Reflecting that the state of being unestablished remains exactly as it was, he says:
"But when there is a connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), both the proponent and the opponent have doubt regarding the presence of the reason in the subject;
for even when a means of valid cognition is absent, the non-existence of the object is not established."

Therefore, [the reason] is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*) because its locus is doubtful, as in the example: "There is a peacock in this bower, because of the sound of its cry. However, when there is an absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish the subject, the reason's state of having a doubtful locus is clearly established as *āśrayāsiddha* (unestablished in its locus) once a means of valid cognition that subverts the subject (*dharmibādhakapramāṇa*) is operative.
The phrase "like the quality of being perceived everywhere" serves as a collective illustration when the self is to be proven as omnipresent;
for in that case, [the subject] would be intended as unestablished either because the establishing proof does not apply— as in the argument "the nature of the subject is unestablished"—
or because the subverting proof does apply.
In the former position, the fault was stated explicitly; in the latter, it is joined with the word "and.
Here, he anticipates the response of Audyotakara by means of the passage beginning with "because it depends on both," and so forth.
Since the meaning has already been explained, all of this is easily understood;
however, he refutes it with the words "not in all cases" and so forth, as was previously stated in the passage beginning with "the two types of faults."

Now, if it is established that contradiction of the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*) consists merely in the thesis itself being [inconsistent] without depending on a reason—as in the case of "O ascetics, there is no self; a woman is pregnant"—then he says: "And if [the contradiction] were independent [of a reason], the mention of a reason would be irrelevant, because it would provide no assistance."

Furthermore, regarding this example of contradiction with the reason (*hetuvirodha*) given by the words "sound is eternal," etc., he says "na ced... (if not... and so forth, in order to state that it is improper [to claim] that there is a contradiction with the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*) by means of the reason.

It might be thought: "Even if this is so, because contradiction relies upon both [the reason and the thesis], it does not arise from the reason alone"; therefore, he says "ubhayāśraye 'pi... (even though it relies upon both), etc.
Having introduced the examples thus demonstrated, he speaks in order to extend the refutation to what was previously stated:

"And as for what was said—that by this [reasoning] 'contradiction with the example' and so forth must also be stated for the proposition, according to the maxim of a clown's painting" (11b5)—the word *iti* is to be understood as meaning "must be stated"; otherwise, because the opponent would not have employed a reply, [the objection] would be ill-connected.
The mention of "jugglers" (*bhaṇḍa*) is for the purpose of illustrating the "eternal person" (*nityapuruṣa*).

For just as jugglers, in order to amaze common folk, paint images such as wooden statues of monkeys endowed with various characteristics, and—having mastered the skill of diverse arts and crafts—instruct [the audience] that "other objects of this kind, produced by our skill, such as figures of elephants and so forth, should be understood to exist within the space of a single palm-clap," so too is this [argument] of Uddyotakara of that same nature.
For indeed, this very [argument] exhibits a contradiction with the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, while being endowed with characteristics distinct from those of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
But what need is there for further deliberation regarding that which has been extended by analogy?

He begins to state that the very same [definition] applies to what is extended by analogy, showing its lack of a definition distinct from the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)—such as contradiction with the example (*dṛṣṭāntavirodha*) and so forth—with the words "In that case also... and so on.

Where there is a contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there too, a contradiction of the proposition by the example would occur if the example possesses the opposite of the property that has been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta-dharma*). This is the implied meaning. The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that which possesses the opposite (*viparyaya*) of that which is both the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*) and the property (*dharma*). And the term "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) here refers to an example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Since the intended dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) possesses precisely the opposite of the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma), what contradiction is there in that?
An illustration for this is as follows:

In the case of the [fallacious] contradictory example, "Sound is eternal, like a pot," if the presence of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being non-common (*ananyasādhāraṇā*), then it is a contradictory fallacy of the reason (*viruddho hetvābhāsaḥ*).
The term "non-common" (*ananyasādhāraṇā*) means that which is not shared with anything else.

The meaning is as follows: by the word "other" (anya), that which possesses the opposite of the property under consideration (*pakṣīkṛtadharma*) is intended to be distinct from that which possesses the property under consideration; thus, if it is being proved that [the reason] exists only in that which possesses the opposite of the property under consideration—for example, in these very same cases of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), [the reason] such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) does not exist in space (*vyoman*) and so forth, which are the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) possessing the opposite of that property, but it does exist in a jar, which is the opposite of those—then, when this common occurrence (*sādhāraṇā vṛtti*) has been established, the phrase "in both the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)" is to be supplied as the remainder.
The inconclusive [reason] known as "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) is, for example, "because of being an object of cognition" (*prameyatvāt*) in these same two cases of the probandum and the example.

As long as the restriction of its non-occurrence in those two—namely, the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)—has not been established, it is inconclusive; for it might occur only in the similar instance or only in the dissimilar instance. Thus, it is inconclusive, being either one where the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is doubtful or one where the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.

Just as [the reason] "because he is a speaker" [is inconclusive] regarding whether a person intended to be spoken of is either omniscient and free from passion or not— like a common street person— so too,
when there is non-occurrence in both the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), it is the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) [inconclusive reason],
such as "sound is eternal because it is audible."

The opponent says: "When there is an occurrence of a contradictory example and an occurrence of the reason in the opposite [of what it is meant to prove], there is no fault in the reason whatsoever. For example: 'Sound is impermanent because it varies according to differences in its conditions, like space'—this is by way of similarity;
and by way of dissimilarity, 'like a jar.
Here, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhatva*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*), because the reason exists therein."
Nor is there inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva), because [the reason] does not occur in either case;

nor is there contradiction (viruddhatva), because it does not occur in the opposite manner in both the similar instances (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), since the necessary connection (pratibandha) exists.

However, the objection that "there is a contradiction of the proposition by the example" does not refute this point— that the scope of the proposition has not transcended the faults of the reason, and thus there is a contradiction of the proposition by the example.

Even then, because it does not transcend being a cause for doubt—since there is no contradiction with the proposition (*pratijñā*) in the example of similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), that is a fault in the example of similarity, but not in the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
Why? Because contradiction is intended [only] in the case of similarity.

The intention is that a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is indeed defined as one that possesses the opposite of the property to be proven (*pakṣīkṛta-dharma*). Even if this were not the case, he asks: "How then is there no departure from the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*)? He replies: In a similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) that possesses a contrary property, such as the ether (*nabhas*), it is impossible to demonstrate the state of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra-dharmatā*);
and it is for that purpose that an example is presented.

As it has been said: "The reason is stated to have three characteristics; when it is established as residing in the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), the remaining two characteristics are demonstrated by means of an example" (32).
Now, one might ask: how can it be impossible, given that being differentiated by the variation of conditions (*pratyayabhedabheditva*) is in reality non-deviant from impermanence? To this, he says:

In reality, even if there is non-deviation from the probandum (sādhyāvyabhicāre 'pi)— the sense being that although non-deviation exists, it is as good as non-existent because it has not been established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)— therefore,
the ascertainment of the probandum does not arise from a reason that is not connected through a demonstrated invariable concomitance (avinābhāva).
Therefore, even the contradiction of the example with the proposition does not escape the category of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*),
because at that time its exclusion from the opposite class remains doubtful; this was already indicated by the word "also" (*api*), which implies that it is not merely a contradiction of the reason.

In both cases— whether by way of the reason (*hetu*) or by way of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)— it is not by way of the reason that [the fault applies], because once the opponent has been defeated through the incidental occurrence of a fault in the example prior to the reason, there is no further defeat of one already defeated, since another fault (such as contradiction with the example) need not be stated. This is the intended meaning regarding the Naiyāyika who maintains a specific order for the members of a proof (*sādhanāvayava*), for he adheres to the sequence of proposition (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*udāharaṇa*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*).
What, then, is its excellence?
To this he says: "The similarity with the example" (udāharaṇasādharmyam), etc.
This was stated while accepting [the opponent's position], but there is no contradiction with the example, as it does not touch upon the nature of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
As it was stated immediately above,

by this the formulation of faults based on conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has been refuted. Thus, it is established that in this way, the contradiction of the example with the proposition does not escape the category of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).

Furthermore, as for what was stated in the *Bhāṣyaṭīkā* by Aviddhakarṇa— that [the world] clearly has a single material cause because it is finite, like a bowl and so forth— even there the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), because the reason "being finite" does not exist in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and,
conversely, exists in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), such as bowls which have multiple material causes.
Since clay is divided both moment by moment and part by part,
even the reason (hetu) now stands in contradiction with the example (dṛṣṭānta);
thus he states that when a reason contradicts the example, it is an uncommon [inconclusive] fallacy (asādhāraṇa-hetvābhāsa) because it does not occur in either instance.
Or rather, when is there contradiction? He says:

"If it were [the case] in the dissimilar instance (vaidharmya), then an example for this has been stated by that very same [author]: 'Substance is distinct from quality, because it is not perceived as a separate entity, like a jar. Here too, if the qualification 'while being visible' is applied to the reason, it is contradictory, because it does not exist in the similar instances (sapakṣa)."

Furthermore, since [the subject] exists in its own nature as form and so forth even in the case of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), if no qualification were provided, there would be a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*); for even non-perceived entities such as *piśācas*, which are distinct from one another, exist as separate things. Moreover, the example "like a jar" is not appropriate here, because that very jar has been made the subject (*pakṣa*) precisely because it is a distinct substance.

The apprehension of that [self] as distinct from form and the other [sensory objects] has already been refuted; and since such apprehension is unestablished, the fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) remains as we maintain.

Now, he asks: "What is the fallacy of the reason when there is a contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? He replies: "It is 'unestablished' (*asiddha*), because coldness does not exist in fire."
Furthermore, as for the other example given here— "fire is not hot because it is a substance, like water"— that is incorrect;
for direct perception does not subvert the reason (hetu),
since [the nature of fire as hot] is established in the subject (dharmin).
But if it is argued that non-heat is the meaning of the proposition,

and because the meaning of the proposition is sublated by perception, there is no pervasion (vyāpti) of the reason by that [proposition], and thus the reason is said to be contradicted by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—

then, in that case, since there is no pervasion by the contradictory property to be proven (sādhyadharma), the reason-fallacy is one whose negative concomitance (vyatireka) is doubtful; thus, our own position is indeed supported.
Because of simultaneous conjunction with six [other atoms], the atom would become a fly; because the six occupy the same location, the entire mass would be no larger than a single atom.
There is no unity in that which is examined as each individual entity.
"Therefore, there are not even many [reasons] by which even one is not found;
thus it is said that the reason has three forms. Being established as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), the remaining two forms are demonstrated by means of the example. (31–32)
Because a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not exceed the category of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
As it has been said:
"Those contradictions with perception and so forth which occur at the time [of establishing] pervasion (*vyāpti*)," [are fallacious].
It might be thought that none of these are joined with a contradictory pervading property (vyāpti-dharma).

Thus, there may be the view that contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñā*) with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-virodha*) cannot be subsumed under the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), because it occurs solely due to the [proposition] itself. To this he says:

"Contradiction of the proposition with a means of valid cognition is explained by contradiction with one's own words" (12a2). A counter-argument has already been made there; in that context, this very point constitutes the ground for defeat (*nigrahādhikaraṇa*), namely, the employment of a proposition—which is not a constituent part of the proof—within the statement of the proof, and so forth.

Thus, he concludes with "therefore all [are valid]"; as for the other objection raised by the proponent—that the response is contradictory—he introduces it [only] to show that it is entirely irrelevant, because [he says] "if indeed," etc. (12a3).

When one person—whether a Buddhist or someone else—puts forward the argument, "Sound is non-eternal because it is perceptible by the senses, like a jar," a Mīmāṃsaka or a Vaiśeṣika might seek to establish the fallibility (*vyabhicāra*) of the opponent's reason (the Buddhist) by means of a universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*), which is established for his own side. If he were to say to the opponent, "Cowness is also perceptible by the senses; therefore, according to you, it too would follow that it is non-eternal"—thus attributing [this consequence] to the opponent to demonstrate a fallacy—then that universal (*sāmānya*) of the Buddhist would be both perceptible and eternal. Since the Buddhist does not accept eternal categories, such a thing is not accepted by him and contradicts his own position. Therefore, how can there be a fallacy? This constitutes a contradiction, an inconsistency, or rather, an irrationality. One must supply the words: "it is appropriate for the respondent [to point this out]."

But he does not, like another, merely cast a burden upon the opponent to manifest a fallacy; so how could there be a contradiction in the response? For that respondent, being himself uncertain because the reason—sensory perceptibility—is present in "cowness" (*gotva*), which he has personally accepted as eternal, expresses his own lack of apprehension and indecision by saying: "Is sound impermanent due to sensory perceptibility like a jar, or is it eternal like cowness and the like? Thus, by putting forward his own position—that in the case of the true side (*satpakṣa*), cowness is indeed both sensory and eternal—he raises the objection of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).

Therefore, the collective meaning would be that the answer is indeed correct; however, since for the Buddhist there is no such thing as an eternal *gotva* (cowness), the answer is actually contradictory. To this he says:
"And that reason, because it is non-sensory (*atīndriyatvāt*)," whether *gotva* exists or does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

One whose capacity to prove [the probandum] has not been established is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it causes doubt due to the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the opposite case. The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that which has its capacity for proving—characterized by the state of being inseparable from the probandum—not established. The word *sādhana* here is used in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*).

However, when one establishes the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the reason through the force of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) by means of a universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), [the argument is as follows]: whatever is graspable by sensory cognition is impermanent, because it produces a cognition that bears its own appearance; for if it were permanent, it would follow that the cognition of its object would either exist at all times or never exist at all. This is because, regarding the production of a cognition within itself, that which is capable is always capable, or else, if it is incapable at some time, it is incapable at all times.
35. Whether its capacity or incapacity exists by its very nature, since it is eternal and incurable, who is able to destroy it? 36.
Thus, that which is capable of producing knowledge within itself is indeed capable.
Or, if it is incapable at some time, then it is forever incapable;
for who is able to remove that capacity or incapacity which exists as its very nature, since it is eternal and incurable? (35-36)
At that time, since even eternal properties such as "cowness" (gotva) are split apart by a single stroke, as it were, the reason does not reside in "cowness"; thus, there is no doubt at all.

By this [statement], "ityādi" and so forth, it is easily understood that even in that case, there is no departure from the status of being a non-conclusive fallacy of the reason (anaikāntika-hetvābhāsa); such is the summary.

Since the reason (*hetu*) has not been established, its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*)— by way of being a cause for doubt— is equal even in other cases, that is, even in a thing accepted as belonging to only one side; thus, there is no distinction in the inconclusiveness between a thing established for both parties and one established for neither,
just as was stated immediately above.
And that reason— whether it exists or does not exist, and so forth— would be explained as "inconclusive" (anaikāntika) because its object is admitted by one of the two opposing parties;
however, that is not a fault, as it is undesirable [for the opponent], whereas what is established for both is indeed a proof.
Or rather, how is it that this [objection] regarding "refutation" (dūṣaṇa) is not contradicted? It is not so, because the statement was made with the intention of pointing out a certain refutation;
for that very reason, immediately after that, another says: "On the other hand, one perceives [the point] as being still to be proven."
However, this might be the case:
neither victory nor defeat would belong to either of the two parties.

Furthermore, that which was stated by Uddyotakara while explaining the very sūtra on the contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*)—namely, "the fallacious examples" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) and so forth—is also untenable for the Naiyāyika who maintains that there are other constituent members (*avayava*) of the syllogism.
The intended meaning is that it is only the Buddhist who speaks thus who appears consistent;
for by his statement of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), a fallacious example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) is implied, since it would follow that [the example] is not distinct from that reason—
this being the case for the "example," as is understood from the context.

Now, one might object: "If it has been indicated that fallacious examples (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa) are included within fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), then the statement that 'the reason does not require another member [of the syllogism] in the example' is indeed incoherent. To this, he says:
"Of the fallacious examples," and so forth;
the following application of this argument unfolds in the mind.

If something is a different entity from another, it is not logical to state that it is included within the latter by means of the term "appearance as that"; nor is there an inclusion of appearances of one thing within appearances of another, just as, for example, there is no inclusion of fallacious perceptions (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) within fallacious inferences (*anumānābhāsa*).

And yet, according to your reason, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is a different entity from the reason (*hetu*). This is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). Therefore, the inclusion of the example within the reason must necessarily be accepted.
And in that case, the example would not be a separate member of the proof, because it does not function separately, meaning it possesses a single function;
he explains this very point with the words beginning "the example which... (12b1).

Having stated that the elaboration of the contradiction between the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) is already subsumed under the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), and thus need not be mentioned separately, [the author] now says "Moreover... and so forth, in order to demonstrate that the same principle applies to cases such as the abandonment of opposition (*pratighahāni*) and the like; the mention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) is for the purpose of explaining that even for the proponent of the final position (*uttarapakṣavādin*), there exist instances of ignorance and other factors that come into contact with fallacious reasons.
"Connected with that" means connected with the proponent of the prima facie argument regarding the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*); or,
it may be argued that since [faults] such as shifting to another subject (*arthāntara*) do not touch upon the fallacious reasons, they are not included therein.
And that [reason] is non-existent, because it is possible for even a reason such as "going to another object" to be thus incapable;
for how could there be proof of the probandum by the force of logic for a proponent who possesses an incapable [reason]? (The word "proponent" is the ellipsis.)

The intention is that [the fault arises] because of deviating from the subject matter through false engagement and so forth. "The subsequent" means that which occurs later as the result; "and that is the abandonment of the proposition"—in relation to that, "what is it not? means "it is nothing at all."

The determination of those whose activities are like the prattling of eunuchs is impossible; that is, the activities of those disputants whose speech is like that of eunuchs and the like—such as the abandonment of a thesis and so forth—what is the point of presenting them?
To the question, "But what is the fault in this case? he says:
"For in this way, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)."
The phrase "and so forth" includes fainting, trembling, fear, and the like by means of the word "etcetera.

Therefore, the intention is that this [objection] is also irrelevant, because such a manner of speaking is too coarse for an assembly of learned scholars. Regarding this, Bhāvivikta himself anticipates the objection and provides a rebuttal: "If it is argued that this is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) due to its coarseness, [we reply that] one who denies the matter already proposed does so in the presence of the judges and the opponent."
It is said that [the objection] is irrelevant because the intended meaning has not been understood.

We do not say that sound is perishable; rather, the point of our proposition is that it is not manifested by conjunction and disjunction. He states this because a universal is manifested by its own substratum, and thus there is no dispute [on that point].
However, [the opponent’s claim] constitutes a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because it concerns a matter not previously proposed.

Regarding the claim that one is defeated because they negate the intended meaning of their proposition when the reason is refuted by the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), it must be said here: if the proponent, while still having a legitimate expectation for his argument, is challenged in the interim by some ill-informed person with the charge of inconclusiveness, and he then clarifies his own intention by demonstrating the validity of his intended conclusion, then there is no fault whatsoever; how much less, then, could there be the defeat called "abandonment of the proposition" (*pratijñā-saṃnyāsa*)?

If, being free from further desire [to elaborate], he later qualifies his proposition when challenged, he is defeated by the very same fault of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*); so what is the point of referring to the "abandonment of the subsequent proposition" (*uttarapratijñā-saṃnyāsa*)? Nothing has been resolved. Furthermore, it is clear that this is included within "shifting the proposition" (*pratijñāntara*), and thus it need not be mentioned separately by us.

In the Nyāyabhāṣya (2.1.59–60), the sūtra beginning with "aviśeṣokte hetau" [when the reason is stated without distinction due to a slight difference] serves as an illustration; that is to say, it is an example.
Here, the follower of Kapila (the Kāpila) offers this as a proof in the hope of establishing the existence of the Pradhāna.

"This manifest world has a single primordial nature (*ekaprakṛti*), because it is finite, like a jar, a bowl, and so forth"—this is the analysis [of the compound]: "that which has one primordial nature.
Primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).

And that which is indeed said to be the nature (*prakṛti*) of the collection of transformations is called *pradhāna*; this is the Sāṅkhya’s false presumption. [The proponent] states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—that things such as the small, the square, or the circular are preceded by clay—and the opponent raises an objection against this reason by pointing out its deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

When the opponent has raised an objection by pointing out that measurement is observed both in things of diverse natures, such as limbs, horses, and so forth, and in things of a single nature, such as jars, water-jars, and so forth; and when the Proponent of Primordial Matter (Pradhānavādin)—having been thus challenged or refuted—replies:
"Because measurement is observed when there is a correlation with a single primordial nature," he intends that there is no fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) because the reason is qualified.
But how is there an endowment with a single primordial nature? To this he says:
"For this manifest world, which is finite, is perceived as being endowed with pleasure, pain, and delusion, because its effects are seen everywhere"—this is the intended meaning.
For instance, for those in whom *sattva* (the quality of goodness) predominates, there arise clarity, lightness, cheerfulness, devotion, joy, and delight;
for those in whom *rajas* (the quality of passion) predominates, there arise desiccation, heat, piercing pain, agitation, distress, and aversion;
and for those in whom *tamas* (the quality of ignorance) predominates, there arise concealment, intoxication, indolence, disgust, dejection, and heaviness.
And since all these [qualities] are perceived everywhere according to their respective variations of increase and decrease,
he states the reason for [the opponent's argument] being a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) with the words, "Therefore, this universe has the three qualities as its nature," and so forth.
The negation of the phrase "here too" and so forth is easily understood;
the meaning is that because there is no cessation, no interruption, and no completion of the statement of the proof (*sādhana*).

By the phrase "possessing the characteristics as previously stated," he recalls the definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) as two contradictory properties residing in a single substratum.

When the acceptance [of these] has been made by the proponent (*vādin*) and the opponent (*prativādin*), and the matter at hand is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) through the reason (*hetu*), within this context—where the establishment of the probandum depends upon the reason—the subject under discussion is the permanence of sound (*śabdanityatva*); [the opponent's position] is irrelevant because of its lack of connection with that.
The meaning is that because it is unconnected [to the word] and because it does not assist it;

for instance, even without the establishment of the form [of the word], the meaning is established from the very meaning conveyed by the base (prātipadika) and so forth, however explained. He permits this as being consistent with his own view, since it is logically sound.
And when is it that the former and latter disputants incur a logically valid point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)? He says:

"When a fault has been pointed out, there would occur for both the proponent and the opponent, respectively, the failure to state a member of the proof and the failure to expose a fault. Otherwise, as it has been stated, neither of the two could have victory or defeat.
Thus, by saying "having abandoned the subject at hand," he demonstrates the logical validity of this very [point].

What is relevant here is the statement of the probandum, the means of proof, and the reason; having failed to do so, when a fault has been pointed out, there is no justification for another [point], such as the establishment of its form (*rūpasiddhi*) and so forth,
even if it were not invariably concomitant with that [fault].
The meaning is: "of that which has been presented as a supporting factor for the justification of the means [of proof]";
the phrase "the mention of another [point], such as the explanation of names and so forth, is a ground for defeat" continues [from the previous rule].
"Meaningless [speech] is like the instruction on the sequence of phonemes," Nyāya Sūtra 2.1.8;
that is, where only the phonemes themselves are indicated in their sequential order.
Neither a word nor a sentence [constitutes this],
for it is said that speaking of a different meaning here— namely, the mere utterance of phonemes— is the statement of an irrelevant matter;
thus he expresses its very lack of connection.

It is not merely from the presentation of a sequence of syllables that something is useless; rather, whatever statement consists of a non-essential member of the proof—such as the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and so forth—or the mere establishment of the form of words, that alone is useless.
What is the reason?
Because it lacks a subject matter that is useful for the establishment of the thesis (*sādhya*).

One should not think that there is any other purpose [for the treatise] even in the absence of the means for establishing the probandum (*sādhya*); this is what he expresses by the words "and because it would be purposeless" (*niṣprayojanatvāt*).
The intention is that since the establishment of the probandum alone is the subject at hand, even if there were another purpose, the discussion here would still be irrelevant.
Therefore, the opponent has stated that [the example] "like the description of the sequence of letters in the recitation of a specific type" is irrelevant;

for what is intended as "meaningless" (nirarthaka) in the context of proving the probandum is not that which is useless or irrelevant to the proof, but rather that speech which possesses no meaning whatsoever, such as the cawing of crows and the like.

And thus, since even irrelevant (*arthāntara*), meaningless (*apārthaka*), and other such fallacies are already included by this very [definition] because they contain some slight element of meaning, the Teacher says: "Why would there not be defeat (*nigraha*) for anyone at all—even for one who speaks something entirely devoid of sense?"*13b3* *The original Sanskrit text here is likely: *yasya kasyacid apy ādinopi nirarthakābhidhāne vāhita iva kiṃ na nigraho bhavati*. This reflects a commentary on the definition of defeat (nigrahasthāna) regarding the utterance of nonsense.*
He asks, "How could this be? and replies:

because there would be no distinction between the proponent and the opponent regarding that futile statement which is a ground for defeat, [the opponent] says "no" to the proponent in this context of debate.
The teacher says: "It has arrived.
For him, since the debate remains in that state with that very same meaningless statement, it is equal.
It must be supplied that for every speaker who states what is not a constituent of the proof, there is the quality of stating the meaningless; in some places, the reading is *tatra*,
in which case nothing is required by way of supplementation.
This very statement of meaninglessness is the response to one for whom there is no meaning whatsoever.
This too is irrelevant,
because even the instruction of the sequence of phonemes is not without purpose in certain contexts, such as in the case of *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated terms), since it is meaningful there; therefore,
it is only in this specific instance that the sequence of phonemes would be purposeless.

Since that [reasoning] applies equally to other objects and so forth, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the mind is characterized by jumping and signaling" includes such things as leaping, clapping hands, dancing, and the like; thus,
he demonstrates the logical principle that because it has been stated three times, the expression must be taken as threefold.
Since even that which has been stated once may sometimes not be understood despite its clear meaning, the recitation must be performed three times.
To the question, "Why, then, is a sentence not understood by those who are experts in words, sentences, and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?", he says:
"Because its words are difficult," and so forth.
Others say that the word *kliṣṭa* is used because it was slightly mispronounced and thus constitutes a corruption of speech (*apaśabda*).
To the question "Why was it employed in this way? he replies:
"Those who conceal their incapacity" (13b9) means that one employs [the argument] out of fear that the opponent will point out a flaw in the application of a clear meaning;
and this is common to both the proponent and the critic of the proof.
For even a statement of refutation that causes such a defeat to occur does not differ from the "meaningless" (nirarthaka) [fallacy];
for one might indeed state a reason that is connected to the relevant subject by means of ambiguous words and the like.

Or, even if it is the opposite of the aforementioned manner, it is not due to a lack of capacity on his part; rather, it is because the members of the assembly and others, out of dullness, do not comprehend what was said. Therefore, for this reason alone, a learned disputant does not deserve defeat; for it is the dullness of the listener that prevents him from understanding. 37.
Then the opponent, with the underlying intention that "this person is indeed deserving of defeat," says:
"[The assembly] knows the wisdom [of the proponent].
To this, he replies: "This refers to the proponent of the reasoning" (Nyāyavādin).
The connection is that this was stated by the proponent of logic (*nyāyavādin*).
However, because the disputant, due to dullness, does not understand the capacity of the proof for the sake of the assembly and so forth, he would not be the victor;
for victory is established through the convincing of the assembly and the opponent.

Regarding that whose capacity for proof is not understood by both the assembly and the opponent, he speaks with reference to the second alternative: "In the case of an irrelevant statement, it is indeed meaningless. (14a1)
Regarding the phrase "of many words":

when one refutes the capacity of a sentence to convey a coherent meaning by asserting that it conveys unrelated meanings, there is an absence of comprehension of the context and the chapter if the sentence conveys unrelated meanings.
Furthermore, it is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because there is no comprehension of a collective meaning;

for example: "Ten pomegranates, six cakes, a bowl, a goat-skin, a lump of minced meat, and this is Rauruka; the father of Sphaiyakṛta’s daughter is ill. Regarding this, Bhāradvāja raised the objection that there is no difference between the "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*) and the "incoherent" (*apārthaka*), and he provided a rebuttal there, stating: "In that case, it is merely the phonemes [that are meaningless], whereas here, they are connected with something else [but not with each other]."
The Teacher also introduces this very point with the words "this, indeed," and so forth;
the analysis of the compound is: that in which the phonemes are unconnected is "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*).
The word *kiṃ* (what) is intended to demonstrate lack of desirability;
indeed, it expresses that very lack of desirability.

[Objection: But surely, because these words lack a connection, an "unconnected sentence" (*asambaddhavākya*)—like the "meaningless" (*apārthaka*)—should be stated as distinct from the "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*).

It might be argued that "the irrelevant" (*apārthaka*) need not be mentioned separately, because it is already included within either "incoherent words" (*asambaddha-pada*) or "incoherent sentence-meaning" (*asambaddha-vākyārtha*). To this it is replied: it is not correct to say it is included in both. Why? Because if it were so included, then even "the meaningless" (*nirarthaka*), which is characterized merely by a sequence of phonemes, would necessarily be included within "the irrelevant," since the latter consists of incoherent words. Thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of over-extension.
Now it is asked: what is called "meaningless" (nirarthaka)?
It is that for which there is no meaning at all, consisting merely of a sequence of syllables.

However, although disconnected words and sentences are of no use for establishing the probandum (*sādhya*), they are not entirely useless; therefore, because they are equal in their nature as meaning-bearers, both are treated as one.
To this, he says "from such [a case]" and so forth;
here, the "over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*) is stated in the sense that it would follow that even things like "lip-flapping" (*kapolavāditā*) should be mentioned separately.

The intention [of the author] is that a distinction cannot be demonstrated anywhere by a mere [partial] similarity. Now, if you think that Akṣapāda did not provide a collective definition because he perceived the fault of such a definition in the case of *nirarthaka* (meaningless) and *apārthaka* (incoherent), and saw the merit in providing a distinct definition for each, you do not think correctly; thus he says:
"And there is no collective definition," and so forth.
The meaning is that it is according to the definition [of the thesis] for the sake of the purpose. This is its capacity:

so that the application of the proof might not be without an object when the object has not been shown, the proposition (*pratijñā*), which is defined as the indication of the probandum (*sādhya*), is stated first.

Immediately after that, for the purpose of establishing that [subject], the *hetu* (reason) is stated, characterized as "the means of proving the probandum (*sādhya*) through similarity with the example.

Then, for the sake of demonstrating the external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) from that reason, the *udāharaṇa* (example) is stated: "The example is that which possesses the property of that [probandum] due to its similarity with the probandum" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.36).

36. Thus, having stated the definition and the example (*udāharaṇa*), there follows the application (*upanaya*), which consists of the conclusion "it is so" or "it is not so," depending on the example, for the purpose of reflecting [the property] or for the purpose of demonstrating its presence in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.38)
The application (*upanaya*) has such characteristics as these.

Thereafter, for the purpose of removing any erroneous implications by reviewing all the members [of the syllogism], the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the statement of the reason (*hetu*) is the conclusion (*nigamana*). (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.39)
Thus, the conclusion (nigamana) has this definition;
this is the sequence according to its definition, as it follows from the requirements of the sense.
For even in the world, the following principle holds: first the material cause, such as a lump of clay, is taken up, and afterwards the instruments, such as the wheel and the staff.

In this regard, when this [five-membered] sequence is established according to the proper method, the statement of the members—such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth—in reverse order constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*);
for example: "Because it is produced, like a jar, it is impermanent."
Bhāradvāja himself raises and then resolves this objection by stating, "Even so,
[the goal] is established," and "This would not be like a word devoid of application," by means of which [he refers to] the term *goṇī*.
Just as...
Just as a child being taught the sound "ambamba" manifests indistinctly at first, yet through that very knowledge, certainty arises regarding the distinct [form],
so too indeed words such as *goṇī* and others serve as causes for the production of comprehension by means of inference from the correct [words].

This is indeed the description of one madman by another madman, just as one madman describes a second madman; for this [work] is exactly like that. If it is a description of the madman Uddyotakara by the madman Vaiyākaraṇa, then the grammarian himself is indeed mad, because he speaks of things that are contrary to valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, it is intended that the investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇacintā*) serves as an indicator for that very procedure (*prakriyā*).
To explain how the grammarian’s statement is improper,
he says "yadi" (if), etc., which is easy to understand.
The words *strī* and *śūdra* are terms for the ignorant;

how indeed could one who does not even know that the word *nakka* or *mukka* is a synonym for "nose" understand the correct word from an incorrect word (*apaśabda*), and how could he understand the meaning from that correct word?
Why is it said that he does not attain such an awakening? He says:

"For even in the case of Sanaka and others who do not experience both [the object and its cognition], there is a realization. Therefore, the realization of the object is not through a causal succession.
This is the summary here.
This might be the case for the unvirtuous being indicative of the virtuous,
provided that their possession of the three characteristics (trairūpya) were as certain as it is for smoke and the like;
however, that is not possible.
Because Sanaka and others, who do not perceive both [the pervaded and the pervader], do not apprehend this relationship of pervaded and pervader even though it exists;
and since that [relationship] is not known, it cannot serve as a means of cognition, for it must be a cognizer.
Even those who are skilled in distinguishing between correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*) merely conceptualize it because it does not actually exist.
For in this way, the relationship between the non-virtuous and the virtuous must be either identity (*tādātmya*) or the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*),
since there can be no rule of non-deviation for that which lacks both of these;
and in that regard, identity cannot be accepted, because a real difference is clearly perceived through direct perception.

Furthermore, because there is no distinction [between them], it would follow that even corrupt words (*asādhu*) possess denotative power just like correct words (*sādhu*); thus, the theory that [corrupt words] arise from [correct ones] is utterly discarded,
since corrupt words do not arise from correct ones.

Since those [words] have as their sole cause the mere desire of the speaker to express the qualities of their causes, they lack eternality; for they are perceived only occasionally. Even if they were eternal, there would be an even greater absence of their production. Or, even if a relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) existed and were fully known, there would be no inference from corrupt words—just as there is none from "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*)—due to the deficiency of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).
For in this case, no such property exists from which the "property-of-the-subject" (pakṣadharmatva) could be established;
for it is not only virtuous persons who possess the status of being the subject (dharmin), since they themselves are what is being inferred.
Nor is it logical that this [quality] belongs to the subject (dharmin),

because the property of being both existent and non-existent is vitiated by the fallacies of the unestablished (asiddha), the contradictory (viruddha), and the inconclusive (anaikāntika); or else, how could that quality belong to virtuous persons?
For at that time, those [words] do not exist;
and it has been well said that non-existent things cannot possess the status of a subject (*dharmin*) or the capacity to denote meaning.

As for the claim that "the person is the subject, the desire to speak with correct words is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), and the incorrect word is the property of the locus (*pakṣadharma*)," that too is incoherent.
Because the relationship of pervader and pervaded does not exist at all,
we do not observe an intention to use the word "cow" at the time of employing the word "gony"; now, if it is argued as follows:
Just as even the indistinct speech of children, despite being deficient in the property of residing in the subject (pakṣadharmatva) and other requirements, leads to the inference of what is distinct,
so too do the unrefined lead to the inference of the refined.
That is incorrect, because the same objection applies there as well. We, however, maintain that even from that unmanifest [source], the meaning such as the *mātrās* is understood directly;
therefore, one should not think that it is improper for the meaning to be understood because the relationship between the name and the named has not been previously experienced.

Because in beginningless saṃsāra, such a relationship belonging to the succession of linguistic usage has been indicated; for indeed, even in the case of words such as "cow," the restriction of meaning is not generally established by explicitly grasping the object (like seizing it by the horns), but rather the learned determine it through the continuity of linguistic usage—
and this is exactly the same here as well.
Therefore, this is like the crying of "Mother, Mother" in the forest by a child being taught;
that which is indistinct becomes distinct through the instruction of one who knows it— of this there is no doubt.

39. Thus, when a correct word (*sādhū*) ought to be employed, whatever corruption (*bhraṃśa*) is used instead, some meaning is understood through that [corruption] which is mediated by the correct word. 40. This is just as a child being taught says "ambamva" [instead of "amba"].

By means of that which is unmanifest, the one who knows it attains certainty through the manifest. Likewise, when a correct word ought to be employed, whatever corruption is used instead, some meaning is understood through that which is mediated by the correct word.
As for what was further stated by Kumārila: "When the word 'go' is established, our cognition of 'gāvī' and so forth—though produced by incapacity—is nonetheless based on the original word. (41)
"When the word 'go' is established for us, the cognition of 'gāvī' and the like is produced by its incapacity [to denote], yet it follows the original word.
Having taken up all this, he concludes with this very same refutation.

Regarding the claim that there is no cognition through a succession [of stages], he provides further reinforcement for this very point: because that which is incapable of conveying the meaning is not valid, it is likewise incapable of generating cognition even with respect to a valid word.
In this regard, one might argue: "We do not deny that corrupt words produce comprehension regarding objects; rather, we deny their status as *vācaka* (denotative).
And a corrupt word is indeed a producer of comprehension, but it is not a *vācaka*. To this, he says:
For the expressive power of a word toward its object is indeed nothing other than this:
if it is maintained that even an ungrammatical form (*asādhu*) generates the cognition of the meaning,
then by this much alone we shall be fully satisfied.
"What is the point of postulating a distinct designation for us as being denotative?"—this is the underlying intention.
If it is argued that "in that case, this [apaśabda] is not capable of producing the cognition of the meaning, but rather only the *śabda* [is so capable]," he replies with the words:
"If it is an *apaśabda*... (14b4).

Now it is said: [If it is argued that] the word has an inherent connection with its own form (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) and not with the object, and therefore it expresses only that [form] and not the object—just as the eye, by its very nature, illuminates visible form (*rūpa*) and not sound and so forth—[the author] says: "For one who has not made a convention," and so on, ending with "because of non-perception."
For words such as "siṃhala," whose relationship [to their referents] is not recognized, do not function in the linguistic usage of noble persons; rather,
it is convention (*samaya*) alone that produces cognition,
and since that relationship is conventional, there is no obstacle to its application to that object.
One might ask: "Why does a thing that is non-virtuous by convention not function as something virtuous when it exists in a virtuous state, such as a cow or the like?
For there is no fault whatsoever in that; rather, it would be a mere quality. To this, he says: "For in this way... (14b6, etc.).
This is what is meant:

those things which are luminous by their very nature do not depend upon a convention (*samaya*), just as the eye, a lamp, and so forth [do not depend on a convention] for the perception of form and other objects.
If an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) were by its very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*) a signifier of a word,
then it too would not require a relationship [with that word];
however, since it does require one, it does not possess an inherent capacity (*svābhāvikam sāmarthyam*) with respect to the word.
Likewise, this can also be inferred:
those whose activity depends upon convention and sensory perception have their scope unimpeded everywhere according to that convention, and they become direct communicators,
just like bodily intimation and so forth.
Likewise, since corrupt words (*apaśabda*) also function in dependence upon linguistic convention (*samaya*), it is established that they convey meaning without any mediation;

this is because we observe the opposite [in the case of correct words]. This is another supporting argument: for instance, when "tree," "fire," or "lotus" are uttered, children whose intellects are untrained remain suspended in inquiry.

By such questions as "What is this tree?", since there is no other means of instruction, they are taught by means of ungrammatical words (*apaśabda*) themselves—such as *rukkha*, *aggī*, and *uppala*. Thus, in this case, a reversal is observed: it is the ungrammatical forms alone that are expressive, while the grammatical forms, even though they exist, are not.

Now, if you maintain that the refinement of words is the means for accomplishing dharma—as established through tradition from the learned—that which is accomplished is the means for accomplishing dharma; yet, while there is no difference in the communication of meaning, ungrammatical forms are the opposite [of that]. Thus it is said: 42.
That which is established through the tradition of the learned is the correct means (*sādhana*), the means for establishing the dharma;
those that are the opposite are incorrect (*asādhava*).
A mantra that is deficient in accent or phoneme, when wrongly employed, does not convey its intended meaning. (42)
That thunderbolt of speech destroys the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [did] due to a lapse in accentuation (43). Those gods, having uttered "he'layo he'laya," were cast down;
yet even a single word, when correctly employed, leads the virtuous to the heavenly world.

"One who has maintained the sacred fires, having uttered an incorrect word, should perform an expiatory sacrifice," and so forth; for a mantra that is deficient in accent or phoneme, or is wrongly employed, does not convey its intended meaning.
That is a thunderbolt of speech which destroys the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [Vṛtra] was destroyed due to a fault in the accent. 43.

In the *Paspaśāhnika* of the *Vyākaraṇamahābhāṣya*, the first chapter of the *Mahābhāṣya*, this [objection] is set aside: "The refinement (*saṃskāra*) of words is not a means to dharma. Why is that? He says:
"Because [words] enjoin false conduct," and so forth.
It is taught that those by whom a false course of action is enjoined [are liable for the sin].

For instance, even when it is said, "Having cut off the head with a sword-blade darker than a blue lotus of this twice-born man who is lying beneath the Aśoka tree—which is resplendent with rows of beautiful clusters and tender shoots as lovely as a profusion of fresh coral sprouts"—the instigator indeed incurs the connection with the sin of killing a Brahmin.
This is because, in contrast to others, there is no lack of possibility [of the act occurring] through the injunction of a correct course of action in the opposite case.
Just as that cow might be given to the brahmin,
so too all this is merely a statement; because it is immeasurable, you have spoken with a mind full of doubt,
saying [in verse 14b9] "only through the correct application of words," and so forth.
[Objection:

"In such cases as, 'Indeed, one who causes a shrine to be built on a level stretch of ground generates Brahma-merit and rejoices in the heavens for an eon,' there is likewise an absence of valid authority; thus this same consequence applies to you as well. [Response:

It is not the same, because in these cases there is a purification of the two objects [the subject and the predicate], a purpose, and non-contradiction; therefore, discerning persons proceed with full satisfaction even toward the third category [of statements].
But this is not so in your own view, because both of the two points just mentioned are contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that contradiction has been demonstrated immediately above.
Therefore, this [position] is like the rivalry between a pauper and a lord.

The expression "impelled by qualities such as having known what is to be known" (*viditavedyādiguṇaprayuktā*) is a designation in which the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is included within the compound.
Those by whom that which is to be known—the nature of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted—is known are described as such;
by the inclusion of "etcetera," compassion and other qualities are encompassed.
These very ones [are] both conditioned and other, unconditioned.
This is what is meant:

for speech has as its purpose worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) and as its fruit the communication of meaning; and just as this is accomplished through refined words by virtue of convention, so too is it accomplished through unrefined words. Why, then, are the learned (*śiṣṭas*) so stubbornly attached to what is not the case?

For this very reason, I think that because they differ from those possessed of discernment (*prekṣāvat*), these names were applied to them for the sake of conformity; or rather, what concern is it of ours if they reject [these names]? For there is no certainty in the matter that "they employ only these and not others."
As it has been said:
"And there is no witness here who is beyond the senses, because we determine that witnesses employ only these [words] and not others.

(15a3) But was it not already stated in the *Mahābhāṣya*, in the first *Āhnika*: "The purposes of its grammatical exposition are preservation (*rakṣā*), elimination of errors (*hā*), addition (*āgama*), economy (*laghu*), and absence of doubt (*asaṃdeha*)"? (1)
To the question, "How then can it be said that there is an absence of superior qualities? he replies:

"Furthermore, the preservation of the Vedas and so forth is entirely purposeless for a follower of the Tathāgata who does not abide by those [Vedic] conventions, because such [preservation] is not consistent with reason."

He clarifies this very introduction of the example— that the nature of that [word], namely the form of a correct word, [is known] "even from another source," meaning through the traditional lineage of the elders' discourse.
Having thus demonstrated the madness of Śābdika with the words beginning with "prākṛta," [the author] now states the view of Bhāradvāja with the words beginning with "avayavaviparyaye'pi."

Regarding the phrase "the cognition of the connection": the "connection" is the relationship of mutual benefit between [the members], by virtue of which the intended meaning is communicated—this is the implied sense.
Now, one might object that the sequence of the thesis and so forth is not being altered in order to maintain the methodological principles of the system of Akṣapāda; to this, he says:
For here there is no established doctrine or rule of his that is endowed with valid means of cognition; thus the opponent says:
"There is no cognition of the probandum by way of its opposite."
However, the negation of the claim that "there is a cognition of sequence from the opposite of that" is this:
there is no cognition of sequence from those whose relations are not being cognized. (15a8)
The passage beginning with "yeṣām" (of those... explains that very point.
Furthermore, we have already previously rejected the employment of the proposition (*pratijñā*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*) within the proof-statement (*sādhanavākya*);
therefore, he explains how there could be any reversal [of the order] caused by them.
The inclusion of the term "proposition" (*pratijñā*) by the passage beginning with "it has been explained" (15a10) is for the purpose of illustration;
he states this [next] because if it were employed even when already obtained through implication (*sāmarthya*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

And there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of employing [the dissimilar instance] when the meaning is already implied; that is, in a formulation possessing the property of the subject (*dharmyavat*), there would be the consequence of employing the dissimilar property (*vaidharmya*) as well, which is not accepted.
Furthermore, it is a logical fallacy (*nyāya-sūtra* 5) to state again in one's own words what has already been established by implication.

[Objection: Since the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) have been mentioned, there will then be a fixed order for the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), even in the absence of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth. To this, he says:
In the *Pariśiṣṭa* (15b1), beginning with "etc.," he states another fault regarding the position that the connection [of words] is not perceived:
"This does not differ from the 'meaningless' (*apārthaka*)," and thus it would not need to be mentioned separately.

A statement in which any one of the members, from the proposition (*pratijñā*) up to the conclusion (*nigamana*), is absent is deficient; [the author] states the reason why this constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
He refutes this [objection]— namely, that "because the probandum is not established in the absence of the means of proof"—
with the passage beginning with "not [the case] for the thesis and so forth."
The mention of the "proposition" (pratijñā) is for the purpose of illustration; by it, the "application" (upanaya) and the "conclusion" (nigamana) are also included.
He sets forth the opinion of Uddyotakara:
"That [syllogism] is indeed deficient. (15b3)
Regarding the point that one deserves defeat even when there is a deficiency in that proposition (*pratijñānyūna*) because of the deficiency of the proposition itself, he states its incorrectness:
"He who employs in his proof a word expressing the probandum—which is redundant since the object is already understood through the power of the proof—deserves defeat. (15b4)
For instance, when the investigation into the impermanence of sound has been introduced, if one says,

"It is observed that produced things are impermanent, and sound is produced," then the meaning to be proven is understood from these two statements alone; thus, the statement of the thesis (pratijñā) is redundant.

It is not the case that the author of the *Vārttika* has made an unconsidered statement merely by expressing the connection of the property with the subject (*pakṣadharma-sambandha*) of that which is endowed with meaning and joined with reason; for this very reason, [the author] says "and therefore. Since one deserves defeat when a word is employed whose meaning is already understood, Abiddhakarṇa here objects by means of the logic of the "obstructer" (*pratibandhaka*).

If this is so, then even the statement "sound is produced" should not be uttered. Why? Because by the very [statement] "what is the reason for its impermanence?", both the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*) are understood in relation to sound. Since the state of being produced had already been accepted by the opponent regarding sound previously, and sound was thus established in the mind through that production, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) sentence merely generates a recollection (*smṛti*).
Furthermore, for one who has not yet understood the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), even from the statement "sound is produced," nothing follows;
rather, one should simply say "sound is produced.

Since the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) of being produced with impermanence is already established for the opponent, they will thereby understand that sound is also impermanent. Thus, [the proponent] has acted quite appropriately.

For instance, if the proponent somehow becomes certain that "sound is produced" (*kṛtakatva*) according to this [opponent's] understanding, then he need not apply the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) at all, because it would be fruitless;
rather, he should merely demonstrate the logical connection (*pratibandha*).
However, if it is not certain in that way...

Nevertheless, if this opponent, when I have stated the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*), should raise the objection that it is unestablished (*asiddha*), then I shall refute it by means of arguments such as its being differentiated by the difference in cognitions; or else, even without being prompted, having anticipated this [objection] in my mind, I must certainly state the presence of the reason in the subject, namely, "and sound is produced.

Even when the proponent has reached the conclusion that the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) of "being produced" with "impermanence" is well-known to the opponent, even in that state, he should simply say: "Sound is produced."

As it has been said: "For the existence [of the probandum] and the state of being the cause for its manifestation are explained by means of an example to those who do not know them; however, for the learned, only the reason itself needs to be stated.
(44) For the existence [of the probandum] and the state of being the cause for its manifestation are indeed [explained] by means of an example to those who do not know them.
"For the wise, only the reason itself is indeed to be stated"—

this very [statement] establishes as an additional point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) the "acceptance of a restrictive rule" (*niyamābhyupagama*) regarding a specific subject; and he states that specific subject as follows:

Regarding the passage beginning with "yatra" (15b5), [the opponent objects]: "But this must be understood as being stated by the author of the Bhāṣya itself in the context of accepting a restriction; so what refutation has the Teacher stated here? [The reply is: True, nothing at all has been stated.
The Teacher, however, restates what was said by Pakṣila for the sake of granting his approval.
He states an exception to the rule that "the repetition of words and meanings is tautology" with the words: "except in the case of a restatement."
The restatement is the conclusion;
for a restatement does not receive the designation of "repetition," since a specific meaning arises from the two words.
Since it has been stated that the "proposition" (pratijñā) is the statement of what is to be proven and the "conclusion" (nigamana) is the statement of what is already established,
and furthermore, the word "again" (punaḥ) is observed to indicate multiplicity.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that "the light of Yama issues forth" once again;
if this is so, then there is simply no possibility of redundancy here, so why is this exception being initiated?
It is true that this is so.
However, those eminent logicians themselves should be asked how this is so;
as for us, what is the use of considering the household concerns of others? Enough of this digression.
