In this regard, there is also this second sūtra: "The restatement by its own word of that which is already established through the force of the meaning" (Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.15).
This was not cited by the Teacher because it is intended as an illustrative example.
Having set aside that commentary, he will refute it with the words "Furthermore, the restatement of what is already understood... (15b9) and so forth;
he begins the critique with the words "In this regard... (15b7).
This is what is meant:

where there is identity of wording but no difference in meaning, that does not fall under the category of "repetition of meaning" (*arthapunarukta*). However, where there is a difference in meaning despite the identity of wording, even in the case of "repetition of words" (*śabdapunarukta*), nothing [of the former fault] has been committed.
Is such a possibility conceivable—that there could be a difference in meaning even when there is a repetition of words? To this, he says:
Just as in the case of "hasati hasati" and so forth (15b7),
for here the first word "hasati" ends in the locative case while the second is a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), and thus there is a difference in meaning;
so it is in subsequent cases as well.
In response to the doubt that such a possibility exists for poetry but not for formal debate (*vāda*), he provides an example beginning with "just as" (*yathā ca*).
[Objection: But surely here too, just as there is a difference in meaning, there is also a difference in words, by virtue of being nominal stems (*subanta*) or verbal forms (*tiṅanta*).

It is true that even here there is a distinction; for in the cases of "sound is impermanent" and "sound is impermanent," there is indeed a difference in the sound itself due to the difference in its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Otherwise, there would be no sequential hearing [of the words].
If tautology is established here on the basis of identical phonetic form, then it is exactly the same in this case as well;
for there is indeed a difference in meaning,
just as there is a difference in action due to the difference in the expressed meanings.

For the distinction between words is indeed constructed based on that [meaning]; moreover, the second sūtra defining "repetition" (punarukta)— which states that "the restatement of a meaning already understood is repetition"— is indicated here,
and its example was stated by Vātsyāyana in the Nyāyabhāṣya.

Regarding the application of the method of similarity (*sādharmya*), the Teacher [Dignāga], anticipating that the same [objection] applies even to the thesis (*pratijñā*) in the method of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), and desiring to demonstrate that the thesis is not to be presented in the statement of the proof (*sādhanavākya*), employs a roundabout expression and presents the very statement of the thesis as an example: "In a proof-statement where the employment of words is fixed, it is like the statement of the thesis. The compound *niyatapadaprayoge* means "that in which there is the employment of fixed words. This is the analysis of the term.
This [objection] is rejected by the fact that its meaning is already understood through mere repetition of meaning (*arthapunarukta*), and thus need not be stated separately.

For just as a synonym is useless when employed to express a meaning already conveyed by a single word, so too is it useless when the meaning is already apprehended through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*). Thus, this is subsumed under *arthapunarukta*—this is the collective sense.

To the question, "In what case does this statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, being redundant because it is already obtainable through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), become a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)?", he explains this very point by way of an alternative: "In a formal argument (*sādhanavākya*) where the usage is restricted. (15b9)

This fault, arising from the restatement of a meaning already understood, applies specifically to the syllogistic statement (*sādhana-vākya*), wherein the employment of words must be strictly regulated.
This is what is meant:
when the judges (*prāśnikas*) are experts in investigating words, meanings, and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and are discerning persons whose minds are exceedingly attentive.

They say that the opponent is likewise of such a nature; therefore, only that which is indispensable for the establishment of the thesis (*sādhya*) should be employed, and nothing more. Thus, this fault occurs only in that case and not otherwise, because those whose minds are dependent on compassion and who are affectionately disposed without cause strive to lead the opponent—who is as if an exceedingly rare disciple—onto the path of logic (*nyāya*). In that context, even a repetition is not a fault.
He says this very thing:

For a proponent who is explaining [the argument] might indeed say it again and again, out of the concern that the witnesses and others have not heard or understood it correctly—this being the instrumental cause for ensuring correct hearing and understanding.
[The opponent objects: "Because it is not the object [of the proof].
He explains this very point: "This proponent is not a teacher to the respondent."
The student is not the opponent,
for both are established by their mutual desire for victory;
therefore, the proponent need not strive to establish the opponent.
The Teacher [Dharmakīrti] says "not so" (na) and so forth:

even if the opponent (*prativādin*) is not necessarily persuaded through effort, the witnesses (*sākṣin*) must certainly be persuaded through effort; for it is precisely by their being informed that the proponent (*vādin*) wins, and otherwise he loses. Why then would he not persuade the witnesses themselves? Furthermore, the opponent must also necessarily be persuaded, just like the witnesses.
Why is this? Because faults are stated when that [the witness] is not presented;

by means of this pretext, witnesses and others are being considered. For if witnesses and others were not to be presented, then that which has been stated by you—namely, that "when something has been thrice uttered by the assembly and the respondent, and it remains uncomprehended, it is the ground for defeat called *avijñātārtha*" (Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.19)—would be contradicted.
The meaning is that this contradicts [the previous statement].
Furthermore, as for what was said— that "this is not a disciple"— that is unproven.
Because the person to be instructed is a disciple (16a1),
and since it is for the sake of attaining knowledge of reality that the very person to be instructed is the disciple— given the absence of any other defining characteristic thereof—
how could the opponent, being likewise such a person, not be a disciple?

As for the claim that "this respondent is not [acting] out of a desire to compete for the sake of knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna)," that is incorrect, because the *jigīṣu-vāda* (debate for victory) was previously refuted.
Even so, this [meaning] is not something to be established through effort, because the Great Sage has established the rule of stating [the matter] three times; therefore, he says:
"Because of the statement 'three times,' etc.
By this, he demonstrates the following:
As he will say:

"If activity is for the sake of instructing another, why is it stated thrice? He should be made to grasp [the meaning] in whatever way his understanding occurs. Or, if it is for the sake of tormenting another, even so, why is it stated thrice?"

Having whispered [the objection] into the ear of the witness, the defendant should harass the plaintiff with difficult, unintelligible, rapid, or overly concise speech, such that he becomes bewildered in formulating a reply and falls silent;
furthermore, this includes the repetition of words and their meanings,
as well as the repetition of what is already implied.
By the passage beginning with "viniya te" (16a1), it establishes precisely their non-difference; [otherwise],
there would be the fault of redundancy regarding the reason and the example (16a2).

Because of the statement that "since [the meaning] has been established by one, the other is redundant," even though there is a repetition, the meaning of the subsequent word is already understood by the preceding word alone; thus it is said that for such a word,
its superfluity is indeed a fault— this is the subject under discussion.
If it is asked, "But why is this fault mentioned specifically regarding the employment of fixed words? he replies:
the connection is that there is no fault in the case of "prolix discourse" (*prapañcakathā*). Of what [is there no fault]? Of the multiplicity of reasons and so forth.
Furthermore, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "repetition and so forth," the inclusion of numerous examples is intended;
in what kind of locus (*adhikaraṇa*), where a single object to be proven (*ekārtha-sādhana*) has not been determined, is the meaning (*artha*) to be established?
Because it is sought after (*arthyate*), the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is the reason (*hetu*); the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the subject (*dharmin*).
The means of accomplishment together with the object (*artha*) is "the means of accomplishing the object" (*arthasādhana*).
By the elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopa*), it is called "that which accomplishes a single purpose" (*ekārthasādhana*).

The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of that is what is meant by "the locus for the accomplishment of a single purpose" (*ekārthasādhanādhikaraṇa*), which has not yet been determined. This refers to that discursive debate (*prapañcakathā*) in which the opponent does not desire to prove even a single property—such as selflessness (*nairātmya*)—of the subject (*dharmin*), such as the living body, but rather multiple properties, such as momentariness, non-selfhood, and non-divine agency; and likewise, not by means of a single reason, but by multiple reasons as well. Such is the meaning.
He explains this very point in due order:

"In the case of a listener who desires the proof of various objects, or who desires various proofs" (16a2). Here, the former word *sādhana* expresses "accomplishment" (*bhāvasādhana*) because it denotes the act of establishing;
the latter, however, expresses the "reason" (*hetu*) because it denotes the instrument (*karaṇasādhana*).
Therefore, while there is an abundance of reasons and so forth, as well as an abundance of words, there is a fault in the formulation of the proof regarding the specific terms;
for what reason? Because there is an absence of what is commonly understood (*pratīta*).
Considering that the fault is equivalent [to the fault of redundancy], it is logical that only the summary (*saṅgraha*) should be employed.

The meaning is that either "the redundant" (*adhika*) or "the tautological" (*punarukta*) alone should be stated, because one of these two is included within the other. To the question, "How is the redundant included within the tautological? he says:
Indeed, another [type of] reason, which is like a synonymous term (paryāyaśabdakalpa), being a second [reason] operating upon a subject already established by a single reason, [is redundant];
for what reason?
Because there is no distinction in that which is to be established.
If it is asked how, then, "repetition of meaning" (*arthapunarukta*) is included within "excess" (*adhika*), he says: "Meaning is not distinct from the act of restating.
By the word "meaning," he indicates the repetition of meaning;
for that by which something is restated is "restatement" (*punarpratipādana*), which is precisely the excess of reasons (*hetu*) and examples (*udāharaṇa*).

This is what is meant: it is quite clear that this [example] is included within the section on examples. For instance, in a formal argument based on similarity (*sādharmya*), the non-employment of an example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) has been stated as an example of "redundancy of meaning" (*arthapunarukta*).

Furthermore, that which has been stated as "the negation of the initial objection is easily understood" means that the meaning of the sentence is well-known or understood when it has been uttered three times; such is the case here.
Or, it should be understood that this refers to a *viśeṣaṇasamāsa* (descriptive compound) meaning "that which is both known and the meaning of the sentence"; thus, the word "three" (*tri*)—
to be connected with the phrase "repetition of the words by the opponent"—
is intended to indicate that there is no defeat (*nigraha*) even if one fails to restate what was stated only once by the proponent.
He states the reason why non-reproduction—whether by way of the word or by way of the meaning—is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*):

"If one does not reproduce [the opponent's statement], on what basis could one state a refutation of the other's position? (16a7). The meaning is that there would be no presentation of a critique regarding the subject matter.
Having formed a judgment regarding what has been stated by you, a refutation must be voiced;
likewise, the proponent of the proof (*sādhana*) must also restate the statement of refutation and then provide a rebuttal.
Therefore, this constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for both parties.

Here, Bhāradvāja first offers a refutation in detail: "If it is argued that this is not a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because there is a thorough understanding [of the matter] up to the conclusion," he explains this statement with the words beginning "This might be so" (*syādetat*).
"Because there is no thorough knowledge of the subject matter of the answer"—this very [author] provides the rebuttal;
"if this... (16a8) and so forth is the analysis of that very [point], and "because it is not a formal proposition" (*apratijñānāt*)—this too is his [rebuttal].

Furthermore, since there is no further basis [for argument] and no introduction of another's position, it is incorrect; thus, failure to restate [the opponent's point] constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Such is the extent of the opponent's text.
Here, the Teacher begins to state the refutation: "Even if the proponent, under the guise of explaining his own proof, should proclaim one thing after another by way of incidental digression..."

As was previously illustrated, there [in that case], by means of the pretext of explaining the body and so forth under the proposition that "the instruments and worlds are preceded by the cause that is the intellect," one should proclaim the entire Vaiśeṣika system (16a10).

Likewise, having stated merely the matter desired to be known, if the proponent should expand the discussion—this is what "if the proponent" implies—one asks: having done what should he expand it? To this he says:
By introducing other matters that are useless for establishing [the point] through a succession of qualifications of the meaning in the thesis and so forth—
as previously illustrated in the dispute over whether "sound is eternal" or "sound is non-eternal," the follower of Jaimini (Jaiminīya) provides proof by means of the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇa* and so on.
And he explains the twelve characteristics just as the followers of Akṣapāda do:

"In the dispute as to whether all these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary or not, [the opponent argues that] because they are the substrata of universals such as 'form-ness' (*rūpatva*), the cognitions— such as direct perception— that have those [universals] as their substrata and objects do not perish immediately after attaining their own existence."

[The word *śabda*] is denoted by the term "effect-sound" because it is produced by conjunctions and disjunctions with substances that are either similar or dissimilar [to itself], just like prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth.
Now, in the phrase "in the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth," what is included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*)?
It cannot be the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*udāharaṇa*), for there is the statement: "having stated only those two."

And since no other [member] is introduced here, this is not a fault; for it should be understood that the words "even having stated merely the reason and so forth" (hetvādimātram apy uktvā) imply that by the mention of the word "etc.
(ādi), the reason and the other members are indeed included, according to some.
Others, however, say that this objection raised regarding the use of the *ktvā* suffix here is misplaced;

for the meaning here is as follows: having stated the mere object of inquiry—such as non-momentariness—which is devoid of other qualifications, the proponent, thinking "I shall prove this," subsequently formulates the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and, by introducing further objects through a succession of qualifiers to the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth, might expand the discussion.

The meaning is as follows: "In that case" (taccet) means that when, through a succession of qualifications such as the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth, the opponent has been induced to state something entirely irrelevant—like the mere proclamation of a play or a narrative—then what is the basis for debate? Since it is merely a matter (*artha-mātra*) such as non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*), there is no impairment whatsoever of one's capacity to provide a response. Therefore, a respondent who does not repeat the opponent's discourse is not capable of countering the proponent.
However, the connection is that whatever is invariably concomitant with the establishment of the object sought to be known must necessarily be demonstrated;

for the reason that refutation has as its object the members of the proof, since refutation proceeds only when a proof has been presented by the opponent. To the question, "What, then, is invariably concomitant with the establishment of the object sought to be known? he says:

Just as the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is merely for the sake of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*), so too "pervasion-establishment" (*vyāptiprasādhana*) means that by which pervasion is established; namely, the presentation of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*). To the question, "Why should another point be introduced even when employing such a proof? he says:
"In that case as well, there is no introduction of another consequence (*prasaṅga*)," because it would be purposeless—this is the intention.
Only that much is shown here: why is it not the case that [the opponent] first follows the sequence [of the argument] and only afterwards offers the refutation?

He says "no," because even in the rejoinder (*anubhāṣaṇa*) intended for the purpose of indicating the object of the refutation, one does not state the refutation of everything that was presented by the proponent.
It should have been uttered previously in its proper sequence; why [is it not so]? Because there would be the contingency of uttering it three times.
To demonstrate precisely the contingency of uttering it twice, he undertakes the initial procedure.
With the words beginning "dūṣaṇa" (refutation), [the author] says:

if one does not announce the sequence of the statement, it would follow that the refutation is now without an object; therefore, because of its necessary concomitance (*nāntarīyakatva*), the refuter indeed performs the presentation of the object.
What is meant by "the statement of each respective fault" (*pratidoṣavacana*)? It means that for whichever fault is stated, its specific object (*viṣaya*) is explained;
this is precisely what [the author] says.
If it is asked, "What is the reason that this fault of the opponent's statement is not stated as a refutation all at once after repeating everything? he says, "For indeed...
(na hi), and so forth.
Why?
Because the defects differ according to each respective object; that is to say, the defect differs just as the object does.
Thus, having established the method beginning with "āracita," he demonstrates the consequence of repeating [the recitation] twice, [showing that] it is not merely once, unproclaimed.

Since it is impossible to state the fault of the subject once the "repeating everything" (*sarvānubhāṣaṇa*) has been demonstrated, he says that this is merely a ground for defeat based on a useless [objection].

When a proponent of refutation must state a refutation, that which involves a recitation of the entire sequence is useful for agitating the opponent's position; its expression consists of this "pointing out the repetition of words" (*dviruktapadodbhāvana*) and so forth, and thus the arrangement of words should be done in such a way as to cause confusion. Therefore, a recitation of the entire sequence should be declared a ground for defeat (*parājaya-adhikaraṇa*). At this point, Ākṣapāda, considering that all this refutation has already been countered by us through the non-acceptance of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), grants permission [to the opponent], saying, "Let it be so.
He explains this very point with the words, "It might be thus" (*syād etat*).

Since there is no possibility of [the opponent] introducing a series of qualifications for the meaning of the thesis and so forth under the pretext of explaining the meaning of the proof from some source or other, the statement of what is not a necessary consequence (*anantarīyaka*) is merely a deviation to another subject (*arthāntara*). If it is asked, "Why is the proponent, while speaking incidentally (*prāsaṅgika*), subject to defeat?", he says:
"For there is no one who does not employ some incidental argument (*prasaṅga*) in some context."
As was stated previously, for one who propounds selflessness (*nairātmyavādin*),

there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [the proof of it] would apply even to dancing, singing, and so forth; nor has this been presented as a consequence by the proponent of that [self].
The meaning is that for that opponent, what ought to be restated is not fit to be restated because it is useless;
thus, by this, that which was previously stated— namely, "even if the proponent, under the pretext of explaining the meaning of his own proof," and so forth— is admitted.

Regarding what was just stated— that not everything should be articulated in sequence and that the refutation should be voiced afterwards to avoid the contingency of double articulation— that [objection] is understood;
for this too has been addressed by us starting with the words "na cedam apy asmābhiḥ" (16b8) and so forth.
The Teacher said:
"If this is also desired by you, then non-repetition should not be mentioned as a separate [ground for defeat]. Why?
Because it is included within 'inability to respond' (*pratibhā*)."
It demonstrates that the [opponent's] position has already been understood, for "non-reproduction" (*apratibhā*) is defined as the failure to respond to a subsequent argument (Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.18).
Then, he explains how [the debate] proceeds: "Furthermore, without demonstrating the subject matter of the response, the opponent is not capable of apprehending, knowing, or stating the answer."
To the question "Why is he not capable?", he says "For not... and so forth;
the meaning is that the subsequent realization is the "subsequent realization" (*uttarā pratipattiḥ*).

That [objection] was not raised by him through the failure to repeat [the opponent's argument]; rather, because of those two negations, it is determined that it is a positive injunction. Thus, what is meant is that it is precisely the non-comprehension of the answer that has been implied.

For indeed, one who offers a rejoinder must necessarily have understood the subject matter as well, since he recognizes, "this is the refutation of that. And how could a conscious person, having understood the subject matter, not repeat it? Therefore, wherever there is non-repetition, there non-rejoinder (*apratibhā*) must be present; thus, non-rejoinder is pervaded by non-repetition, just as the *khadira* tree is pervaded by trees in general. Since the status of being a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) has been established for that [non-repetition], it implies its presence in the pervaded [non-repetition]; this he states under the guise of a conclusion with the words beginning "by that" (*tena*).

Right here he states an illustration: "Just as [the property of] possessing a dewlap and so forth, which is prescribed for that which is not specifically qualified as a cow but is of the nature of a universal, is found even in a bāhuleya (a brown ox) which is pervaded by that [universal]; such is the application.

Furthermore, when something is obtainable even though it is not explicitly stated—by virtue of the power of the prescription of one thing—it should certainly not be prescribed again by one who acts with foresight.

For example, just as the possession of a dewlap and so forth—which is established in the case of the genus "cow" by the force of its definition—is precluded from being a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) such as "inability to respond" (*apratibhā*) by the force of the definition of that ground; and just as the state of being "non-reproduction" (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) is likewise precluded [from being a ground for defeat] by the force of its definition—this is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

But surely, even when a respondent understands both the subject (*viṣaya*) and the reply (*uttara*), his mind may be distracted by extreme fear, trembling, and so forth, such that he fails to restate [the opponent's position]. That subject is not touched by "non-restatement" (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) because it is not touched by "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*). Therefore, how could that [non-ingenuity] be its pervader (*vyāpikā*), such that this reason [of yours] would be established? It is simply not possible; for one who understands the subject and the reply to that subject does not fear or tremble from any cause, since fear, trembling, perspiration, and the like are produced by ignorance of that [subject].
Furthermore, if even one who has become such [an expert] is agitated by fear and the like, then he would not even run toward engaging in debate at the outset;
moreover,
it is only fools who are of such a nature.
Furthermore, logical treatises (*nyāyaśāstra*) are not composed with reference to the conventional practices of fools;
thus, even in this way, their inclusion within "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*) is by no means contradicted,
because the realization of various types of responses consists both of the form of ignorance regarding the response and the form of non-utterance of the response.
Therefore, this [objection] is trivial;
even if it were for the purpose of tormenting others, why would it be stated three times? Rather, he says what the actual task is:

Having approached the witnesses with a bribe and whispered into their ears, "This is the matter I intend to state," he should subsequently harass the wretched defendant— who has no protector— by means of words that are difficult to understand, rapid, or abridged; for why [should he not do so], since they are difficult to pronounce?

Unfamiliar, such as the Sinhalese language and so forth; unexpressed, being unintelligible; rapid, being uttered quickly; and concise, having their meaning condensed and rounded up like a thread of a sūtra.
By the inclusion of the word "ādi" (etcetera), there is the inclusion of meanings that have been concealed;
for example:
*satvādurvāyuste diśyāyotāyāñcārātyasvantaṃ pakṣe nolaṃvam vijñāyaiḥ veṣṭātoyāspṛṣṭeśaḥ śamiti*.

Just as the proponent, being confused regarding the apprehension of a reply, remains silent; this is "the unintelligible" (avijñātārtha), when that which has been stated three times by the assembly and the opponent is not understood— Nyāya Sūtra 5.1.23.

If it is argued that because the Sage did not prohibit the use of words that are punning (*śliṣṭa*) or difficult (*kaṣṭa*) in this [verse], one cannot therefore act unrighteously, he replies: "For this is not a method for afflicting others," and so forth. Furthermore, the virtuous do not engage in activities to afflict others, nor are scriptures composed by them for that purpose; as it was stated in the section on the opposition of the wicked (*durjana-vipratipatti-adhikaraṇa*): "Because the scriptures of the virtuous do not function [in that way]."

Since the virtuous do not engage in activity for the purpose of afflicting others, it must therefore be stated that [the statement] should be repeated only as long as it has not been grasped by the opponent, and not more than three times; this is the rule.

Now, if it is determined that the respondent is unable to grasp [the argument] despite the proponent’s repeated exposition even a hundred times due to extreme dullness, and once that incapacity for grasping has somehow been ascertained, then before the formal application of the proof (*sādhana*), the proponent should withdraw, thinking, "I shall not engage in debate with this person. Thus, the proponent determines the incapacity—known as extreme dullness—belonging to the respondent.
To the question, "How can one who avoids [the objection] in such a manner be suspected of being incapable?", he says:
"Having awakened the witness of the supreme breath, this person is not capable of understanding the meaning of the sentence; rather, the reality is established in this way.

"Non-cognition is ignorance" (Nyāya-sūtra 5.2.17); since the suffix -ta is prescribed here in the sense of a state (*bhāva*), the failure to understand the meaning of the argumentative statement constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
For this very reason, the commentators on the Bhāṣya explain that "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) is the non-arising of the cognition whose object is the meaning of the sentence.

Or, even if the suffix *-niṣṭhā* is prescribed only for the [past] action, nevertheless, it remains the case that the very statement employed by the proponent—which is qualified by the non-arising of the cognition whose object is the meaning of the sentence—constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the opponent; thus, nothing is contradicted.
Others, however, seeing the word "meaning" (*artha*) in the *Vivaraṇa*, mistakenly read the word "meaning" (*artha*) even in the Sūtra.

Regarding the reading "and ignorance is the non-understanding of the meaning [of the statement]," there is another reading: "the meaning is understood. In this case, the arrangement of the words is as follows for the abstract (bhāva) sense: "that which is not understood—that is, the lack of comprehension—by the opponent (prativādin) from the assembly regarding the statement of proof (sādhanavākya) is 'ignorance' (ajñāna). However, in the objective (karman) sense, the word "tasya" ("of that") need not be supplied; rather, it is explained as a single syntactical unit.

Regarding the statement "The assembly has understood," for what purpose is it made? It is to indicate that even when the assembly does not understand, the debater incurs a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because his meaning remains uncomprehended.
He states the reason for its being a point of defeat: "Indeed, if the meaning is not understood, the opponent would not be able to state a refutation of it."

Others, however, connect this with the subsequent section on refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), but that is incorrect; since this is a passage from the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika*, it establishes that [the opponent's] understanding is indeed what is being proven. Just as in the case of non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), the status of a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) arises precisely through the failure to understand the reply, he asks: "How is there a failure to understand the reply? He says: "Because the subject matter has not been demonstrated. This should be understood to mean that the opponent's ability to understand the reply is impossible because the subject matter has not been demonstrated by him; or it may be understood as a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).

For instance, one restates [the opponent's argument] for the purpose of making the object of the refutation known; yet, if one were to restate whatever web of words the proponent has not even brought forward, abandoning that [relevant point], then such a restatement would be useless in the absence of the occasion to demonstrate the subject matter of the response. Therefore, it follows that it constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) precisely because it fails to assist [the proponent] and because it is not understood [as relevant]. Alternatively, [it is a point of defeat] because it is impossible [to respond].
He concludes the illustration:
likewise, even in the case of knowledge, it constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) precisely because of the failure to provide a reply;
for how could one speak of the refutation of the opponent, its object, and the object of the reply to someone who does not understand?

The object of the rejoinder (*uttara-viṣaya*) is the one to be refuted (*dūṣya*); however, in some places the reading is "how is it that the rejoinder is both the rejoinder and the object of the rejoinder?"

In this regard, since one who lacks a connection [to the subject] and does not know the scope of the response could not possibly provide a response, therefore both ignorance of the subject and ignorance of the response are grounds for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because they are understood through non-replica (*apratibhā*) itself.

The term "inexpressible" (avācya) continues [to apply here]. What is the reason? Otherwise, since this would lack any means of valid cognition (apramāṇa), there would be no object for the "non-appearance" (aprati-bhā).
To the question, "How is it that there is no object? he says:
"For one whose object is not determined," and so forth.
If a respondent does not recall the prior position regarding the *tīrtha* (the point of debate) nor its refutation because he failed to attend to them,

then, failing to recall them, he would be unable to demonstrate the subject matter and thus unable to formulate a response; consequently, he would not arrive at a reply, would not understand it, and would not be able to state it.

Why is it that when there is ignorance regarding the answer and its object, there is no comprehension of the answer? To this he says: "Because it is impossible for there to be no comprehension of the answer when the answer and its object are known," meaning that by which [the respondent] has understood both the answer and its object;
therefore, both of these constitute the ignorance of the answer.
Furthermore, ignorance regarding the subject matter is indeed the cause of *apratibhā*—which is synonymous with "inability to respond.
But if it is simply ignorance of the answer that constitutes *apratibhā*, how can that very [ignorance] be taught as its own cause?
[This is not so], because what is intended here is *apratibhā* characterized by the failure to state an answer.

"In the absence of that" means that when there is an absence of those two— the ignorance of the subject matter of the reply and the failure to provide a reply— there is indeed the understanding and the articulation of the reply; therefore, if apratibhā (lack of ingenuity) were stated as a separate ground for defeat from the ground for defeat called ajñāna (ignorance)— which consists of the ignorance of the subject matter of the reply and the ignorance regarding the reply itself— it must be stated what the scope of apratibhā is, if no such scope is declared.

Others explain that, because it would then lack a specific object, non-representation (*apratibhā*) would indeed be inexpressible as distinct from ignorance (*ajñāna*) and non-reproduction (*anubhāṣaṇa*); thus,
the opponent speaks in order to establish a distinction between the objects of ignorance and non-representation.

Non-knowledge is said to be the lack of superior knowledge (*anuttara-jñāna*), because from that [lack] there arises a failure of eloquence (*apratibhā*) due to the absence of an object, which would thus become inexpressible.
To the question "What then is non-knowledge?", he says:
Even so, one might ask: how can non-apprehension have an object? To this he says: because, when the object has been known, there subsequently arises a further non-cognition [of that cognition].
If the opponent were unable to comprehend or express that [point],
then there would be a scope for *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity),
which is characterized by ignorance.
Even so, because it is inexpressible, you are not liberated; thus he says,
"In that case, then," thereby establishing the very objection that [the opponent's] restatement is due to ignorance.
For no conscious person, when correctly understanding the subject matter, would fail to repeat it; thus, non-repetition should not be stated as distinct from ignorance.
Furthermore, in this way, non-elucidation (*apratibhā*) should not be stated as distinct from ignorance, just like non-repetition; for he says: "because it is implied by the ignorance of the reply."
He explains this with the passage beginning "viṣaye" and so forth;
the opponent [responds] with "jñāte viṣaye" and so forth.
(Nyāyabhāṣya, p. 262).

I could not find the footnote reference for this statement: "It has been said that [the opponent's ignorance] is twofold: that which accompanies ignorance regarding the answer itself, and that which accompanies ignorance regarding the subject matter. Since the first does not imply ignorance regarding the subject matter, the answer remains unimplied; therefore, *aprati-bhā* (inability to respond) is mentioned separately with respect to the second [type].
Thus, he says that an infinite regress of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) would otherwise result."
The passage beginning with "evam tarhi" (if that is so) is an analysis of the very same [point] introduced by "yathā" (just as);
likewise, the phrase "jñānayor api" (also of the two cognitions) refers to the object and the subsequent cognition.
If it is argued that there is a fault in the summary statement regarding the ignorance of the entire subsequent subject matter and the inclusion—
by means of the term "and so forth" (ādi)— of two, three, or four parts, etc.,
[the author] says:
If it is argued that just as there is no fault, so too there is no quality, he says:
"And there would be a quality known as lightness"; thus, the statement of summary is logical.
The meaning is that because they fall within the scope of *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity), there is no separate mention of them; they are included by the very term *apratibhā*.
It is not only these two that are mentioned separately.
But others say that it is also logical for them [the other two],
as he states with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth,
by means of the statement of both of those.

By the mere mention of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and lack of rejoinder (*apratibhā*), all [other faults] such as abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*) and failure to restate (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) are already included;

for it must be stated that no one other than the proponent of the proof (*sādhana-vādī*) ever admits the property of the counter-position (*pratipakṣadharma*) or employs the thesis itself as a means to prove that very thesis. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever that is not already evident when one fails to restate [the opponent's position].

If it is argued that the opponent diverts the discussion and the proponent allows it, and that even when both do so, such proliferation (prapañca) is virtuous, and therefore the Sage did not speak of it— then [the author] says:

Since no distinctions projected by those two [categories] are perceived without an excellence of quality (*guṇātiśaya*), there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of applying the term "proliferation" (*prapañca*) even to qualities; furthermore,
it would entail the undesirable consequence of having to name things such as "the back of the armpit" (*kakṣapiṭṭitā*).
Therefore, the elaborate elaboration was rendered useless by the Great Sage.

When an opponent, while a refutation of their own position ought to be made, neither finds a response, nor understands one, nor articulates one, they should then be known as defeated; such is the extent of the opponent's argument.

Thinking that this is indeed a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), and that for this very reason we have also stated here that "this is the pointing out of a non-existent fault," he [the opponent] grants permission with the words "sādhana" and so forth.
Immediately after the statement of the proof (*sādhana*), the opponent (*prativādin*) must state the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).

If, without doing any of that, he wastes time by restating the entire sequence [of the proof], reciting verses, describing the assembly, or other such means, then, by wasting time fruitlessly and without purpose—failing to undertake the understanding of the refutation that ought to be performed—he is defeated. This "time" is a qualification of the action of "wasting."
Distraction by business, the mention of something else to be done, the interruption of the narrative, and the cessation of the narrative—as for example:
"An old ailment afflicts me."
"I am unable to speak now; I shall speak later"—by such means as these, one cuts off the discussion during its unfolding.
He states the reason for this being a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*):

when either the proponent or the opponent brings the discussion to an end in defeat by failing to state a constituent of proof (*asādhanāṅga-vacana*) or by failing to point out a fault (*adoṣodbhāvana*). This is a discussion that culminates in defeat.
And when that [situation] has occurred in such a manner—that he himself reaches the end of the discussion, the conclusion of the discourse—this is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Regarding this, the Teacher says:

"This too is a diversion from the task (*kāryavyāsañjana*), if the proponent of the prima facie case (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) should do so because of a lack of power to state the proof; that is to say, by means of some pretext, merely through a deceptive objection."

The phrase "he should not do so" continues [from the previous rule]. That is to say, if there exists a matter that obstructs such a discussion—one whose nature is to interrupt a discourse in the form of a formal debate (*udgrāhaṇikā*)—and if, by its very presence, at that very time, ailments such as indigestion, pain in the stomach, or burning in the house occur, then this is not a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). This is the meaning.

When, however, one acts by mere prevarication alone, then that proponent (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) would experience distraction simply from the realization of the incapacity of his own proof; to the question "What follows from this?", he says:

"And thus, this point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as 'distracting' (*vikṣepa*) would be included within 'irrelevance' (*arthāntara*) itself, because the presentation of what ought to be done is identical to the explanation of names and so forth in the case of the [defeat called] *rūpasiddhi*."
It follows that it would be included among the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*);
for why is it not so? Because it is designated as both "inefficacious" (*asamartha*) and a "proof" (*sādhana*).
Furthermore, how does this differ from the "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*) and the "incoherent" (*apārthaka*)?

What is the reason? It means that there is no perceived connection between this [proposition] and the statement of the proof (*sādhana-vākya*), because it is unrelated to both the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) and its proof (*sādhana*). It is like the statement "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*) or the sequence of phonemes "ja-ba-ga-ḍa," which have no connection with the proof-statement.
If it is argued that it is stated separately from the other members due to a slight difference in form or a minor causal factor, he replies:
"And there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)," and so forth.
Those who possess comprehension through an unconnected statement of proof are "those who comprehend an unconnected statement of proof";

these are both those [persons] and the varieties [of distraction], and [the term refers] to them. Thus, it has been stated that there is no separate mention of distraction in connection with the proponent (pūrvapakṣavādin).
Now, he speaks also in connection with the opponent (prativādin):

Now, if the proponent of the rejoinder (*uttarapakṣavādī*) should divert the discussion by means of such a sequence as "it destroys the throat which consists of the entire mass of phlegm," then, since a rejoinder ought to be understood immediately after the proof (*sādhana*) [of the first proponent], the fact that he does not understand it—that is, his failure to state that rejoinder—is an admission of diversion (*vikṣepa*), which is included either within "inability" (*aprati-bhā*) or "irrelevancy" (*arthāntara*). However, the opponent, unable to accept this aforementioned inclusion, objects:
"But surely, not necessarily so," and thereby confirms that very point.

For indeed, there exists debate even by means of a syllogistic statement that is unconnected, or even by a discourse that is irrelevant—even down to the accusation of one’s mother’s infidelity for the purpose of depriving an opponent of their presence of mind;
thus the Teacher says:
"Not so, because such a debate is impossible."

Since there would be a dispute between two parties—a proponent and a respondent—who hold mutually contradictory assertions regarding permanence, impermanence, and so forth, with respect to a single locus such as sound, [the author] asks, "Whence does this follow? and replies:
"Those two whose assertions are not contradictory are thus; those two persons for whom there do not exist contradictory and non-contradictory assertions possess such assertions."

Since there can be no dispute between the two when this determination of the logical rule has been established, in that case, one of the two— the proponent or the opponent— must necessarily initiate the speech first.
"Why do they not speak simultaneously? To this he says:
"Because for those whose minds are composed, there is no simultaneous activity"—this is the connection [of the sentence].
Why is this so? To this he says:
Because the activity [of speech] would be futile due to the impossibility of hearing, comprehending, and responding to one another's words— [impossibility] which serves as the instrumental cause—

if indeed the hearing of one another's words were possible without confusion, then one could comprehend their meaning and offer a response; however, since simultaneous activity, like the clamor of Digambara reciters, makes all of this impossible, it follows that one person must necessarily initiate the speech first.

Therefore, when that proponent of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣavādin), being composed in mind, has presented his own accepted position by stating, "I shall prove that sound is impermanent," and so forth, he must necessarily state a proof (*sādhana*); otherwise, if the reason (*hetu*) is not stated, there would be no comprehension for others, such as the witnesses and the like.

And by the other—the proponent of the rejoinder (uttarapakṣavādin)—a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) related to that, namely related to the proof spoken by the proponent, must be stated; this is the sense that follows.

Therefore, when both the proponent and the opponent proceed incorrectly, there is the inclusion of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*). Thus, every presentation of the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the response (*uttara-pakṣa*) conducted according to logic does not exceed these two: fallacious reasons and lack of ingenuity.
Now, if logic is indeed proceeding, how can there be scope for these two [fallacies] therein?
And how can two contradictory presentations occur within a single subject (*dharmin*) while logic is proceeding? For in that case, one presentation must necessarily be in accordance with logic.
Otherwise, the subject (dharmin) would possess a dual nature;

this is not due to a failure to understand our intention, for you have failed to fully comprehend that the Master did not intend to assert that this [subject] functions according to formal logic (nyāya).

For when reasoning proceeds, since the presentation of the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final position (*uttarapakṣa*) does not occur simultaneously, and because there is an absence of the experience of contradiction regarding the mother [the thesis], that which was intended is established;
by this, the objection that "there would be a dispute between two contradictory admissions in a single locus" and so forth—which was leveled against the *vitaṇḍā*—is refuted.
He asks: "How is it refuted? and then says:

Since there can be no dispute in the absence of a thesis, this is what is meant: a collection of statements that lacks the establishment of one's own position is called *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), according to Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.3.
2.3 Furthermore, if a vitaṇḍāvādin has no position of his own, it must be explained how there can then be a dispute.
If it is argued that the caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*) proceeds for the sake of refuting the opponent's position,
then the very refutation of the opponent's position would constitute his own establishment of a position; thus, the definition of the cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) collapses,
for whatever is accepted by someone is that person’s own position.
Furthermore, since the refutation of the opponent's position accepted by him does not transcend the status of being his own position,
it follows that when he enters into a debate and— due to the fruitlessness of his mere thesis and because he is distracted by timidity before the assembly—
does not state any proof or even the effort required for it, [he is defeated].

Or if one utters some other nonsensical babble distinct from both a valid means of proof (*sādhana*) and its fallacy (*tadābhāsa*), such as: "The crow is crying discordantly; surely this portends some calamity in my house;
enough of this dispute, I shall go home first to see whether my father’s death or something else has occurred," and so forth.
Likewise, how could there be an inclusion within the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*)?
Since there is an absence of a proof (*sādhana*), he considers that the fallacies of the reason are impossible;
the intention is that even the "failure to understand the reply" does not exist at all, because [the opponent] is the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣavādin*).
With this, the opponent wishes to refute the statement that "one does not fall beyond these two";
the Teacher says:

"This was stated regarding the formulation of a proof that has not been established; that is to say, it was stated that one does not fall beyond these two only when the aforementioned proof has been [successfully] set forth."
To address the question of how one should proceed when [the reason] is unspoken, he says:
even when there is both non-expression and expression [of the reason], there is indeed defeat; this was already stated at the very introduction of the section, and he now recalls that very point.
Regarding the statement "because of the utterance of what is not a member of the proof" in the context of an *abhyupagamya-vāda* (acknowledged discourse),
it has been explained therein as the non-utterance of a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*).
Whatever statement is made regarding something other than the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) is all "statement of what is not a member of the proof" (*asādhanāṅgavacana*).

By this—namely, by the mention of another [member] as a ground for defeat (*parājaya*)—the status of the excessive, the redundant, and the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth as points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is explained.
To the question "How so? he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tadapi hi" (for even that), he says this by it:

whatever point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) has been stated by Akṣapāda as being consistent with reason, that has already been subsumed by us under the very term "stating what is not a member of the proof" (*asādhanāṅgavacana*). If this is so, for what purpose was the statement "and of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth" made? For indeed, the statement of the proposition, the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*) were not declared by Akṣapāda to be points of defeat.

[Objection: If that is so, then this is for the sake of an illustration: just as that [statement] is designated by the term "stating a non-member of the proof" (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) because it lacks the capacity to convey what has not been understood, so too it is with the redundant and the superfluous.
And for that very reason, the second *ca* functions in the sense of "as if" (*iva*);
otherwise, the meaning would have to be understood as "and [the repetition]," whereas some do not read the subsequent *ca*.
Furthermore, they [the opponents] must explain that the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth is indeed a case of repetition;

yet even this is not tenable, because Akṣapāda (Gautama) does not accept such a form of repetition. There is no fault, however, because this too is included within the category of repetition by virtue of its possessing the same characteristics as the previously mentioned types of repetition.
Matānujñā (conceding the opponent's position) is the attribution of a fault to the opponent's position by accepting a fault in one's own position; Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.21.
20. When a fault (*doṣa*) ought to be refuted, because he does not fully understand the fault, he accedes to the opponent's position and is thereby defeated.
Thus it is said: having followed the fault urged and questioned by the opposing proponent and having refuted it [superficially], he says, "This fault belongs to you as well.
For example, when the proponent has said, "You are a thief because you are a human being, like a hunter (*śabara*) and so forth," that respondent might reply to that proponent:

"You too are a thief"—by this application of the word, the opponent also admits his own status as a thief and, while attributing that fault to the other's position, incurs the defeat called *matānujñā* (admission of the opponent's view). For he thereby consents to that which the other proponent has asserted regarding the opponent being a thief; indeed, one who is not free from suspicion cannot possibly admit his own status as a thief, nor could he speak of it otherwise.
However, whether that [alleged fault] exists or does not exist must be considered by the proponent himself; therefore, *matānujñā* is a point of defeat.
The Teacher refutes this as follows:

"In this case as well, if the intention of the opponent is that 'you must be a thief because you are a human being, just like me,' yet you yourself do not accept being a thief, then 'because of being a human being' is not a valid reason for proving theft; for it is vitiated by the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), since it occurs even in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) of one who is not a thief."

Therefore, in this intention of the opponent, there is no fault— neither the one characterized as "admission of the opponent's position" (matānujñā) nor any other— because the reason is refuted by the method of demonstrating its presence in the proponent’s own self, which is the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) for that which is not intended [as a thief], namely,
through the manifestation of a fallacy of non-deviation (avyabhicāra) consisting of a clever artifice. This is the meaning.

He anticipates the objection of Ādyaudyotakara: "Why do you not state, in a straightforward and honest manner, that 'the reason is also non-deviant in your case, since the property of being a human (puruṣatva) exists even in one who is not a thief; therefore, it is inconclusive'? Consequently, he is defeated precisely because he practices crookedness when he ought to act without crookedness.
[Note: The reading in the *Nyāyabhāṣya* is "non-defeat of one who has reached a point of defeat" (*nigrahasthānaprāptasyānigrahaḥ*).]
The teacher says:
"This statement of Uddyotakara is trivial (yatkiñcid). For there certainly exist in the world such transactions initiated by cleverness;

for instance, when one says, 'Your mothers are prostitutes because they are women, like other prostitutes,' even cowherds and others, following a cleverness common to people such as the *jaḍa* and *janaṅgama*, offer a rebuttal."
Nor can it be said that "your mother would likewise be so," for they do not, by this means, establish the status of their own respective mothers as mere prostitutes;
rather, they merely refute the opponent through an indirect method by pointing out the deviation of the reason (*hetu-vyabhicāra*).
Therefore, by casting aside even the light of worldly convention—which is evident even to children and plowmen—Uddyotakara has, at best, only illuminated his own nature as a "light-maker" (a lamp).

Now it is said: he does not indicate a deviation (vyabhicāra) by way of this [rejoinder], but rather, having accepted the validity of that proof, he defames the opponent with that very same fault. To this he replies:

"If he accepts him [the opponent] as saying, 'You are a thief because you are a man,' even then he is subject to defeat solely due to his failure to provide an answer to that proof; he is not subject to defeat because of the introduction of the opponent's own fault—namely, being a thief. This is the sense.
This very point is further supported by the fact that, once the faultlessness of that proof has been accepted— this being the ellipsis—

the very admission of that [objectionable] proposal constitutes the failure to provide a response; for it is by that alone, namely by the mere failure to respond, that one incurs the charge of error regarding the other [position].
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "of one who has incurred (āpanna) or reached (prāpta) a defeat (nigraha), which is the refutation (nigraha) of a previous proof.

The sense is that there is no defeat of one already defeated, because the raising of another's fault—which is characterized as "admission of the opponent's position" (matānujñā)—is not to be taken into account.
Nyāyavārttika 5.2.21, page 559.

"Overlooking the one who deserves censure" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) is the failure to censure one who has reached a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). One who "deserves censure" (*paryanuyojya*) is defined as one who has reached a point of defeat; it is the failure to state, "You have reached a point of defeat. But who, then, points out this point of defeat called "overlooking the one who deserves censure"?
It is not logical to say that it is the one who deserves censure himself.
Because it is impossible;
for there is no possibility that one who has incurred defeat would admit his own possession of faults for the sake of pointing out the faults of another,
yet be overlooked by the opponent due to the latter’s failure to recognize the ground of defeat.
Therefore, it is not right to say that he is either "faulty" or "to be ignored," because he indeed knows that this [opponent] has incurred defeat;
for it is precisely due to a lack of understanding that he does not press him, saying, "You have reached defeat."
Or, if there is full comprehension, how could one be indifferent?

And if one is indifferent, how could one have an even mind? Furthermore, how could one manifest this [indifference] by saying, "This person has been neglected by me"? Therefore, that fault is subject to inquiry: "Negligence is a point of defeat.
Nor is there any third alternative here as a consequence; so, by whom should this be challenged? Anticipating all these objections, the master Pakṣilasvāmin says:

And this "neglecting what is to be censured" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) must be stated; the meaning is that when the proponent and the opponent have been questioned in this manner—"Who has lost?"—the assembly (*pariṣad*), having been properly addressed or questioned by them or by others, must declare [the result] through the judges (*prāśnika*).
The word "and" (*ca*) is for the sake of emphasis, signifying that this alone [is so], whereas other points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are brought forth by the proponent and the opponent themselves.
Furthermore, why is this not stated by those two [the disputant and the opponent] themselves? To this he says:
"Indeed, one who has reached a point of defeat would not expose his own private parts—that is, his own fault. (18b10) He would not reveal it.
Regarding this, the Teacher says "here too" and so forth:
if, however, one considers the logic of the matter, then it is not logical for even one [of the two] to have both victory and defeat.
To the question "How then is there victory for the proponent?", he replies: because the object of inquiry has not been established by means of a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*).

For this very reason, there is no defeat for the opponent either, because the determination of the opponent’s defeat is made in relation to the establishment of the meaning intended by the proponent. [The author] asks: "In that case, what is the victory of the opponent? and answers:
"And because of the non-statement of faults regarding what is real" (19a1).
For this very reason, there is no defeat for the proponent, since that [defeat] is established in relation to the refutation of his argument;
furthermore, even if many defects exist in the respondent, if he points out some defect in the proof stated by the proponent but not another,
he does not deserve defeat.
"What is the reason?"—the meaning is that it is because the subsequent response has been stated.
The opponent says: "He certainly deserves defeat, because not all of the faults have been pointed out."
The Teacher says:

"Indeed, sir, it is not the case that all faults must necessarily be stated by the opponent simply because they exist; for if they are not stated, there is the defeat consisting of another fault. This is how it continues.
Why should not all defects be pointed out? To this he says:
because even by a single defect, such as "unestablished" (*asiddha*) and so forth, once it has been pointed out, there is no obstruction to that proof (*sādhana*) employed by the proponent;
the meaning is that its incapacity to establish the probandum (*sādhya*) is thereby demonstrated.

Alternatively, the word "sādhana" (means of accomplishment) here has a nominal sense (*bhāvasādhana*); he provides an illustration for this very point: "like the expression of a single means of accomplishment. 19a3

The phrase beginning with "just as" (*yathā*) is a detailed analysis of this very point: although there exist many means of proof (*sādhana*), such as existence (*satva*), being an effect (*kāryatva*), and arising from effort (*prayatnotthatva*), for the purpose of establishing a single object—such as momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*)—one need only employ any one of these, such as existence, because that object, momentariness, is established and ascertained through it alone; thus, not all means of proof are employed.
Similarly, since the proof of that [object] is thwarted by even a single fault (*doṣa*), not all [faults] are employed. This is the similarity illustrated by the example.

Thus, for this reason, the proponent of the subsequent position (uttarapakṣavādī) is not deserving of defeat merely because he fails to point out another fault after having already pointed out one fault;
for, as in the previous case, he has neither demonstrated [the opponent's flaw] through a fallacious proof (sādhanābhāsa) nor stated an actual fault.
But surely, how can there be victory for the proponent when he has not employed a fallacious proof, whereas the opponent merely points out a non-existent fault? To this he replies:

[it is so] because he does not drive away—that is to say, does not cause to turn back—the proponent of the counter-position who is speaking a fallacious fault, by demonstrating that what was stated by him is a fallacious refutation with respect to his own proof.
Why is there no victory for the proponent? Because his members of proof are not properly connected.
That which possesses the state of having unconnected members of proof is [the proponent];
why is this so? He says:
Because the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) are established by demonstrating the absence of all defects,
the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.21, either in the sense of a characteristic (*ittthambhūtalakṣaṇa*) or as an instrument (*karaṇa*).
The concise meaning is that because it has not been established, what was employed by him is merely a semblance of a proof (*sādhanābhāsa*);
nor does victory belong to the proponent of the subsequent position (*uttarapakṣavādin*).

Therefore, even in this case—by the word "even" (*api*), it is indicated that it is not only in connection with the opponent (*uttaravādin*) that the proponent of the prior position (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) fails to defeat one who has reached a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
19a6: Pressing for a point that should not be pressed;
stating "you are defeated" when one has not reached a point of defeat.
But why do you speak thus? He says:

"Because of a false determination regarding the definition of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)," which means because of an incorrect thorough understanding of the previously stated definition of the points of defeat;
and thus one is defeated due to a lack of comprehension.
Regarding the phrase "In this case also," and so forth, the Teacher [Dharmakīrti] says:

if one were to charge the proponent with that proof by means of non-existent, false defects— saying, "The proof you have employed is vitiated by defects such as *savyabhicāra* (inconclusiveness), therefore you are defeated"— then that [charge] is an exposition in the wrong place (*asthāne*), because this [defeat], being a faultless point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), is already included within the very classification of this [point].

The term "accuser" (*abhiyoktṛ*) is explained as "one who brings forth" (*udbhāvayitṛ*). Thus, when one states a false defect while failing to understand the rebuttal characterized by the bringing forth of that defect, the respondent is defeated by means of "inability to respond" (*apratibhā*) acting as the instrument. Since this is not the defeat-ground called "objectioning against one who is not to be objected to" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), it is not a separate defeat-ground from "inability to respond. To explain when this person is defeated by inability to respond, he says:

Alternatively, when the other disputant has demonstrated that what was stated by the former is a fallacious rejoinder (*uttarābhāsa*), otherwise neither of the two would have victory or defeat as before—this is the underlying intention.
Having thus established that this [refutation] is not mentioned separately from its connection with the respondent (*prativādin*), he speaks also in connection with the proponent (*vādin*):

"Then, the 'other'—that is, the proponent of the prima facie case (*pūrvapakṣavādin*)—should charge the respondent, who is revealing a real (i.e., true) defect in the proof such as *savyabhicāra* (inconclusiveness) and so forth, with the statement that no such defect exists."

The meaning is: if the opponent should charge, "You have employed a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*), an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*), or some other fallacy; therefore, you are defeated," then, once that fault—such as the inconclusiveness—has been pointed out and its status as a genuine defect has been established by the respondent, it amounts to saying that the character of being a futile rejoinder has been refuted.

Since the proponent is defeated by the very mention of a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*), this [fallacy of the thesis] does not differ from the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) even when related to the opponent; therefore, it should not be stated separately.

This is merely a reinforcement of that very point: for one who maintains that there are twenty-two points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), the fallacies of the reason must necessarily be stated as distinct points of defeat.
He asks, "For what purpose? and says:

"For the sake of attaining another category [of defeat], namely, the inclusion of those not already encompassed by the points of defeat such as 'accusing one who is not to be accused' (niranuyojyānuyoga) and so forth. The intention is that otherwise, the acceptance of twenty-two points of defeat would be contradicted.
And thus, when they are stated—that is, when those fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are stated as points of defeat—there is no further statement [required].
The statement of another [fallacy], namely "urging what should not be urged" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), is redundant because it is already subsumed under the mention of "pseudo-reasons" (*hetvābhāsa*).

Regarding the sūtra: "Deviation from a tenet (*apasiddhānta*) is the consequence of a debate resulting from a failure to adhere to a tenet once accepted" (NS 5.2.23). This means that having accepted a tenet—that is, having undertaken the adoption of a thesis—there is a lack of consistency; specifically, by obstructing the previously established subject matter and disregarding the systematic arrangement of the treatise.
In the context of a discourse, when one describes another matter—
that is, having asserted a different property (*dharmāntara*) of a subject (*dharmin*), the contradiction (*virodha*) consists in the reversal of the asserted meaning;
this he clarifies by means of an example.

Just as there is no destruction of an existing entity that is without residue, but rather it merely becomes hidden, and nothing non-existent— such as a donkey’s horn— is produced, but rather that which already exists is produced through manifestation; having thus presented the established tenet of the Kāpilas, he formulates his position.
There is one primordial nature (prakṛti) characterized as unmanifest (avyakta) for that which is manifest (vyakta)—namely, for the great principle (mahat) and so forth;
he states the reason for this here: because of the observation of the persistence (anvaya) of modifications (vikāra), such as sound and the rest.
The example beginning with "of those things consisting of clay," and the application "and so too is this [world]," namely "endowed with pleasure,
pain, and delusion" (19b3), demonstrates that it is composed of pleasure and the other qualities.
And it has already been demonstrated previously, according to the Sāṃkhya view, that the manifest possesses the nature of pleasure and so forth;

therefore, the conclusion is that "because of pleasure and so forth, [the manifest] has a single primordial nature"—this is the distinction of the manifest. Here, the instrumental case in the word "sukhādibhiḥ" is used in the sense of a characteristic (itthambhūtalakṣaṇe).
The meaning is that its single primordial nature (prakṛti) consists of the modes of pleasure and so forth, and has pleasure and so forth as its characteristics;
others read it differently.
"There is one primordial nature (prakṛti), manifested, because of the observation of the persistence [of that nature] through its manifest transformations.
And thus they explain:

"There is one primordial nature, undivided, which has the self-nature of all things, because of the observation of the persistence [of that nature] through its manifest and unmanifest transformations."

"Because one observes the persistence [of the cause] even in those manifest transformations such as the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth, as well as in those unmanifest things that abide within the nature of Pradhāna"—thus say others; however, some read it as:
"The single unmanifest Prakṛti..."
"Of the transformations of the manifest" means "of the transformations that have a manifest form";
he says this in order to demonstrate how this [doctrine] has proceeded by way of a reversal of the intended meaning; that very follower of Kapila, having spoken thus, is being questioned. 19b4
Then, having been questioned thus— "How are both 'primordial nature' (prakṛti) and 'evolution' (vikāra) to be characterized and understood?"— he replied:

The Sāṅkhya has stated that that which remains constant while one property ceases and another property arises is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of fixed form; whereas that other property which undergoes arising and cessation is to be characterized as a modification (*vikāra*). This [definition] is undermined by the fault of abandoning the actual meaning of the term *prakṛti*.
The proponent, by reversing the subject matter under discussion due to a lack of consistency, introduces an irrelevant topic;
the meaning is that he abandons what was previously under consideration.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Indeed, he has made a formal proposition"; remember what was said previously.
[The opponent asks: "If this is so, what is the fault? [The author] replies with the words beginning "of the existent and non-existent," and so forth.
The cessation of the activity of no phenomenon whatsoever is established without the absolute disappearance or destruction [of that phenomenon].
If it were to exist in some altered state, that hidden limb would have to be either identical with or distinct from the persisting entity.

If it were identical, then because it is non-different from the hidden part, the persisting entity—just like the hidden part—would be non-existent; and conversely, because it is non-different from the persisting entity, the existence of the hidden part would likewise be suspected.
Even if [the effect] were something other [than the cause], how could there be continuity? There would be no destruction [of the cause], for when one thing persists, another does not persist;
nor can one thing be the continuity of another, because that would entail the absurdity of consciousness being continuous with a jar.
Likewise, the activity of any property cannot be established without the manifestation or production of what was previously non-existent.
But surely, it is only another existing property that is manifested— that is,
brought into the state of being an object of apprehension;
for there is no action of production (*upādāna*) regarding what already exists, nor indeed any perception [of something new], because it already exists.
The Sāṅkhya, having been refuted while persisting in the position that [an effect] is not produced by a causal agent,
falls into the seventh case [of the locative];
this should be explained as "when the opponent has thus persisted."
If that follower of Kapila accepts the disappearance of an existing property and the emergence of a non-existing one, then he falls into the fallacy of *apasiddhānta* (deviation from a tenet);
the meaning is that because his proposition contradicts his own accepted doctrine, he incurs the point of defeat known as *apasiddhānta*.
Alternatively, if he does not accept the disappearance of an existing property and the emergence of a non-existing one...

Even so, this position previously asserted— that there is a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*) for all transformations (*vikāra*)— is not established, because the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the primordial nature and its transformations are unstable. For instance, the definition of those two, which was stated as "belonging to that which is stable," and so forth, is untenable.
The passage beginning with "And of the existent and non-existent" (sadasatośca) and so forth is the opponent's argument;
here, the Master [Dharmakīrti] now offers a rebuttal, the sense being: "For this reason as well, we offer a rebuttal."
Because there is no restriction [on the nature of things], it would follow that the Sāṅkhya position contradicts its own established tenets and logic;
therefore, this was stated in order to support the claim they have accepted—that what is non-existent does not arise, and what is existent does not disappear.
To ask what was said, he replies:
"This manifest world has a single primordial nature, because its commonality is observed.
(19b8) Therein, he analyzes the term "single" as follows:
"This manifest world has an undifferentiated source."

Those [qualities] such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth are "undivided" (*avibhakta*), meaning they are not separate; that which has them as its source (*yoni*), location (*sthāna*), or substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) is "that which has an undivided source. What is the reason for this? It is because their concomitance (*anvaya*) is observed—that is, because identity (*tādātmya*) is perceived with those [qualities] such as pleasure.
What is established by this? He says: the manifest entity (*vyakta*) possesses that nature, namely, the nature of pleasure and so forth.
Regarding the question of how their identity as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is determined therein, he says: "Because they are perceived as non-different" (19b8),
which means that sound and the other [objects] are seen to be non-distinct from pleasure and the other [mental states].
To the question, "Even so, what is established? he says:
"The production and destruction of the entire aggregate of modifications, such as sound and so forth—which consist of pleasure and the like—is impossible.
Why is this so? He says:

Since pleasure and the like have neither origination nor destruction, and since sound and the other [objects] are non-different from them— just as they are identical with their own selves— it follows that sound and the rest are also established as eternal.
And thus, that which was previously asserted— that there is no destruction of what is perishing and that nothing arises from the non-existent— is confirmed.

When the Sāṅkhya has thus established his own position here, Akṣapāda— without pointing out any defects such as the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason consisting in the observation of concomitance (*anvaya*) stated by that Sāṅkhya— responds in this way and permits the inquiry. Then, asking for the definitions of transformation (*vikāra*) and primordial matter (*prakṛti*) by saying, "How is it to be characterized that primordial matter is without transformation?", this Akṣapāda himself proceeds with the discussion by disregarding the subject at hand, because of a lack of restriction and because he obstructs the relevant topic.

The sense is this: since the definition of cause (*prakṛti*) and effect (*vikāra*) has not been introduced here, why is it being questioned after having been mentioned? Therefore, because he questions what is irrelevant, Akṣapāda alone is worthy of defeat. However, [the author] states that there is indeed a sentence here connected to the answer: "In that case, regarding the reason for observing the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), this should be said... (20a1).

The manifest (vyakta) indeed possesses the nature of activity and cessation; however, the pleasure and so forth [of the manifest] do not possess the nature of activity and cessation in the same way as the manifest itself—this is the connection, with the gender and number adjusted accordingly.
