And thus, regarding the connection of the manifest with pleasure and so forth, this is the explanation: if there were identity of nature with pleasure and so forth, then the characteristic of possessing the nature of activity and cessation would be lost for the manifest, because those [pleasures and so forth] would also exist eternally, being non-different from it.

Thus, therefore, there is no such state of having pleasure and so forth as its nature for that which is manifest, being devoid of those two—namely, engagement and withdrawal. "Devoid of those" means lacking those two; "pleasure and so forth" refers to pleasure and the rest; "having that as its nature" means having those [pleasures] as its essence; and the state of having that as its nature is what is meant by "the state of having pleasure and so forth as its nature, being devoid of those."
He asks "Why? and replies:

"Because of the contradiction with the characteristics of the manifest" (vyaktalakṣaṇavirodhāt). The characteristic of the manifest is its nature of having the properties of engagement and withdrawal; its contradiction is that which is the opposite of this, namely, the contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion existing between pleasure and the other [feelings].

And thus, by this proof, it follows that this manifest [evolute] of yours does not have a nature consisting of pleasure and so forth that exists eternally, because its properties are the opposite of those,
like the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). Nor is there a single nature for the manifest and pleasure and so forth,
because they are superimposed with mutually contradictory properties.

If the manifest [world] is thus connected with the nature of pleasure and so forth— just as it is for *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, or for consciousnesses— then since the observation of the concomitance of pleasure and so forth establishes the reason (*hetu*),
why is this objection relevant? To this, he says:

For in this way, by pointing out the defects in the Sāṅkhya’s proof and challenging the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason, the thesis that "this manifest world has a single primordial material cause" is refuted. Yet that Naiyāyika, without withdrawing or demonstrating the defect called unestablishedness in his own proof, prolongs the debate by means of an irrelevant inquiry into the characteristics of the material cause and its transformations; thus, failing to acknowledge his own fault, he casts another point of contention upon the poor Sāṅkhya opponent.

The Teacher says: "In this manner, by means of the inquiry into the characteristics of cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra*), we too shall state the very same fault called 'unestablished' (*asiddhatā*).
This is the domain of those who know the light [of the stars], namely, the astrologers. (20a3)
This is not the meaning of the statement you have uttered;
for people are not capable of understanding a meaning that has not been communicated by words, except through [the aid of] context, purpose, and so forth—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Therefore, this very same "rule of the rogue’s painting" (*bhaṇḍālekhyanyāya*), which was pointed out in the discussion on the contradiction of the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*), is here also [to be understood as] a deviation from a tenet (*apasiddhānta*); the word "also" (*api*) indicates that it is not only in that [previous] case.

For just as magicians, in order to amaze common folk, quickly draw a very small line in the shape of a crescent moon and say, "Behold! We have drawn an elephant the size of a palm tree," some of dull intellect accept it exactly as it is, while others of conceited intelligence inquire:
"Surely its ears, feet, tusks, and so forth are not perceived; how then can this be an elephant, being so deficient?"
They replied:
"We do not believe this is true; however, we have drawn this elephant with all its details fully completed."

Just as all the parts [of an object] submerged in water are not perceived, while only this portion of the pot is perceived, so too is this [position] of the opponent merely a manifestation of audacity; for even if this matter is not understood from that external source, it is nevertheless stated in this manner.

Furthermore, let this very matter be stated in this way—nevertheless, since an unestablished reason is included among the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), its statement constitutes a formal declaration [of that fallacy]. Thus, it would not be necessary to adopt "contradiction with one's own tenets" (*apasiddhānta*) as a separate category; he states this under the guise of a conclusion.
"By the logic as previously stated," and so forth;
"and fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are as previously described"— this is the sūtra.

Vātsyāyana explains this by way of an objection, beginning with "But what [is it]? (20a6). He asks: since they possess characteristics other than those of the fallacies of reason (*hetvābhāsa*), by virtue of that connection, how do they incur the status of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)? To which he replies with an example.

The phrase "just as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) attain the status of objects of valid cognition (prameya) due to another characteristic" continues [from the previous context]. For they are called *pramāṇas* because they are the causes of the activity of valid cognition (*pramiti*); however, when they themselves are cognized by another means of valid cognition, they are then *prameyas* because they are the objects (*karman*) [of that cognition].
From this very fact, since they are categories (*padārtha*), doubt arises.
Regarding this, it is said: "As stated by the Sage";

this is an elaboration of that very point, namely, that the status of a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) occurs precisely through the characteristics of the aforementioned fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).

This is what is meant: the inconclusive (*savyabhicāra*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the equal-to-the-point-at-issue (*prakaraṇasama*), the unestablished (*sādhyasama*), and the mistimed (*atītakāla*) [are fallacious reasons], Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.4.

Thus, having introduced the classification of "pseudo-reasons" (*hetvābhāsa*), the individual definition for each was stated: "The inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) is that which deviates" (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.5).
The contradictory [fallacy] occurs when, having accepted a tenet, one acts in contradiction to it (Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.6).
"That for which there is an investigation of the context is the 'equal to the point at issue' (prakaraṇasama), stated for the purpose of reaching a decision" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.7).
"That which is not distinct from the probandum, because it is itself yet to be proven, is the 'equal to the probandum' (sādhyasama)" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.8).
2.8 *Kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (the fallacy of mistimed application) is defined in Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.9 as *kālātīta*.
"Thus, by that very definition, these constitute points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*); no further definition is required beyond that.
Regarding this point as well, the Teacher says, "How is this to be considered? (20a7).
"Are they exactly as their distinctions have been characterized by you, or rather otherwise?"—this is the analysis [of the compound]: "those whose distinctions have been characterized.

To the question, "If that is so, then what is it that is being considered here?", he says: "But that, when being considered here, leads to an over-extension (atiprasajyate), and therefore it is not elaborated upon."

Some indeed acknowledge only this much: that certain pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are not applicable here, while others are not even included among the pseudo-reasons. In such an investigation, the entire *Hetvābhāsavārttika* would have to be introduced, which would result in it becoming a separate treatise altogether. However, those of pure intellect [should understand] that because of its extreme distance from the definition of pseudo-reasons as formulated by us, it is entirely different.
Therefore, equanimity alone is appropriate;
nevertheless, since the treatise is also spoken for the sake of awakening those of dull intellect,
we shall now describe how the fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is untenable in the two cases of the "mistimed" (*kālātīta*) and the "inopportune" (*prakaraṇasama*).
Among these, the "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) is that which has passed its proper time.

Having set aside the opinion of the elder Naiyāyikas on this point, because it was stated by the venerable teacher Diṅnāga, contemporary scholars such as Vātsyāyana and others maintain this very position;
regarding this, we say the following:
That whose portion of the meaning being stated is connected with the lapse of time is called "stated after the lapse of time" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), or "past its time" (*kālātīta*).
An illustration is: "Sound is eternal, because it is manifested by conjunction, like color."
The form of sound exists prior to and after its manifestation; it is manifested through the conjunction of a lamp and a jar.
Likewise, sound exists in a latent state and is manifested through the conjunction of a drum and the ear, or through the contact of wood and a leaf.
Therefore, because it is manifested by conjunction, sound is eternal.

This is not a valid reason, because it points to a lapse in time (*kālātyayāpadeśāt*). The manifestation of the manifestor, which is conjunction, does not exceed the time of the manifestation of the manifested color. When there is contact with a lamp, the color is perceived; when the contact has ceased, the color is no longer perceived.

However, when the conjunction between the wood and the leaf has ceased, the sound is heard by one standing at a distance. This manifestation of sound does not exceed the time of conjunction; therefore, it is caused by conjunction.
For the principle that "the absence of an effect follows from the absence of its cause" is indeed inconclusive (anaikāntika),
because [the effect] is manifested by conjunction (saṃyoga).
Even that which is impermanent is seen to be manifested through conjunction, as in the case of a jar; therefore,
since we do not assert that the persistence [of sound] is established by being manifested through conjunction, we do not say that "sound is eternal."

However, if the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is "the sound persists," then the reason (*hetu*) "because it is manifested by conjunction" becomes inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For nothing that is non-persistent is ever manifested by conjunction; how so? It is because in this manner, the very fact that sound is manifested by conjunction is being refuted. Thus, this [reason] does not avoid the fault of being unestablished (*asiddha*).
Otherwise, one must explain what is meant by the statement: "This manifestation of sound does not transcend the time of conjunction, therefore it is not caused by conjunction."
One might think: "The non-existence [of a property] in the locus at all times constitutes 'unestablishedness' (asiddhatva);

however, this [property] is not unestablished in every respect within the locus, because its being manifested by conjunction exists at the time of its production, though not at the time of its perception."
As it has been said:
because even that which is unestablished in one part is recognized as being unestablished, for example: "Atoms are eternal, because they possess odor."

Furthermore, he who asserts that trees become white from sleep and that sound is impermanent must admit that sound arises from the conjunction of an axe and wood; he does not, however, maintain that it is the manifestation of something already existing. Thus, it is clear that his reason is unestablished for at least one of the two parties.

Now, if it is argued that the reason is not "unestablished" (asiddha) because one accepts the meaning of the reason— that perception occurs when there is conjunction— nevertheless, since lamps, pots, and so forth are perceived when there is a conjunction of oil, light, and wick, as well as when there is a conjunction of a potter, a lump of clay, and a stick,
yet these do not persist there in a state of non-attainment of conjunction, this reason becomes inconclusive (anaikāntika) and thus does not fall into the fallacy of being "mistimed" (kālātīta).
If it is further to be proven that [the entity] persists even after that time, then for the proponent who maintains the exclusion of other aggregates, the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*),
because it does not occur there— due precisely to the absence of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*)— and because the subject (*dharmin*) possesses the property of momentary existence.
Because [the probans] exists in things such as form,
there is both a deficiency of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) and a futility of the proof (*sādhana*) for one who maintains that entities are permanent;

furthermore, against an opponent who asserts a logical position (*nyāyavādin*) but has not accepted the established conclusion (*asiddhānta*), this is the fault demonstrated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In this way, one should state the refutation even at the end of the example, having considered it;

for that [reason] for which there is deliberation regarding the matter (*prakaraṇa*) is designated as "the equal-to-the-matter" (*prakaraṇasama*) for the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*).
Nyāyasūtra 1.2.7:

The *prakaraṇasama* (the "equivalent to the point at issue") is that which, based on doubt, consists of two opposing sides—the thesis and the counter-thesis—remaining unsettled; it is an investigation starting from the initial doubt until before the final determination. When a reason is employed for the sake of a conclusion but, due to the equality of both sides, does not transcend the state of the *prakaraṇa*, it is called *prakaraṇasama* and is not fit for reaching a definitive conclusion.

Why, then, is there an investigation of the context (*prakaraṇacintā*) when the reality is perceived? Because when the reality is perceived, the investigation ceases; therefore, that non-perception of a specific [quality] regarding what has been apprehended in a general sense prompts an investigation of the context.
An example is: "Sound is impermanent, because its permanent qualities are not perceived."

An impermanent object such as a pot, which is observed to possess the property of impermanence while lacking any perceived permanent property, is cited as a common property that serves as a cause for doubt; this is "balancing the doubt" (*saṃśayasama*), which is indeed a case of the "inconclusive" (*savyabhicāra*) fallacy.
However, when a deliberation depends upon a specific distinction and no such distinction is perceived between the two sides, that [deliberation] initiates a "point of controversy" (*prakaraṇa*).
Just as the property of permanence is not perceived in sound, so too the property of impermanence is not perceived;

this non-perception of the specific characteristics of both sides gives rise to an inquiry into the matter (*prakaraṇacintā*). How so? Because if the matter were resolved upon the contrary—that is, if the property of permanence were apprehended in sound—there would be no further inquiry.
If the eternal nature [of sound] were not accepted, even so the context would be set aside;
thus, this reason, while operating upon both sides, is not capable of determining either one,
yet it is not itself non-different from the probandum.
It is not "undistinguished" (aviśiṣṭa),
because that very property which is the cause for the commencement of the discussion is presented as the reason;
where a property identical to the probandum (sādhya) is presented as the reason, that is "undistinguished from the probandum" (sādhyāviśiṣṭa).

Furthermore, where that which is the very cause for the engagement of the inquiry (*prakaraṇa*) is itself [the reason], that is called "equal to the inquiry" (*prakaraṇasama*); here too, the deliberation regarding the inquiry arises only from the non-perception of both eternal and non-eternal properties,
and not from one alone.

Because of the statement that "the [fallacy] ceases when there is a reversal [of the reason]," if the reason were "because of the non-perception of permanent and impermanent properties," it would be a *prakaraṇasama* (neutralized) fallacy.
If the reason is based on the non-perception of one property (*ekadharmanupalabdhi*), how can it be called *prakaraṇasama*?

Even when there is a non-perception of both properties, since the positive concomitance (*anuvṛtti*) in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the negative exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) remain uncertain, it becomes an "uncommon inconclusive" (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason. How then could this be considered a distinct fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*)?
Let it be granted that the reason is indeed the non-perception of one property; yet, [if so], it is precisely this that constitutes *prakaraṇasama*.

Nevertheless, since the proponent who asserts that sound is eternal necessarily understands the properties of eternity out of delusion, this [reason] remains unestablished for the opponent (*prativādyasiddha*).

If, on the other hand, the non-perception of the properties of eternity is established by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through the refutation of those properties of eternity, then because it is determinative, this very [reason] is a cause of right knowledge; how then could it be a "neutralized" pseudo-reason (*prakaraṇasama*)?

For in that case, the meaning of the reason is established as the apprehension of a specific property (*viśeṣa*) alone; and the specific properties of a permanent entity are such things as being produced (*kṛtakatva*), etc.
Nor is there an investigation of the matter (*prakaraṇacintā*) caused by those [properties], because of the statement: "Because the investigation of the matter ceases in the case of the opposite."

Furthermore, regarding the statement "because of the non-perception of eternal properties," is this a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) or is it an affirmation of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi-vidhāna*)?

If it is a simple negation, then like [the fallacy of] "knowability" (*prameyatva*), this would be a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*), because the mere negation of the perception of eternal properties is possible even in things that lack impermanence (i.e., non-existent things). If, on the other hand, it is an affirmation of a counter-correlate, then by the reasoning just stated, it is unfit to be a semblance of a reason (*hetu-pratirūpaka*).
But another explains these two sūtras differently:
"The cause that was indicated at the time of its causality passes away;
from what does it pass away?"
Being contradicted by perception, by scripture, or by both, that [reason] is called "mistimed" (*kālātīta*) because its proper time has passed.
If it is asked, "How is contradiction with perception and scripture established?
it is because of the statement: "The reason possesses four characteristics."

For instance, in the *Nyāyasūtra* (1.1.5), it is stated that "the [inference] based on what is generally observed (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is like the former and like the remainder," wherein a fourfold reason (*hetu*) is intended.

As before, [inference] is called *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* when it is pervasive (*vyāpaka*) regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), and *śeṣavat* when it exists in what is similar to that; and it is also [called] *śabdāt* (from verbal testimony) when it is non-contradictory.
Likewise, there is also a statement in the Bhāṣya:
"Furthermore, that inference which contradicts perception and scripture is a fallacy of reasoning (*nyāyābhāsa*).
Thus, when the three characteristics [of the logical mark] are present, that which is sublated by perception and scripture is the *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (the mistimed).
And that [invalidity] is divided into three types: contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣaviruddha*), contradicted by scripture (*āgamaviruddha*), and contradicted by both.
An example of being contradicted by perception is: "Fire is not hot, because it is a substance, like water.
An example of being contradicted by scripture is: "A Brahmin may drink liquor, because it is liquid, like milk."
An example of that which is contradictory to both [the thesis and the reason] is: "The eye-faculty is like a ray [of light], because it is a sense-faculty, like the olfactory faculty and so forth.

Now, this is certainly not a contradiction of the thesis (*pakṣavirodha*), because a contradiction of the thesis has already been rejected; rather, this is merely a lack of clarity regarding the failure to understand the definition of the three characteristics (*trairūpya*).

For when the three characteristics—namely the triad beginning with "being a property of the subject" (pakṣadharmatva)—are fully ascertained by valid means of cognition, and where there is sublation (bādhā), there is an obstruction;
for sublation and invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) are contradictory.

Indeed, invariable concomitance is the presence of the reason only when the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) exists. How then could that reason, possessing such a definition, exist in the subject while the property to be proven is absent? This and other points should be stated here in accordance with the refutation regarding the "unsublated object" (abādhitaviṣayatva).

Furthermore, as for this refutation that has been cited, those [reasons] do not possess even the slightest degree of the three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*), because they lack the necessary logical connection (*pratibandha*).
Moreover, since this is a formal argument (*prayoga*) regarding a thesis (*pakṣa*) that has already been accepted, it is proper to regard this simply as a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*).
As for the extensive and incoherent arguments brought forward to avoid the charge of being a fault of the thesis, they are utterly worthless and are therefore not examined here.
Since it is said that "the investigation is according to the context," the example of that context as defined in the Bhāṣya is as follows:
In the inquiry as to whether or not an atom is produced by another atom, someone asserts:
"An atom is produced by another atom because it possesses color and other qualities, just like a dyad (dvyaṇuka) and so forth."

When that very atom which is cited as the cause is itself possessed of color and other qualities, there arises the inquiry: "Is this [atom] the effect of another atom because it possesses color and other qualities, or is it not? If one asserts that even that [atom] is the effect of another atom because it possesses color and other qualities, then since that too possesses color and other qualities, the same inquiry recurs. Thus, by setting in motion a debate characterized by infinite regress (*anavasthā*), it is called *prakaraṇasama* (the equal-to-the-issue).

Now, if it is argued that the atom does not possess the property of being an effect produced from another atom because it possesses color and other qualities, then the reason (hetu) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Therefore, the "equal-to-the-issue" (*prakaraṇasama*) fallacy is distinct from the inconclusive;
nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it does not establish the opposite; nor is it unestablished (*asiddha*), because its presence as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is observed.
It is not "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because it is not sublated by perception or scripture;
therefore, it is not a "different matter" (*arthāntara*).
Alternatively, the meaning is that the establishment of the cause consists in its operation in a specific location and its relevance to the context (*prakaraṇa*).

This [fallacy] called *pradeśasama* (the "equal to the point of application") is that for which the reason is stated because of a certain location (*pradeśa*). It is "equal" (*sama*) because it establishes that very location;
just as it is not a prover with respect to one part, so too it is not a prover with respect to the other—thus it is "equal" due to the commonality of its lack of proving power.
Therefore, a property residing in only one part is *pradeśasama*.
For example: "Earth, water, fire, air, and space are impermanent because they possess existence (*sattāvat*).

In this case as well, if one follows the opinion of Akṣapāda, one would formulate the proof as follows: "An atom is preceded by another atom because it possesses form and other qualities, like a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth. If that were the case, there would be a contradiction with what [the proponent] himself accepts; therefore, this [type of fallacy] does not differ from the "past time" (*atītakāla*).

If the Buddhist were to formulate [the argument] in that way, even then the reason would be unestablished (*asiddhi*), because atoms are not admitted to exist apart from form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory qualities],
and because [qualities] such as duality and so forth are impossible; thus, the example is devoid of both [the property to be proved and the probans].

Even when a proponent of logic (*nyāyavādī*) speaks while disregarding established tenets (*siddhānta*), the fault pointed out in the second position does not cease; thus, this [fallacy] does not differ from the "unestablished" (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, that property which resides in only one part of the object of inference (*anumeyaikadeśavartin*), such as "earth and so forth are non-eternal because they possess odor," is also included within the category of "contrary tenet" (*apasiddhānta*) and need not be mentioned separately;
it is not "unestablished" because it is a property residing in only one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśadharmatvāt*).

If you argue that [the definition] is like "subsisting in a part of the similar instances" (*sapakṣaikadeśavartin*), this is an unequal comparison. For in the case of the phrase "existence only in the similar instances," the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is indeed conjoined [with "only"], and thus it does not establish that the probans must be a property of all similar instances. However, the statement of existence in the subject (*anumeya*) functions as a regulator by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), thereby establishing that the probans is a property of every member of the class of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*). Since the exclusion of the various types of "unestablished in a part of the subject" (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*) is accomplished by this very [definition], any further effort is useless; therefore, this [objection] is trivial.
Even though the future [reason] is distinct, it falls into this very same "equal to the point at issue" (prakaraṇasama) fallacy; otherwise, he would be establishing it as such.

Because the investigation of the *prakaraṇa*—that is, the consideration of the counter-position (*vipakṣa*)—occurs subsequently, that which is taught for the sake of determining the reason (*hetu*) and possesses such characteristics is called *prakaraṇasama*. It is "equal" (*sama*) in relation to the point to be proven (*sādhya*), whether in terms of existence or non-existence. For example: "The omniscient one exists, because he is free from the opposite of that [non-omniscience], like visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Since this reason is the same in both cases, it is equally applicable even to one who seeks to prove non-existence. Thus, it is equal (*sama*).
"How can omniscience be non-existent? Because it is free from its opposite, like a donkey's horn. [The opponent objects:
"But surely this reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), even though it possesses both properties, because it does not occur in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
This very point has been refuted by the Master himself in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*.
How then does your honor understand the "opposite side" (*vipakṣa*) here as the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*)?

Furthermore, regarding the statement beginning with "how now [could] the reason be present in the opposite side? and "by both properties alone," and what was said in the explanation of the term "object" (*artha*), that must also be stated here.
The refutation of this has already been stated in detail;
thus, the [definitions of] *prakaraṇasama* and *atītakāla* are untenable,
whereas it is appropriate that deviation from the probandum (*sādhyavyabhicāra*) constitutes a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), but not in the manner you accept.

For indeed, you do not admit that a reason is inconclusive when its exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful, because you accept the establishment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) through mere non-observation alone.

And for this very reason, you yourselves, having set aside your doubts, employ the following argument: "The eye and the ear reach their objects, because they are external sense-faculties, like the nose and so forth."
"Conceptual perception is a valid means of knowledge because it possesses the nature of inference," and so forth;
nor is the establishment of negative concomitance (vyatireka) achieved by mere non-observation in the absence of a necessary connection— this has been elaborated elsewhere—
and that which does not establish the existence of the self, clay, consciousness, and so on.

"Is that very non-perception (anupalambha) the prover of the absence of a reason? and so forth—likewise, you yourselves maintain that even when the presence or absence [of a reason] in the similar and dissimilar instances is doubtful, it is indeed a cause for correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and not an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) one, as in the case of the argument: "The living body possesses a self because it possesses breath and so forth. And its validity has been established in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya* and other works. As for the variety of contradiction (*viruddha*) formulated by Bhāradvāja, it was refuted precisely during the discussion on the contradiction with one's own thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*).

Regarding that which is described as "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddha*) even within the context of the "equal-to-the-probandum" (*sādhyasama*), such as the argument: "Atoms are non-eternal because they possess activity, like a jar," this too is indeed considered *sādhyasama*. This is because the possession of activity by atoms is due to their having form, activity, color, and so forth, and not due to their non-eternality. That [argument] is untenable because it is already established in the subject (*dharmin*); for a reason (*hetu*) that exists in the subject cannot properly be called unestablished (*asiddha*).
This is not so, because it would follow that all reasons (hetu) would be unestablished;
for the property of being a characteristic of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) does not consist merely in its existing in the subject,
since the subject's status as a characteristic of the subject is intended by virtue of the probandum (sādhya).

Because the property alone is what is to be proven, if the property to be proven cannot exist in the subject (dharmin) without that means of proof (sādhana), and if that means of proof can exist in the subject even in the absence of the property to be proven, then the reason possesses the quality of being a "property of the subject" (pakṣadharmatva). However, when the property is established in the subject as taken for the purpose of proof in some other way, it lacks the status of a reason; thus, existence (*sattva*) qualified in this specific manner is intended by the term "property of the subject."
It is indeed appropriate that [the reason] be "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha) and thus "equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama).

To this, the following rebuttal is offered: If, in the absence of the property to be proved (sādhyadharma), the non-occurrence of the reason in the subject (dharmin) constitutes such "existence" (satva) as intended by the definition of being a property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva), and not mere existence in general, then is such a property of the subject—being unperceived—capable of revealing the object of inference, or is it only when it is definitely ascertained? In these two alternatives, if that which reveals is unperceived, then it transgresses the logic of a "reason that makes known" (jñāpakahetu).

For a reason (*hetu*) that makes known reveals the object to be known by depending on cognition within itself; yet reasons are capable of dispelling misconceptions through their mere existence. Thus, there would not be a plurality of mutually contradictory scriptures among opponents.

Furthermore, if that which is already cognized can also function as a communicator, its ascertainment must occur either through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or through that very [first] means of valid cognition.

First of all, because that which is not a means of valid cognition lacks the capacity to cause the ascertainment of a real object, there can be no comprehension from what is not a means of valid cognition; otherwise, its very status as a means of valid cognition would be lost, since this alone is the defining characteristic of a means of valid cognition: namely, its capacity to illuminate an object exactly as it exists.

If this [property of being a property of the subject] belongs even to that which is not a valid means of cognition (*apramāṇa*), then how can the existence of a reason—which cannot subsist in the subject to be proven (*sādhya-dharmin*) without the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*)—be understood as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharman*) on the basis of such an invalid cognition? For in that case as well, since the proof of the reason arises from that very same means of cognition, the proof of the property to be proven would likewise arise from it; so for what purpose is this useless form of the reason (*hetu-rūpa*) adopted?
Nor is it reasonable to say that the proof of the reason alone comes from that [cognition], while the proof of the property to be proven does not.

For otherwise, it would follow that the reason (*hetu*) itself remains unestablished; for this reason is established in that subject (*dharmin*) only if it cannot occur there without the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), but rather occurs only together with it.
If that were the case, one must consider why the property to be proven is not also established by that very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And thus, by that very same means of valid cognition, [the reason] is concomitant with this property to be proven.
It follows as a great undesirable consequence that there would be no relationship of indicator and indicated by means of this reason;

furthermore, if one relies upon such a form of "property-of-the-subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*), then as long as the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished, the reason is likewise unestablished, and as long as the reason is unestablished, the probandum is likewise so—thus there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).

Moreover, since the establishment of the property to be proven is already accomplished at the very moment of determining the property-of-the-subject, it is useless to subsequently pursue the other forms of the mark. Consequently, a reason should not be described as having two characteristics, four characteristics, or five characteristics.

In our view, however, once the mere existence [of the reason] in the subject (*dharmin*) has been cognized, and subsequently the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) or the two concomitances themselves are cognized through a universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), then—since the mere existence in the subject was already cognized at the earlier time—the cognition of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) arises there by its very force immediately thereafter.
Therefore, this entire web of faults finds no footing here, like a reflection in the clear sky or pure water; so enough with these unstable, false prattlings, and we shall desist.

*Santānāntarasiddhi*, which does not establish the existence of a self, clay-consciousness, and so forth.
Is that very non-apprehension the proof of the absence of a reason? If this is so, what then is intended here as "intended"? He says:
"But fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are according to the rule," and so forth. Those fallacious reasons which are contrary to the rule—stating them constitutes a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna).
And those which have been mentioned by us—namely, "when there is non-establishment of one [of the two parties] or doubt, it possesses non-establishment and deviation;
when both [are unestablished], or when there is contradiction and non-establishment, it possesses doubt and deviation"—[refer to these cases]. 46.
When there is doubt regarding the non-establishment of one [of the two reasons], it partakes in both non-establishment and inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*);
when there is non-establishment of both, it partakes in doubt and inconclusiveness.

(46) Now, this path of the logic of debate was made into a great royal highway by the noble Vasubandhu in his *Vādavidhāna* and other works, acting as a kinsman who provides no bond for anyone in the world.

Furthermore, this has already been threshed out in the *Mahānyāyaparīkṣā* by the venerable teacher Dignāga, who was adept at splitting open the frontal globes of the elephant-like proponents of false doctrines; therefore, why do you resort to chewing what has already been chewed? To resolve this objection, he presents the following verse (beginning with "loka 20a8"):

"Timira and paṭala... and so forth. "Timira and paṭala" (*timirapaṭala*) means ignorance itself is the *timirapaṭala*; it is called the "film of the darkness of ignorance" (*avidyātimirapaṭala*) because it obstructs the vision of reality.
The connection is that *vādanyāya* is its "scraping away" (*ullekhana*). The word *ullekhana* is derived in the sense of the agent (*kartṛsādhana*).
To the question, "Of what [is it the scraping away]? he says: "Of the film of the darkness of ignorance."
The meaning is that for one who possesses the vision of reality— that is, the vision of truth consisting of the illumination of wisdom—
this very method of debate has just been explained.

The meaning is that [this treatise] was composed by six former masters who were devoted to the welfare of others; because they were dependent upon compassion, they established the world on the correct path, brought it to supreme renown, and made it clearly manifest in the world.
It was not done out of rivalry with one another, nor from a desire for fame and the like.
If that is so, then the aforementioned objection remains in force; therefore, he says:

It obscures—that is, it darkens and veils with the gloom of fallacious objections—the light or illumination of reality (*tattva*) as taught by the masters (*ācārya*). Who, then, is this most audacious person who seeks to block the path trodden by the great *nāgas*? He says: "This person is wickedly clever; due to a total lack of correct discernment, he includes [in his critique] Udyotakara, Prīticandra, Bhāvivikta, and others."

Since this is so, an effort has been made by me here in this treatise on the Logic of Debate (*Vādanyāya*) for the sake of rekindling that [work] which was cast aside by the great kings among the Antarājatas; for I have been occupied with refuting fallacious criticisms and illuminating its principles, and thus I have not ground what had already been ground—this is the summary meaning.
[For this task], like plunging into a priceless woman, requires no small power of intellect.

May the peace that comes from whatever abundant, pure merit I have correctly attained— having clearly analyzed the thought of those who, despite great exertion, do not perceive the essence of the ultimate truth— be for the sake of all beings. 47.
And may I,

having attained the glory of Mañjuśrī— who possesses vast power capable of bearing the burden of the Fully Awakened One upon the mountain of faults through the sequence of awakening to selflessness— become skillful in bringing about the destruction of all obscurations for all sentient beings.
By its great speed, nothing here has been left behind, discarded, or divided;

This *Vādanyāya*, correctly composed by him who seeks the welfare of others, obscures that light of reality for those people who are poorly trained; therefore, I have made this effort here in order to rekindle it. (49)
The *Vādanyāya-ṭīkā* named *Vipañcitārthā* is completed; this work is by the venerable Sāntarakṣitapāda.
It was written by me on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa in the year 402 (N.E. 272 = 1152 A.D.).
In the victorious reign of the illustrious Ānandadeva— the King of Kings, Supreme Lord, and Most Venerable One— on an auspicious day,
the extent of this work was determined by the former scholars to be two thousand nine hundred, as calculated according to the standard measure.
May there be auspiciousness for all the world;
it must be protected with effort by everyone.
Homage to the Omniscient One!
